Presenting complaint: Mechanical fall while stepping out of bathroom. Patient was able to move into a sitting position before calling 999. No pre-fall symptoms: no chest pain, palpitations, dizziness, or loss of consciousness. No post-fall symptoms.

Observations: BP 110/70 mmHg, HR 69 bpm regular, RR 17/min, SpO₂ 98% on air, Temp 36.3°C, GCS 15/15. Random blood sugar 5.4 mmol/L. Systemic exam: heart sounds S1/S2, no added sounds. No obvious injuries. ECG: sinus rhythm, no acute changes.

Impression: Mechanical fall with no apparent injury. Patient declined hospital transfer. Advised to follow up with GP.

bloodTestResults.summary: No recent blood tests available — last routine bloods satisfactory (3 months ago).

patientStory:
You are Mary Trafford, an 80-year-old female.

**Opening Statement:** *Hi doctor, I was told by the paramedics to call you after my fall the other day.*

You had a fall 2 days ago while coming out of the toilet. For the past 7 months, you have been passing urine frequently since starting your water tablet (furosemide). Just before the fall, your legs felt wobbly. You were unable to get up immediately but managed to sit yourself up. Fortunately, your phone was nearby and you called the ambulance.

You did not experience any loss of consciousness, dizziness, chest pain, or palpitations. This was your first ever fall.

You were started on furosemide 7 months ago for leg swelling, which has now improved. If asked about aspirin: you were started on this many years ago when your blood pressure tablets were prescribed — you believe it works alongside your blood pressure medication.

**Social History:** You live alone in a detached three-bedroom house with stairs. Retired accountant. Your son lives about 40 miles away and visits every 2 weeks. You are independent with cooking, cleaning, and shopping.

**Ideas:** You believe you tripped and fell because your legs felt wobbly.

**Concerns:** You are worried about having another fall.

**Expectations:** You would like the GP to advise you on what to do to prevent another fall.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about the episode of the fall: when, mechanism, whether witnessed, what led to it, and whether she was able to get up.
Ask about pre-fall symptoms: dizziness, palpitations, chest pain, or weakness in any part of the body (to suggest stroke).
Ask if any injury or fracture was sustained. Use the ambulance report in questioning: *'I can see from the ambulance records that there were no injuries — is that correct?'*
Ask if she lost consciousness during or after the fall.
Ask if she ever feels dizzy when standing up from a sitting position (to assess for postural hypotension).
Ask about mobility issues, such as arthritis or joint pain, or symptoms of Parkinson's disease (tremor, slow gait).
Ask about recent memory or cognitive changes.
Ask about eyesight and visual problems.
Ask about urinary symptoms — frequency, urgency, incontinence.
Ask about bowel habits.
Ask about diabetic control and upcoming follow-ups.
Ask about home hazards: loose rugs, poor lighting, wet bathroom floors, unstable handrails.
Ask about home situation — living alone, support available.
Ask about mood and whether the fall has affected confidence.
Review current medications (furosemide and aspirin) and ask if she knows why she is taking them.
Ask about diet, nutrition, alcohol, and smoking.
Elicit ICE.
Give a diagnosis of likely mechanical fall, possibly contributed to by polypharmacy and medication side effects (furosemide, antihypertensives).

exampleExplanation:
*Mary, from what you have described, this sounds like a mechanical fall, meaning you most likely tripped or lost balance rather than it being caused by something more serious like a heart problem or a stroke.*

*You mentioned that your legs felt wobbly. One possible reason for this is your water tablet, furosemide. This medicine can cause you to pass urine more often and sometimes make you a little dehydrated, which can make your legs feel weak. It is no longer needed now that your leg swelling has improved, so I would recommend stopping it.*

*I also notice you are taking aspirin. This is usually only used for people who have had a heart attack, a stroke, or problems with their blood vessels. From your records, you do not seem to have had these conditions, so there is no clear reason for you to be on aspirin, and continuing it when it is not needed can increase the risk of side effects like bleeding.*

*In addition, you are taking more than one blood pressure tablet, and sometimes this combination can make people feel dizzy or unsteady. I would suggest stopping one of them — ramipril — and then reviewing your blood pressure in a few weeks.*
management: **Stop furosemide** — it can cause dehydration and wobbly legs, and is no longer required since her leg swelling has resolved.
**Review and reduce antihypertensives** — consider stopping ramipril to reduce risk of postural hypotension. Recheck blood pressure in 1–2 weeks.
**Stop aspirin** — she has no clear indication for secondary cardiovascular prevention. Aspirin is not recommended for primary prevention in elderly patients.
**No immediate face-to-face review needed** — she has recently been assessed by the ambulance crew with observations, ECG, and cardiovascular examination.
Offer **blood tests** to check for electrolyte abnormality secondary to furosemide use.
Offer **referral to occupational therapy** to assess home environment and identify safety modifications.
Offer **referral to community physiotherapy** for strength and balance training.
Offer a **falls alarm** — can be arranged through social prescribers, occupational therapy, or frailty practitioners.
Encourage good **fluid intake** to prevent dehydration.
Arrange **follow-up in 1–2 weeks** to recheck blood pressure and reassess progress.
Safety netting: if she develops dizziness, chest pain, weakness in any part of the body, another fall, or any other concerning symptoms, seek urgent medical advice immediately.
learningPoints:
**Falls in older adults** are common and usually multifactorial. Key risk factors include polypharmacy, conditions affecting mobility or balance (arthritis, Parkinson's, stroke), muscle weakness, poor vision, cognitive impairment, and home hazards.

**Polypharmacy** is a major contributor. **Deprescribing** medications that are no longer indicated or appropriate is essential:
- **Furosemide**: can cause dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, and orthostatic hypotension — stop if the indication (leg oedema) has resolved.
- **Aspirin**: is only indicated for **secondary prevention** of cardiovascular disease (post-MI, TIA, stroke, PAD). It is **not recommended** for primary prevention due to bleeding risk with no survival benefit.
- **Antihypertensives**: multiple agents can cause postural hypotension — rationalise where possible.

**Falls prevention requires a multidisciplinary approach:**
- **Occupational therapy**: home hazard assessment, adaptive equipment
- **Physiotherapy**: strength, balance, and mobility training
- **Medication review**: deprescribing fall-risk-increasing drugs
- **Vision assessment**: addressing visual impairment

title: Patient's Complaint About Your Colleague

patientData.name: Elizabeth Freeman
drugHistory: DuoResp Spiromax (budesonide/formoterol MART) — 1 puff twice daily

recentConsultation.seenBy: Dr Phil Barnes, Clinical Practitioner (2 weeks ago)
recentConsultation.notes:
History: Recent X-ray confirmed osteoarthritis of right knee. Patient reports pain not controlled with topical ibuprofen; sometimes affects sleep. No red flags. Walking freely, not limping.

Plan: Start amitriptyline 25 mg nocte. Worsening advice given.

patientStory:
You are Elizabeth Freeman, a 50-year-old female. You are here to report some concerns about your last consultation with Dr Barnes.

You had booked to see Dr Barnes because your osteoarthritis pain in the right knee was not controlled with topical ibuprofen. During the consultation, you noticed the doctor looked exhausted, had red eyes, and appeared very sleepy — as if he had not rested for many days.

He rushed the consultation and did not examine your knees, which other doctors would usually do.

He then prescribed amitriptyline. You experienced dizziness as a side effect and were not warned about this. When you looked it up, you saw that amitriptyline is an antidepressant and a neuropathic pain medication, and you do not agree with Dr Barnes's judgement. You had to get codeine from the chemist and this is helping with your pain. You no longer feel dizzy since stopping the amitriptyline.

**Ideas:** You think Dr Barnes was not fit to see patients on the day you attended.

**Concerns:** You are worried about other patients he saw that day and their safety.

**Expectations:** You want the GP to tell you how to file a complaint.

**Question to ask:** Was Dr Barnes's decision to prescribe amitriptyline the right thing to do?

markingScheme.heading: History
points: Acknowledge her complaints first: *'Thank you for sharing your concerns. I'm sorry to hear about your experience. We take feedback like this seriously. Can I ask a few questions to help me understand what happened so I can better support you?'*
Ask how her knee pain is now — is it better, does she still need painkillers?
Ask about the amitriptyline side effects — how severe was the dizziness, has it resolved since stopping, and did the medication provide any pain relief before the side effects started?
Ask her to describe more about how Dr Barnes appeared during the consultation.
Ask what specifically made her feel he was sleepy or not fit to practise — changes in speech, actions, or behaviour?
Ask whether this behaviour affected how comfortable she felt or the care she received.
Ask if she has any other concerns about the consultation.
Ask what outcome she would like to see — what specifically was she hoping the GP would address?

exampleExplanation: No example explanation provided
management: **Acknowledge her concern again** and thank her for raising this: *'Thank you for sharing your experience. I'm very sorry to hear the consultation left you feeling uncomfortable and that the amitriptyline caused dizziness. You made the right decision to stop taking it, and I'll work with you to find a better treatment plan for your knee pain.'*
Address her ongoing **knee pain** — offer alternative analgesics, review topical NSAIDs, discuss physiotherapy, or consider joint injection as options.
If she still has dizziness, offer a **follow-up appointment** to assess this in detail.

Explain the **complaint process**: *'I will forward your concerns to the practice manager for review. Your feedback will help us ensure the highest standard of care. If you prefer, we can keep your identity anonymous while addressing this issue. You can also file a complaint using our feedback and complaints email, which is monitored by the practice manager.'*
Advise that: *'We will acknowledge your complaint within three working days. Investigating this thoroughly may take some time, but we will keep you updated.'*
Inform the patient that you will **speak to Dr Barnes** to understand his account of the consultation.
If she wants her complaints to be **anonymous**, reassure her that this is possible.
If further painkillers are prescribed, arrange appropriate **follow-up**.

Respond to her question about amitriptyline: *'Amitriptyline is often used to manage certain types of chronic or nerve-related pain. I cannot fully comment on Dr Barnes's decision as I was not involved in your care, but we can now review your treatment plan to ensure you receive the most appropriate management.'*
learningPoints:
This station tests the ability to handle **complaints about a colleague** professionally and empathetically. Key principles include:

1. **Listen and acknowledge** without being dismissive or defensive — patients need to feel heard.
2. **Do not criticise colleagues** directly, but take concerns seriously.
3. **Explain the complaint process** clearly: practice manager, written complaints email, and acknowledgement within 3 working days.
4. **Offer to speak to the colleague** to understand their account.
5. **Maintain confidentiality** — offer anonymity if requested.
6. **Address the clinical problem** — ensure the patient's current medical needs are met regardless of the complaint.

**Amitriptyline** is a tricyclic antidepressant widely used for neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia, and chronic musculoskeletal pain. Common side effects include dizziness, dry mouth, constipation, and sedation. Patients should be counselled about these before starting the medication.

If a clinician is believed to be impaired or unfit to practise, the duty to **raise patient safety concerns** (whistleblowing) must be considered, escalating to the clinical lead or CQC if necessary.

furtherResources.title: How To Complain To The Nhs

title: Breathlessness In Known COPD

recentConsultation.seenBy: Phil Barnes, Respiratory Nurse Practitioner (5 weeks ago)
recentConsultation.notes: Known COPD — well controlled. Good inhaler technique. Reports mild SOB on exertion. No red flags. Recent spirometry shows no decline. Non-smoker. No recent flare. Plan: continue ongoing management. Advise to book appointment with GP to discuss SOB.

patientStory:
You are Thomas Brown. You've been living with COPD for a number of years, and it's generally well managed. You attended a routine COPD review with the nurse 5 weeks ago where no changes were made.

Recently, you've noticed shortness of breath (SOB) that only happens when you exert yourself, such as climbing stairs or walking long distances. You have also noticed chest tightness during those episodes. No SOB at rest, and it doesn't wake you up at night.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:

You have used your blue inhaler but it doesn't seem to help to relieve the symptoms — only rest helps.

No chest pain, palpitations, dizziness, or fainting. No increased cough, sputum, or wheeze.

**Social History:** Lives at home alone — wife died. Ex-smoker — stopped 10 years ago. No alcohol. Retired postman. Generally independent with ADLs but recent SOB is restricting him.

**Concerns:** You're worried that the SOB might mean your COPD is worsening and this is affecting your independence.

**Expectations:** You'd like the doctor to investigate why you're getting SOB and provide guidance.

markingScheme.heading: History
points: Ask about SOB — does it happen only on exertion or at rest? Is there associated chest tightness? What relieves it — rest or inhalers? How far can he walk before getting breathless?
Ask about orthopnoea (SOB when lying flat, use of extra pillows), PND (waking up gasping for air), and ankle swelling — to rule out heart failure.
Ask about cough, sputum production, chest pain, and palpitations.
Ask about red flags: weight loss, night sweats, fever.
Ask about adherence to medications.
Ask how SOB has affected his daily life.
Ask about social history: smoking, alcohol, home situation.
Elicit ICE.

Explain likely diagnosis of **stable angina** — SOB on exertion relieved by rest but not by salbutamol, with associated chest tightness, in a patient with cardiovascular risk factors (hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, ex-smoker) is highly suspicious for angina.

exampleExplanation: *Mr Brown, from everything you've told me about your symptoms — feeling breathless when you exert yourself, improving with rest, and not responding to your blue inhaler — I am concerned that this could be a condition called **angina**, rather than a worsening of your COPD. Angina happens when the heart muscle doesn't get enough oxygen-rich blood, usually because of narrowing in the blood vessels that supply the heart. This can cause symptoms like chest tightness or breathlessness, especially during activities like walking or climbing stairs.*
management: Offer **face-to-face assessment** — listen to heart sounds and chest, check blood pressure.
Arrange **ECG, bloods** (BNP, FBC, cholesterol), and **chest X-ray**.

Offer **GTN spray** and **aspirin 75 mg once daily** — provide clear safety-netting: use GTN spray during an episode of SOB or chest pain; take a second dose after 5 minutes if the first has not eased symptoms; call 999 if pain or SOB has not eased 5 minutes after the second dose, or earlier if intensifying.
Refer urgently to a **Rapid Access Chest Pain Clinic (RACPC)**.
Safety netting: if worsening SOB at rest, chest pain, or palpitations develop — dial 999 immediately.
learningPoints:
**Shortness of breath (SOB) can be the only presenting symptom of angina**, particularly in patients who already have a respiratory diagnosis such as COPD, where breathlessness may be misattributed to their known condition.

**Key distinguishing features:**

| Feature | Angina | COPD exacerbation |
|---|---|---|
| Onset | Exertional | Often at rest or on exertion |
| Relief | Rest, GTN | Inhalers, time |
| Associated | Chest tightness | Cough, wheeze, sputum |
| Inhalers | Do not help | May help |

Always assess for underlying **cardiac causes** in patients with known respiratory disease who report new or worsening exertional breathlessness — particularly if they have multiple cardiovascular risk factors.

**GTN spray safety advice:** use as soon as symptoms begin, can repeat after 5 minutes, call 999 if no improvement after second dose.

title: Severe Headache In A Young Male

recentConsultation.notes: Patient booked urgent appointment to discuss concerns.

patientStory:
You are Daniel Cooper, a 27-year-old man. For the past four days, you've been experiencing intense, one-sided headaches around your left eye and temple. The pain feels sharp, stabbing, and unbearable — almost like someone is pressing a knife into your head.

Each episode lasts around 30–90 minutes and occurs multiple times per day (up to 6 episodes). You've noticed your left eye becomes red and watery during attacks, and your nose gets blocked or runs on the same side. You also get facial sweating.

You suffered this type of headache 2 months ago and it settled on its own.

You've tried paracetamol and ibuprofen, but they haven't helped at all. You feel restless during attacks and cannot sit still — pacing or moving seems to distract you.

**Social History:** Works as a software developer — spends long hours at a screen. Non-smoker, occasional alcohol. No history of recent head trauma. Lives with his girlfriend.

**Ideas and Concerns:** You are worried about a brain tumour or bleed in the brain.

**Expectations:** You would like the GP to help with a stronger painkiller and to arrange a scan of your head.

markingScheme.heading: History
points: Ask about onset of headache.

Ask about headache characteristics: location, duration (how long each attack lasts), nature (stabbing, dull ache), frequency (how many times per day), and any triggers (alcohol, stress, sleep changes).
Ask about photophobia — does bright light make the headache worse?
Ask about nausea, vomiting, teary eyes, blocked or runny nose, facial sweating.
Ask about red flags: neck stiffness, fever, rash, weakness or numbness, visual disturbances, recent trauma, confusion.
Ask about social history and how this has affected daily life.
Elicit ICE.
Give a diagnosis of likely cluster headache.

exampleExplanation:
*Mr Cooper, I completely understand why you're worried about something serious like a brain bleed or a tumour. It's natural to think that when you have a severe headache that won't go away.*

*From everything you've described — the one-sided, severe stabbing pain near your eye, the teary eye, the runny nose, and the fact that painkillers haven't worked — this sounds very much like a condition called **cluster headache**. Cluster headaches are a type of severe headache that comes in cycles over a few weeks. They cause intense pain around one eye, along with symptoms like a teary eye and a runny nose on the same side. Many people describe them as the worst headache they've ever had.*

*Your headache is very unlikely to be a brain bleed because it was not a sudden explosive pain and you do not have serious symptoms like weakness, speech issues, or confusion. A brain tumour is also unlikely because your headaches are episodic rather than progressively worsening, with no persistent vomiting, vision changes, or memory problems.*

*However, because this is your first presentation with these symptoms, guidelines recommend referral to a neurology specialist to confirm the diagnosis and arrange imaging.*
management: As this is the **first presentation with cluster headache**, make an **urgent advice and guidance request or urgent referral to neurology** for confirmation of diagnosis, neuroimaging, and likely initiation of prophylaxis.
Offer a **face-to-face appointment** to examine the nervous system (neurological exam), perform fundoscopy, and check blood pressure.

For **acute attacks**, offer **sumatriptan intranasal spray** — start with 10–20 mg in one nostril. A second dose can be taken after at least 2 hours if the headache returns. Maximum 40 mg per day. Do not take a second dose for the same headache if the first didn't help.
**Short-burst high-flow oxygen therapy** can also be considered for acute attacks.
If severe or refractory, seek specialist advice to start prophylaxis with **verapamil**.
Advise the patient to keep a **symptom diary** to identify triggers (alcohol, sleep disruption, stress).
Heavily safety net on neurological symptoms (weakness, speech change, sudden onset 'thunderclap' headache, neck stiffness, fever, rash) — seek urgent help immediately.
learningPoints:
**Cluster headaches** are characterised by severe, strictly unilateral orbital or temporal pain occurring in clusters, lasting 15–180 minutes, with ipsilateral autonomic features (lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, conjunctival injection, ptosis, facial sweating). Patients are often restless during attacks.

**Key distinction from migraine:** cluster headache causes restlessness; migraine causes the patient to want to lie still. Migraine is associated with nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia; cluster headache typically is not.

**NICE advises against:** paracetamol, NSAIDs, opioids, ergots, or oral triptans for acute cluster headache — they are too slow-acting for this short-duration, intense pain.

**First-line acute treatments:** sumatriptan subcutaneous injection or intranasal spray, and/or high-flow oxygen (100% via non-rebreather mask, 12–15 L/min for 15–20 minutes).

**Prophylaxis** (initiated by neurology): verapamil is first-line; short courses of prednisolone may be used as a bridge.

title: Pregnant Woman Worried About Down Syndrome

patientData.name: Sarah Olderman
pastMedicalHistory: Previous child with Down syndrome (first pregnancy at age 37)
drugHistory: Nil — not currently on any regular medications

recentConsultation.notes: Patient booked urgent appointment to discuss concerns about her current pregnancy.

patientStory:
You are Sarah Olderman, a 42-year-old woman who recently found out you are pregnant again. You had your last menstrual period 8 weeks ago.

This is your second pregnancy. Your first child, now 4 years old, has Down syndrome. You had him when you were 37 years old. At the time, you were not aware of your risk, and although you love your son dearly, you now want to be better informed about screening options.

Your friend, who is a midwife, told you that because of your history and age, you might be able to get tests earlier than the usual 11–14 weeks. You're not sure if this is true and want to know what tests are available and whether they are safe for the baby.

You are feeling worried and anxious because you do not want to have another child with Down syndrome, as it can be very stressful. You also wonder if your past pregnancy increases your chances.

**Social History:** Lives with her partner — both excited but anxious about the pregnancy. Non-smoker, no alcohol. No history of diabetes, hypertension, or other conditions affecting pregnancy.

**Concerns:** You are worried about the chances of Down syndrome in this pregnancy and want to know if you can test earlier than 11 weeks.

**Expectations:** You expect the doctor to explain all available tests, when they can be done, and whether they are safe for the baby.

markingScheme.heading: History
points: Ask about LMP.
Ask how the pregnancy was confirmed — scan or urine pregnancy test.
Ask about symptoms in early pregnancy: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, PV bleeding.
Ask about history of previous pregnancy and any issues.
Ask about family history of Down syndrome from both her and her partner.
Ask — 'Apart from your son, does anyone in your family have Down syndrome or other genetic conditions?'
Ask if she has any other medical conditions.
Ask if she is on any medications including over-the-counter.
Ask if she has registered for antenatal care.
Ask about smoking, alcohol, home situation, and support.
Ask about anxiety relating to the pregnancy, especially concerning Down syndrome.
Ask about concerns and expectations.
Ask for more details about what her midwife friend told her.
Ask what she already knows about Down syndrome.

exampleExplanation:
*Sarah, Down syndrome is a condition where a baby is born with an extra copy of genetic instructions that affect their growth and learning. It happens naturally and is not caused by anything you did or did not do. The chances of having a baby with Down syndrome increase with age, and at 42, your risk is higher than when you were younger. Since you have already had a baby with Down syndrome, your risk is also slightly higher compared to someone your age who has not had a child with the condition.*

*There are two main types of tests: **screening** and **diagnostic** tests.*

*The NHS offers combined screening at **11 to 14 weeks**, where we do a scan and a blood test to estimate the risk. You also have the option of a second screening test called **Non-Invasive Prenatal Testing (NIPT)**, which is a blood test that can be done from **10 weeks** and gives a more accurate screening result.*

*If screening shows a high chance, we then offer diagnostic tests — these confirm whether the baby has Down syndrome and are done from 11 weeks onwards, but they carry a small risk of miscarriage.*

*If the test confirms Down syndrome, we will fully support you in making the best decision for you and your baby.*
management: Explain **Down syndrome** in simple, sensitive terms.
Explain the two types of tests available — **screening** and **diagnostic**.
Screening tests: **Combined test (11–14 weeks)** and/or **NIPT from 10 weeks** (more accurate screening).
If booked later in pregnancy: **Quadruple test (14–20 weeks)** — less accurate than earlier tests.
If a diagnostic test confirms Down syndrome, explain the options: continue the pregnancy and prepare; continue and consider adoption; or end the pregnancy (termination).
Ensure she is taking **folic acid** (400 micrograms daily, or 5 mg if high risk) and **vitamin D**.
Advise to **register for antenatal care** if not already done.
Offer **pregnancy vaccinations**: flu and COVID at any time in pregnancy; whooping cough from 16 weeks; RSV vaccine from 28 weeks.
Offer patient information leaflets about Down syndrome.
Advise to book a follow-up appointment after screening results are available to discuss further.
learningPoints:
**Down syndrome (trisomy 21)** results from a chromosomal abnormality where there is an extra copy of chromosome 21. The risk increases with maternal age and is also slightly higher in women who have previously had a child with Down syndrome.

**NHS Down syndrome screening pathway:**
- **NIPT (Non-Invasive Prenatal Testing):** a blood test available from 10 weeks, analysing cell-free fetal DNA in maternal blood. It is a screening test — positive results require confirmation with diagnostic testing.
- **Combined first trimester screening (11–14 weeks):** nuchal translucency ultrasound + blood tests (PAPP-A and free β-hCG).
- **Quadruple test (14–20 weeks):** offered if the patient books late; less accurate than first-trimester screening.

**Diagnostic tests** (definitive, with small miscarriage risk ~0.5–1%):
- **Chorionic villus sampling (CVS):** from 11 weeks
- **Amniocentesis:** from 15 weeks

All screening and testing discussions should be conducted in a non-directive, supportive, and non-judgmental manner.

furtherResources.title: Screening For Downs Edwards And Pataus Syndromes

title: Pregnancy And Subclinical Hypothyroidism

recentConsultation.seenBy: Emily Dowry, Nurse Practitioner (3 days ago)
recentConsultation.notes: Patient is 9 weeks pregnant. Reports feeling persistently tired for the past 6 weeks. No other associated symptoms. BP 110/70 mmHg, Weight 70 kg, BMI 24. Urinalysis: all negative. Impression: likely pregnancy-associated tiredness. Plan: blood tests to rule out vitamin deficiency or other causes of tiredness. Advised to rest, stay hydrated, and commence folic acid 400 micrograms OD. Review with results.

bloodTestResults.summary: TSH elevated at 5.8 mU/L with low-normal T4 at 11 pmol/L — consistent with subclinical hypothyroidism. Other bloods normal.

patientStory:
You are Emma Harrison, a 35-year-old woman who is 9 weeks pregnant and has been experiencing extreme tiredness for the past 6 weeks. You saw a nurse practitioner three days ago who ordered blood tests. You are calling today to discuss your results.

You are excited about your pregnancy but worried that something might be wrong. You want to know if there is anything you should be doing differently to feel better.

ONLY SAY IF ASKED: You take folic acid 400 micrograms every morning as instructed. Your sister had underactive thyroid issues in pregnancy. You are registered with a midwife for antenatal care and your first scan is in 3 weeks (at 12 weeks gestation).

**Social History:** Lives with husband — first pregnancy. Works as a secondary school teacher but struggling with energy levels at work. Non-smoker, does not drink alcohol.

**Ideas:** The nurse practitioner said it may be due to pregnancy. You have never been pregnant before and do not know what to expect.

**Concerns:** You are worried the tiredness is affecting your job and you do not want to start maternity leave early.

**Expectations:** You want the doctor to explain your blood results and offer a solution to help you feel better.

markingScheme.heading: History
points: Ask about hypothyroid symptoms: fatigue, cold intolerance, skin/hair changes, weight gain, mood changes, constipation.
Ask if symptoms have worsened since she last saw the nurse practitioner.
Ask about her pregnancy — how many weeks pregnant, is everything going well, was the pregnancy planned, has she registered for antenatal care?
Ask about pregnancy symptoms: abdominal pain, bleeding, nausea or vomiting.
Ask about family history of thyroid disease.
Ask about social history: occupation, smoking, alcohol.
Ask about home situation and support at home.
Ask about use of any medications or over-the-counter supplements, especially folic acid.
Elicit ICE.
Explain blood test results, informing her of subclinical hypothyroidism.

exampleExplanation:
*Emma, your blood test shows that your thyroid function is borderline underactive — a condition we call **subclinical hypothyroidism**. This means your thyroid is working a little slower than expected, but not enough to be considered full hypothyroidism.*

*The thyroid is a gland in the neck that regulates energy levels and metabolism. When it is underactive, even slightly, it can cause symptoms like tiredness, feeling cold, weight changes, and constipation.*

*During pregnancy, your body relies on your thyroid to produce enough hormones to support both you and your baby's development. Even when thyroid levels are only slightly off, it can contribute to fatigue and, if left untreated, could affect the pregnancy. That is why we monitor and manage it early.*

*I would like to arrange a further blood test to check for thyroid antibodies, and I would also recommend starting you on a small dose of thyroid hormone replacement to keep your levels in the ideal range for pregnancy. I will discuss this with a specialist first to make sure we get this right for you and your baby. Most importantly, this medication is completely safe in pregnancy.*
management: Offer a **further blood test for thyroid peroxidase antibodies (TPOAbs)** — pregnant women with positive TPOAbs are more likely to benefit from levothyroxine.

Offer **levothyroxine 50 micrograms once daily** after discussion with a specialist (endocrinologist), as NICE advises seeking specialist input before initiating treatment for subclinical hypothyroidism in pregnancy.
Advise that **levothyroxine should be taken on an empty stomach**, at least 30–60 minutes before food, and at least 4 hours apart from iron or calcium supplements.
Arrange **follow-up blood tests in 4 weeks** to check TSH is within the pregnancy target range (TSH < 2.5 mU/L in the first trimester).
Ensure she is taking **folic acid** (400 micrograms or 5 mg if high-risk) and **vitamin D**.
Offer **pregnancy vaccinations**: flu and COVID at any time in pregnancy; whooping cough from 16 weeks; RSV vaccine from 28 weeks.
Safety netting: if she develops worsening fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, or new symptoms, seek urgent medical advice.
learningPoints:
**Subclinical hypothyroidism** in pregnancy is defined as a TSH above the trimester-specific reference range with a normal free T4. During pregnancy, the TSH target is lower than in non-pregnant adults — typically **TSH < 2.5 mU/L** in the first trimester.

**Why it matters in pregnancy:** even mild thyroid dysfunction can impair fetal neurodevelopment and increase risks of miscarriage, preterm birth, and gestational hypertension.

**TPO antibodies (TPOAbs):** these indicate autoimmune thyroid disease (Hashimoto's thyroiditis). Pregnant women with positive TPOAbs have a higher risk of complications and are more likely to benefit from levothyroxine treatment.

**NICE guidance:** treatment of subclinical hypothyroidism in pregnancy with levothyroxine may help lower the risk of pregnancy complications, especially in TPOAb-positive women. Specialist advice should be sought before initiating treatment.

**Levothyroxine in pregnancy** is safe and should be taken on an empty stomach. Dose requirements typically increase by 25–50% during pregnancy and should be monitored every 4–6 weeks.

title: Suspected Female Genital Mutilation

recentConsultation.notes: Mother (Aisha El-Tayeb) booked routine consultation to discuss concerns.

patientStory:
**Caller: Aisha El-Tayeb (Mother)**

You are Aisha El-Tayeb, mother of Yasmin, a 7-year-old girl. You are unsure if this is the right thing to do, but you need advice.

Your husband has planned for you and Yasmin to fly to Egypt in five days for a family gathering. However, you recently found out that the trip is also intended for Yasmin to undergo a 'girl purification ceremony' — female circumcision.

You underwent this procedure yourself as a child and remember how painful it was. You do not want your daughter to go through the same pain, but your husband is insistent that it is a necessary cultural and religious tradition. You feel powerless, as the entire extended family expects it to happen.

You want to ask for strong painkillers so that you can give them to Yasmin after the procedure to ease her suffering.

You love your daughter deeply and do not want her to suffer, but you are afraid of opposing your husband and family.

**Social History:** You have two children — Yasmin and her older brother Mohammed. Both are doing well at school. Everything is okay at home.

**Ideas:** You know the procedure is painful but were told as a child it was necessary for women to be accepted in your culture.

**Concerns:** You are worried about your daughter's health but feel helpless because your husband has made the decision.

**Expectations:** You want the GP to prescribe strong painkillers for your daughter.

markingScheme.heading: History
points: Start by thanking her for opening up and speaking about this.
Ask when the trip is planned and where exactly they will be going.
Ask what the father has said about why he wants Yasmin to undergo FGM — explore reasons (cultural, religious).
Ask if there is a history of FGM in the family.
Ask if there are other female children at home and if FGM has already happened to any of them. (If FGM has happened to a child under 18, report to police immediately.)
Ask if Yasmin is aware of the trip and FGM, and how she is feeling about it.
Ask how the mother feels about this.
Ask about the home situation — does she feel safe at home? Any form of violence or coercion?
Explain FGM clearly and compassionately.

exampleExplanation:
*Aisha, I understand that this is a very difficult situation for you. You clearly love Yasmin and want to protect her. I can see how worried you are, and I truly appreciate that you've come to talk to me about this.*

*Female genital mutilation (FGM) is a harmful procedure that causes lasting damage to a girl's body — including physical pain, possible infections, and long-term health problems. It is also illegal in many countries, including the UK, because it is considered a form of child abuse.*

*Because you've shared this with me, I am required to follow certain steps to make sure your child is protected. This is part of safeguarding your child's well-being. We need to inform the right people, like child protection services, to ensure your daughter is protected from harm. They will investigate and take the necessary steps.*

*I know that in some cultures, FGM is seen as an important tradition, but it is a dangerous procedure with serious risks, including severe pain, infections, lifelong complications, and even death. The UK government treats this as a serious crime.*
management: **Immediate safeguarding referral** — inform the mother that this is a serious child protection issue and contact the safeguarding team without delay.
Initiate an **urgent child protection referral**.
Inform the mother that Yasmin may be placed under a **Child Protection Order** to prevent her from leaving the country. Authorities may issue an **FGM Protection Order** to block the trip.
Explain that if the father proceeds with the plan, he could face serious **legal consequences** (prison sentence up to 14 years in the UK).
Reassure the mother that she is doing the right thing by speaking up and that both she and Yasmin will be protected.
Offer the mother a **referral for counselling** to address her own trauma from FGM.
Advise that if she feels at risk at home or receives threats from her husband, she should **dial 999**.
Offer patient information leaflets about FGM.
learningPoints:
**Female genital mutilation (FGM)** is illegal in the UK under the Female Genital Mutilation Act 2003. It is a form of child abuse and a serious criminal offence. Performing, aiding, or failing to protect a girl from FGM carries a prison sentence of up to 14 years.

**Mandatory reporting duty:** since April 2015, healthcare professionals in England are legally required to report to the police any cases of FGM identified in girls under 18. This includes information disclosed by a child or a third party.

**FGM Protection Orders** can be issued by a court to prevent a child from being taken abroad for FGM, and to protect those at risk.

**Signs of risk:** planned travel to a high-prevalence country, family history of FGM, requests for 'painkillers for after the procedure', or a family member speaking about FGM in the context of tradition or cultural rites.

All clinicians should approach these conversations with **cultural sensitivity and compassion**, while being absolutely clear that FGM is a criminal act that will be reported to safeguarding authorities.

title: Abnormal Blood Pressure Readings

recentConsultation.notes: Patient booked appointment to discuss concerns about self-measured blood pressure readings taken at work on three separate days.

patientStory:
You are Adewale Okonkwo, a 50-year-old Nigerian man working as a physiotherapist. Recently, you checked your blood pressure at work on three separate days, and the readings were:

Day 1: 150/100 mmHg
Day 2: 155/98 mmHg
Day 3: 160/98 mmHg

You were mostly settled when the readings were taken.

These numbers worried you because hypertension runs in your family — your father has high blood pressure and takes medication for it.

You feel fine with no symptoms, but you are worried you have hypertension and want to start antihypertensive medication immediately.

**Social History:** Non-smoker, does not drink alcohol. Works as a physiotherapist. Married with 4 children. Diet is not great and you rarely exercise — you know it is somewhat ironic as a physiotherapist.

**Ideas:** You believe you have high blood pressure.

**Concerns:** You have read that hypertension is a 'silent killer' and are concerned that if left untreated, it could lead to stroke, heart disease, or kidney problems.

**Expectations:** You want the GP to start you on antihypertensives immediately.

markingScheme.heading: History
points: Ask about headache.
Ask about blurry vision.
Ask about weakness in one part of the body (to screen for stroke).
Ask about chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath (hypertensive heart disease).
Ask about urinary symptoms and any blood in urine.
Ask about ankle swelling.
Ask about family history of hypertension, heart attack, or stroke.
Ask about smoking, alcohol, diet, occupation, caffeine, and stress levels.
Make a diagnosis of possible hypertension — pending confirmation with ABPM or HBPM.

exampleExplanation:
*Mr Okonkwo, I understand your concerns, and you have done the right thing by checking your blood pressure. Based on the readings you have taken, it is possible that you have high blood pressure, but we cannot diagnose hypertension from three readings alone.*

*Blood pressure fluctuates throughout the day due to factors like stress, exercise, caffeine, or even the way it is measured. A single set of high readings does not always mean hypertension.*

*To diagnose high blood pressure accurately, we need more data. There are two ways we can confirm this: **Ambulatory Blood Pressure Monitoring (ABPM)** — a small device that measures your blood pressure over 24 hours while you go about your daily activities — or **Home Blood Pressure Monitoring (HBPM)** — checking your blood pressure twice daily for 7 days and recording the readings.*

*If this does confirm hypertension, we will then discuss medication and lifestyle changes together.*
management: Offer a **face-to-face appointment** to check blood pressure in clinic and perform a full assessment.
Arrange **blood investigations**: FBC, U&Es, HbA1c, lipid profile.
Other investigations: **urine ACR** (first void/early morning sample), **ECG**, and **fundoscopy**.
Offer **ABPM or HBPM** to confirm the diagnosis of hypertension before starting treatment.
Inform the patient that if hypertension is confirmed, medication will be offered at that point.
Provide **lifestyle advice**: regular exercise, healthy balanced diet, low salt intake, limit caffeine, stress management.
Arrange **follow-up in 1–2 weeks** to discuss results of blood tests and ABPM/HBPM.
Safety netting: if severe headaches, chest pain, breathlessness, visual problems, or limb weakness develop before the appointment, seek urgent medical help immediately.
learningPoints:
**Hypertension cannot be diagnosed from a single set of readings** taken in a clinic or at work. NICE recommends confirming the diagnosis using either:
- **ABPM (Ambulatory Blood Pressure Monitoring):** measures BP over 24 hours during normal daily activities — reduces the effect of 'white coat hypertension'.
- **HBPM (Home Blood Pressure Monitoring):** twice daily for 7 days, with the first day's readings discarded. Average of remaining readings used for diagnosis.

**Diagnostic thresholds:**
- Stage 1 hypertension: clinic BP ≥ 140/90, confirmed by ABPM/HBPM ≥ 135/85
- Stage 2 hypertension: clinic BP ≥ 160/100, confirmed by ABPM/HBPM ≥ 150/95
- Severe hypertension: clinic BP ≥ 180/120

**Full cardiovascular risk assessment** is essential before initiating treatment, including lipid profile, renal function, HbA1c, ECG, and urine ACR.

**Lifestyle modifications** (diet, exercise, low salt, reduced alcohol) should be advised regardless of whether medication is started.

title: Skin Lump In African Lady

patientData.name: Tatenda Ndlovu
pastMedicalHistory: Previous abdominal laceration following road traffic accident (2 years ago, sutured in Zimbabwe)

recentConsultation.notes: Patient sent a photograph of the lump and booked a routine telephone appointment to discuss concerns.

patientStory:
You are Tatenda Ndlovu, a 25-year-old female. You have noticed a lump in your tummy that has been gradually increasing in size over the past few months.

The lump first appeared two years ago, approximately three months after you had a deep cut to your tummy following a road traffic accident in Harare, Zimbabwe. The wound was sutured and you recovered well, but the lump gradually formed afterwards.

The lump feels rubbery and soft. It is not painful. In recent months, it has become more noticeable and increased in size.

**Social History:** Works as a model. Non-smoker, no alcohol. Lives with her parents.

**Ideas:** You do not know what the lump is but feel it is related to the past injury.

**Concerns:** You are a model and worry about the cosmetic appearance. Wearing bikinis is important to your career, and this lump makes you feel less confident about your body.

**Expectations:** You want a solution — ideally surgical removal or any treatment that can make your tummy look normal again.

markingScheme.heading: History
points: Ask about onset of the lump.
Ask for any history of trauma prior to onset of the lump (classical for keloid or hypertrophic scar).
Ask if the lump has increased in size.
Ask if the lump feels soft, firm, or hard.
Ask for any associated tenderness or pain.
Ask for any discharge, redness, or skin changes over the lump.
Ask for any weight loss or loss of appetite.
Ask for other lumps and bumps anywhere else in the body.
Ask for any family history of keloid scars or similar lumps.
Ask how this has affected the patient's life.
Ask about occupation.
Elicit ICE.
Give a diagnosis of keloid scar.

exampleExplanation:
*Tatenda, I understand your concerns, and you have done the right thing by seeking medical advice.*

*Based on what you have described, the lump is most likely due to scar tissue called a **keloid**. A keloid is a type of raised scar that grows larger than the original wound. It happens when the body produces too much collagen during healing. In your case, the lump likely formed after your injury from the accident. Keloids are not dangerous, but they can keep growing and affect appearance.*

*There are treatments available that can help reduce or flatten the keloid, and I will refer you to a specialist in skin conditions — a dermatologist — who can discuss these options in more detail.*
management: Offer **routine referral to Dermatology** for assessment and management.

Explain that first-line treatment includes **intralesional steroid injections** (given every 2–6 weeks until improvement). Inform of side effects: skin lightening or darkening (hypopigmentation or hyperpigmentation — more noticeable in darker skin tones), telangiectasias (visible small blood vessels), skin thinning, or slight denting.

Other treatments include **steroid-impregnated tapes** (e.g. Haelen tape [fludroxycortide] or Betesil medicated plaster [betamethasone valerate 2.25 mg]) — applied for 12 hours per day to help flatten keloids.

If the patient asks about surgical excision: inform her that **surgery alone carries a high risk of recurrence** — the new scar can sometimes be even larger than the original. Surgery is therefore only considered in combination with other treatments.
**Cryotherapy** (liquid nitrogen) can also be considered — freezes and shrinks the keloid.
Advise that as she is prone to keloid scars, she should **avoid body piercings, tattoos, or unnecessary cosmetic surgery**, especially in high-risk areas (chest, shoulders, earlobes).
If she ever requires surgery, she should **inform the surgeons** about her keloid history so extra precautions can be taken.
Safety netting: if the lump changes rapidly, becomes painful, red, or warm, or causes new symptoms, seek urgent medical attention.
learningPoints:
**Keloid scars** grow beyond the boundary of the original wound, continue to enlarge over time, and do not regress spontaneously. They are more common in individuals with darker skin tones (Fitzpatrick skin types IV–VI), and in certain anatomical sites (chest, shoulders, earlobes, upper arms). They can appear months after the initial injury.

**Hypertrophic scars**, in contrast, remain within the wound boundary, appear soon after injury, and may improve over time.

**Key differences:**

| Feature | Keloid | Hypertrophic |
|---|---|---|
| Extends beyond wound | Yes | No |
| Regresses spontaneously | No | Sometimes |
| Onset | Weeks to months | Weeks |
| Risk of recurrence after excision | High | Lower |

**Treatment** is aimed at flattening and reducing the keloid — options include intralesional corticosteroid injections, pressure therapy, silicone gel/sheets, steroid-impregnated tapes, cryotherapy, and laser therapy. Surgical excision alone is not recommended due to high recurrence rates.

title: Chronic Kidney Disease

patientData.name: George Thompson
pastMedicalHistory: Chronic kidney disease (CKD stage G4 — eGFR 26–27, likely secondary to diabetic nephropathy and hypertension)

recentConsultation.seenBy: Lucy Adebayo, Diabetic Nurse Practitioner (3 months ago)
recentConsultation.notes: Routine diabetic review. Blood tests showed eGFR 27 and HbA1c 60. Patient is compliant with medications and asymptomatic. BP 130/70 mmHg, pulse 65 bpm, BMI 27. Foot examination normal. Plan: repeat blood tests in 3 months to reassess eGFR and perform urine ACR.

bloodTestResults.summary: eGFR remains critically reduced at 26 mL/min/1.73m². Urine ACR elevated at 6.5 mg/mmol. HbA1c improved to 55 mmol/mol. Cholesterol borderline at 5.0 mmol/L. Electrolytes and creatinine stable.

patientStory:
You are George Thompson, a 65-year-old male.

**Opening Statement:** *Hi doctor, I would like to discuss my blood test results.*

Three months ago, during a routine diabetic check, you were told that your kidney function was not as good as expected. The nurse explained that it was likely related to your diabetes and advised you to repeat the blood tests. She also mentioned checking your blood sugar.

ONLY SAY IF ASKED: You feel well and do not have any symptoms.

**Social History:** Non-smoker, drinks minimal alcohol. Lives with his wife. Retired bus driver. Maintains a healthy diet and exercises regularly to control his blood sugar.

**Ideas:** You are not sure what to expect from today's results.

**Concerns:** You are worried about kidney failure and whether you might need dialysis in the future. Your friend had kidney failure, required dialysis, and later died, which has made you anxious.

**Expectations:** You would like to understand your blood test results, how serious this is, and what can be done to prevent your kidney function from getting worse.

**Questions to ask:** If the doctor does not address dialysis — ask whether you will need dialysis in the future. Ask whether you need a referral to a kidney specialist.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about symptoms of chronic kidney disease: nausea, vomiting, shortness of breath, itching, fatigue, muscle cramps, blood in urine, reduced urine output, and other urinary symptoms.
Ask about symptoms of diabetes and its complications: blurred vision, increased thirst, urinary frequency, tingling or numbness in the legs, non-healing wounds or ulcers.
Ask about use of over-the-counter medications such as NSAIDs and supplements such as creatine — both can worsen kidney function.
Ask about family history of kidney disease (e.g. polycystic kidney disease).
Ask about social history including smoking, alcohol, diet, occupation, and stress levels.
Ask about adherence to medications.
Make a diagnosis of chronic kidney disease (CKD stage G4), likely secondary to a combination of diabetes and hypertension.

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you George for taking the time to speak with me today. I understand you are worried about your kidneys, especially given what happened to your friend, and I want to address that fear directly.*

*From your blood results, your kidney function is reduced, and this is what we call **chronic kidney disease** — or CKD. This means that your kidneys are not working as well as they should. There is no cure for this condition, but the most important thing is that we can **slow it down** and protect your kidneys by managing your blood pressure, blood sugar, and lifestyle.*

*I want to reassure you that not everyone with reduced kidney function goes on to need dialysis. To give you a clearer idea of your risk, I will use a medical calculator to estimate your chance of needing dialysis or a kidney transplant over the next five years. If your risk is low, we will continue to monitor you closely. If the risk is higher, we would involve a kidney specialist earlier.*

*One important change is that we will need to stop your metformin, as it is not suitable at your current level of kidney function. Instead, we will start two alternative medications — dapagliflozin, which helps control blood sugar and also protects the kidneys, and linagliptin. We will introduce these one at a time, starting with dapagliflozin.*
management: **Stop metformin** — it should not be used if eGFR is below 30 due to risk of lactic acidosis.
Offer **dapagliflozin 10 mg once daily** first. After 1–2 weeks, once tolerance is confirmed, introduce **linagliptin 5 mg once daily**.

Inform of side effects: dapagliflozin — increased UTI risk, and rare risk of **Fournier's gangrene** (redness, swelling, pain around genitals — seek urgent help if this occurs); linagliptin — occasional cough.
Explain **sick day rules for dapagliflozin**: if vomiting or diarrhoea develops, stop temporarily and restart 24–48 hours after able to eat and drink normally.
Offer to calculate the **5-year renal replacement therapy risk** using the 4-variable Kidney Failure Risk Equation. If >5%, refer to nephrologist. If <5%, continue monitoring in primary care.
Offer **vaccinations**: pneumococcal, influenza, and COVID.
Lifestyle advice: **avoid NSAIDs** (worsen kidney function), maintain regular exercise, follow a healthy balanced diet.

Safety net for **diabetic ketoacidosis**: feeling very unwell, excessive thirst, passing large amounts of urine, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, fast or deep breathing, confusion, fruity breath — contact GP or NHS 111 urgently.
Safety net for **worsening kidney function**: severe leg or facial swelling, very little urine output, severe tiredness, confusion, shortness of breath, chest pain — seek urgent medical attention.
Arrange **follow-up in 3 months** to reassess symptoms, blood results, and response to treatment.
learningPoints:
**Chronic kidney disease (CKD)** is classified by GFR (G1–G5) and albumin-to-creatinine ratio (A1–A3). This patient has CKD stage **G4A2** (eGFR 15–29, ACR 3–30 mg/mmol), likely secondary to diabetic nephropathy and hypertension.

**Metformin** should be **stopped when eGFR < 30** (use with caution from eGFR 30–45) due to risk of accumulation and lactic acidosis.

**SGLT2 inhibitors** (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) offer both glucose-lowering and proven **cardiorenal protection** — they reduce progression of CKD and are now first-line agents in diabetic CKD. They should be initiated before DPP-4 inhibitors.

**DPP-4 inhibitors** (e.g. linagliptin) are safe in CKD and do not require dose adjustment for linagliptin specifically.

**Kidney Failure Risk Equation (4-variable):** uses eGFR, urine ACR, sex, and age to estimate 2- and 5-year risk of renal replacement therapy. If 5-year risk >5%, refer to nephrology.

**Avoid NSAIDs** in CKD — they reduce renal perfusion and can precipitate acute-on-chronic kidney disease.

title: Heart Failure

recentConsultation.seenBy: Dr Ann Drinkwater (Clinical Practitioner Access Role) – 7 days ago
recentConsultation.notes:
**History**: Patient reports worsening shortness of breath with cough ongoing for 2 months. Cough is worse at night and SOB is worse when laying down. She now has to use up to 3 pillows to sleep. She has also noticed ankle swelling. No chest pain and no other red flags

**Examination:** BP 139/80mmHg, Pulse 65bpm, Bilateral pedal oedema noted, HS- s1, s2 nil added sounds, chest clear, no crepitations, No raised jugular venous pressure.

**Impression:** Suspected heart failure

**Plan:** Bloods and chest X-ray. Review with results. Meanwhile, trial furosemide 20mg OD

bloodTestResults.summary: Raised NT-proBNP at 1,800 pg/mL (above 400 threshold). Cardiomegaly on CXR. Other markers within normal limits.

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *"I'm here to discuss my blood test and X-ray results, Doctor."*

You are Mary Johnson, a 75-year-old retired teacher. You saw the GP 7 days ago because of increasing shortness of breath over the last few weeks, which is worse at night when lying down and requires extra pillows. You also noticed swelling in both ankles and a persistent cough, worse at night, sometimes producing frothy white sputum.

The doctor gave you some water tablets which seemed to help reduce the swelling in your feet, but you still feel short of breath.

No fever, chest pain, or palpitations. SAY NO TO ANY OTHER SYMPTOMS ASKED.

**Social history:** No history of smoking or alcohol consumption. Lives alone but has family nearby. You are divorced.

**Ideas:** The doctor said it may be coming from your heart, but she said she would also check your lungs, which is why she sent you for the chest X-ray.

**Concerns:** You are worried that this breathlessness is limiting you from doing things you love, like gardening. You are normally independent and fear losing your independence.

**Expectations:** You want a solution for your breathlessness.

**Questions for the doctor:** If the doctor mentions heart failure, act surprised and ask: *"Am I going to die?"* Also ask the doctor what caused the heart failure.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask patient about symptoms that led her to have the blood test in the first place
Ask about SOB – exertional, at rest, or lying flat
Ask about waking up suddenly gasping for air (paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea)
Ask about associated symptoms – cough, chest pain, palpitations, ankle swelling, distended neck veins, fatigue
Ask about family history of heart disease
Ask about smoking and alcohol
Ask about home situation and how she is coping at home
Ask if the furosemide given by the previous doctor made any difference and if she feels better
Ask if she is compliant with her medication
Explain blood test results and chest X-ray findings
Make a diagnosis of heart failure

exampleExplanation:
*Mrs Johnson, your blood test showed a raised level of a heart marker – this is a chemical that tells us how hard your heart is working. When this level is higher than normal, it suggests that the heart is under some strain. Your chest X-ray also showed that your heart is slightly larger than usual, which can happen when the heart isn't pumping as strongly as it should. Taken together, these results suggest that your symptoms are due to a condition where your heart might not be pumping efficiently, called heart failure.*

*I know the term 'heart failure' can sound scary, but I want to reassure you – it does not mean that your heart is stopping. It simply means that your heart needs some extra support to pump blood around your body more effectively.*

*Mrs Johnson, in your case, the most likely **cause** of your heart working harder than usual is high blood pressure over time. When blood pressure is high for many years, the heart **has to** pump harder, and over time, this can make it weaker or stiffer, leading to fluid buildup in the lungs and legs.*

*The good news is that now we know what's happening, we can take steps to support your heart, reduce the strain, and help you feel better.*
management: As her symptoms are not better on 20mg of furosemide, offer to increase this to 40mg OD and recheck renal function in 1–2 weeks

Offer referral to cardiology for echocardiography and confirmation of diagnosis – referral should be within 6 weeks. As per NICE: if NT-proBNP is above 2000 ng/L (236 pmol/L), refer urgently to be seen within 2 weeks. If NT-proBNP is between 400–2000 ng/L (47–236 pmol/L), refer for specialist assessment within 6 weeks
Advise her that the cardiologist may start new medications depending on what they find on echocardiography (reduced or preserved ejection fraction)
Advise her to avoid excessive salt intake – adult daily intake should not exceed 5g of salt per day
Offer vaccinations – pneumococcal, influenza, COVID
Follow up after cardiology clinic review
Advise to seek urgent help if: severe breathlessness (unable to speak in sentences), chest pain, sudden worsening swelling in the legs or face, confusion or dizziness
learningPoints:
Heart failure is a clinical syndrome in which the heart is unable to pump sufficient blood to meet the metabolic demands of the body. **NT-proBNP** is a key diagnostic biomarker – levels above 400 pg/mL (47 pmol/L) are suggestive of heart failure and should prompt echocardiography.

**NT-proBNP thresholds for referral (NICE):**
- If NT-proBNP is **above 2000 ng/L (236 pmol/L)**: refer urgently for specialist assessment and echocardiography within **2 weeks**
- If NT-proBNP is **between 400–2000 ng/L (47–236 pmol/L)**: refer for specialist assessment and echocardiography within **6 weeks**

Common causes of heart failure include hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, valvular disease, and cardiomyopathy. Management involves diuretics for symptom relief, ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists for disease modification, guided by ejection fraction.

title: Breathlessness in a Young Adult

patientData.name: Charlotte Clarke
pastMedicalHistory: Smoker – 5–10 cigarettes per day for 4 years
drugHistory: Symbicort 100/6 – 1 puff twice daily; also 1 puff as required for relief, up to 6 puffs PRN, max 8 puffs per day

recentConsultation.seenBy: Divya Sharma (Asthma Specialist Nurse) – 6 months ago
recentConsultation.notes:
Patient seen for regular asthma review. Inhaler technique good and uses a spacer device. Nil complaints and no recent flare.

**Impression:** Good asthma control

**Plan:** Continue ongoing management, update personalised asthma plan, safety netting advice given.

Patient booked urgent appointment to discuss concerns.

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *"Doctor, I've had sudden shortness of breath for the last 4 days that's been getting worse, and I really need to know what's going on."*

You are Charlotte Clarke, a 28-year-old air hostess for Etihad Airways, currently on a week off. You developed sudden-onset shortness of breath over the last 4 days, which has gradually worsened. SOB is present at rest and worse on exertion and when you cough.

You feel tightness in your chest when breathing. Your last flight was 3 days ago.

ONLY if the doctor asks: You have noticed chest pain (worse when breathing in) and a racing heart. You have been using your inhaler, but it has not improved your symptoms.

SAY NO TO ANY OTHER SYMPTOMS ASKED.

**Social History:** Job: air hostess, currently on your week off. Occasional smoker, 5–10 sticks per day for the last 4 years. Does not drink alcohol. Lives with her boyfriend. Takes the contraceptive pill – Microgynon.

**Ideas:** You think it might be a chest infection or an asthma flare-up.

**Concerns:** You are due to return to work in 4 days. If you do not improve, you need a sick note to apply for early leave.

**Expectations:** You expect the GP to prescribe steroids to help with your symptoms.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about onset, duration, and progression of SOB – is it intermittent or constant? Worse with movement or activity? Worse when lying flat (orthopnoea)?
Ask about other respiratory symptoms: cough (if present, ask about haemoptysis), sputum production, wheezing, fever, recent flu-like symptoms
Ask about pleuritic chest pain (worse on inspiration) and palpitations
Ask about asthma control: frequency of inhaler use, night-time awakenings
Ask about previous exacerbations or hospital admissions
Ask about smoking history (frequency and duration)
Ask about job/occupation – air hostess with long-haul flights is high risk for PE
Ask about use of over-the-counter medications or other medications, including COCP
Ask for red flags – dizziness, worsening SOB
Ask ICE (Ideas, Concerns, and Expectations)
Make a diagnosis of potential pulmonary embolism

exampleExplanation:
*Charlotte, I can hear that you're really concerned about your symptoms, and I want to explain what might be happening. You mentioned that you've had shortness of breath that hasn't improved with your inhaler, along with a racing heart and chest **pain that gets worse when you breathe in. These symptoms, combined with the fact that you are an air hostess who flies long distances and that you smoke occasionally, raise a concern about a condition called Pulmonary Embolism.*

*A Pulmonary Embolism, or PE, happens when a blood clot forms in the lungs, blocking blood flow. This can make breathing difficult and painful and put extra strain on the heart, which may explain why your heart is racing. It's a serious condition that needs urgent medical attention because, if left untreated, it can become life-threatening.*

*I don't want to alarm you, but I do want to stress that it is important we get you into hospital. I will organise and get you admitted via the Acute Medical Unit, where they can do urgent tests, including a scan of your lungs, to check for a clot. If a clot is found, they can start treatment immediately with blood-thinning medication to dissolve it and prevent further complications.*
management: Offer same-day referral to the Acute Medical Unit
Inform her that initial investigations will include a D-dimer blood test, chest X-ray, and ECG. If the D-dimer suggests PE, she will be offered a CTPA to look more closely at the lungs
Inform her that if PE is confirmed, she should not fly for 4 weeks – offer a fit note if needed

Advise her to stop taking the combined oral contraceptive pill for now; use condoms as an interim alternative. Once discharged from hospital, arrange a follow-up to discuss longer-term contraception options
Offer smoking cessation advice
For future flights, advise preventive measures: class 2 compression stockings, staying well hydrated, and moving around the cabin regularly, especially on long-haul journeys
learningPoints:
In line with NICE guidance, patients with suspected PE who are haemodynamically unstable, pregnant, or recently postpartum (within 6 weeks) should be admitted urgently via the emergency department.

For all other cases, a structured assessment using the **Wells Score** should be performed:
- If Wells Score **>4** (PE likely): arrange urgent admission for CTPA. If immediate imaging unavailable, start interim anticoagulation (e.g., apixaban or rivaroxaban)
- If Wells Score **≤4** (PE less likely): offer a **D-dimer test** within 4 hours. If not possible, start interim anticoagulation while awaiting results
- If D-dimer **positive**: refer for imaging. If **negative**: PE unlikely, no further investigation needed

In primary care, if a patient's history strongly suggests PE (smoker, recent long-haul flight, on COCP), same-day hospital referral for urgent CTPA is appropriate without needing to calculate the Wells Score first.

title: Recurrent Reflux in a Child

patientData.name: Noah Adams
pastMedicalHistory: Gastro-oesophageal reflux – onset at 1 week of age
drugHistory: Gaviscon Infant – 2 sachets as required, mixed with feeds; maximum 12 sachets per day

recentConsultation.seenBy: Dr Anjali Patel (Clinical Practitioner Role) – 2 weeks ago
recentConsultation.notes:
Patient seen with Mum. Mum reports that child is bringing up milk after feeds, looks uncomfortable during feeds and occasionally cries during feeding. He is wetting nappies okay and no weight loss has been reported. No rashes. No red flags.

**On examination:** Weight 5.7kg (previous weight 5.5kg), vitals stable. Abdomen soft, non-tender, no masses. No rashes.

**Impression:** Reflux

**Plan:** Gaviscon Infant – 2 sachets as required, mixed with feeds; maximum 12 sachets per day. Worsening advice given.

**Reason for consultation:** Mother (Lucy Adams) booked routine appointment to discuss concerns about patient.

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *"Hi Doctor, I'm calling about my baby Noah. He's still having reflux symptoms despite the Gaviscon and I'm worried there might be something else going on."*

You are Lucy Adams, mother of Noah Adams, an 11-week-old baby boy. You booked a telephone consultation because Noah has been suffering from reflux symptoms since 1 week of age.

His symptoms include: bringing up milk after feeds, crying and irritability, particularly after eating, fussiness and discomfort after feeds.

You met a lovely doctor 2 weeks ago who prescribed Gaviscon, but this has not stopped his symptoms. He is still managing to eat.

You are now worried it might be something else.

SAY NO TO ANY OTHER SYMPTOMS ASKED.

**Social history:** Noah is your first child. You live with him and your husband (his dad). No family history of eczema or asthma.

**Ideas:** You are not sure but worried there may be something else going on.

**Concerns:** You think there may be some other condition causing his symptoms besides reflux.

**Expectations:** You want the GP to do further investigations and find out exactly what is happening. Ask if your child needs referral to a specialist.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about onset of symptoms – when the vomiting, regurgitating, crying after feedings or reflux symptoms started
Ask if symptoms are getting worse or still the same
Ask if there are any relieving factors
Ask about feeding – is child breastfed or formula-fed or mixed? How much and how often? Does he seem uncomfortable during or after feeds?
Ask if there is any weight loss or issues with weight gain
Ask about vomiting – projectile vomiting (suggestive of pyloric stenosis), bilious vomiting (suggestive of obstruction), blood in vomit
Ask about other reflux-associated symptoms – difficulty breathing, choking episodes, arching back during feeds, hiccups, excessive crying
Ask about bowels – loose stools or constipation (side effect of Gaviscon; also seen in CMPA), blood in stools
Ask if child is wetting nappies okay (to ensure he is not dehydrated)
Ask if he is still managing to feed or refusing food
Ask about rash after feeds (common in CMPA), lip/tongue swelling, difficulty breathing (anaphylaxis)
Ask about family history of atopy – eczema, asthma
Ask about PBIND (pregnancy, birth, immunisation, nutrition and development)
Ask what mum has tried – e.g. smaller but more frequent feeds
Give a diagnosis of likely Gastro-oesophageal Reflux Disease (GORD)

exampleExplanation:
*Lucy, based on what you've described, Noah's symptoms are very typical of infant reflux, which happens when milk comes back up from the stomach. This is very common in young babies and usually improves as they grow. However, since Gaviscon has not helped, we may need to try another approach.*

*I completely understand your concerns and need for further investigations or referral, but I want to reassure you that what Noah is experiencing is very common in young babies.*

*The good news is that we can manage this very well in primary care without needing a hospital referral. Since Gaviscon hasn't worked, we can try a different approach.*

*Another possible cause of reflux-like symptoms in some babies is cow's milk protein allergy (CMPA). This can sometimes cause vomiting, reflux, or digestive issues. However, **at the moment**, Noah doesn't have symptoms that strongly suggest this, such as persistent diarrhoea, blood or mucus in his stools, or significant distress after feeds. Because of this, we're not considering CMPA as the main issue right now. However, if Noah's symptoms do not improve with our current management plan, or if he develops other signs suggestive of an allergy, then we may need to explore this further.*
management: If symptoms have changed from when child was previously seen, or there is clinical concern, offer a face-to-face examination; otherwise no immediate need as no red flags were identified

Offer a 1–2 week trial of smaller, more frequent feeds (while maintaining appropriate total daily feed volume) AND/OR a 1–2 week trial of thickened formula (pre-thickened formula or a thickener such as Instant Carobel added to formula)

**Note:** pre-thickened formula or thickeners should NOT be used with Gaviscon, as both thicken feeds and using both together creates risk of choking and worsens constipation. If switching to a thickener, discontinue Gaviscon
You can continue Gaviscon with a trial of smaller but more frequent feeds
If mum has tried smaller feeds or is not willing to try, stop Gaviscon and offer a 4-week trial of omeprazole
Inform mum of possibility of CMPA but explain his symptoms are not fully suggestive of this currently
Keep baby upright for at least 20–30 minutes after feeds
Review in 1–2 weeks
Safety netting – seek urgent help if: projectile vomiting, blood in vomit or stool, signs of dehydration (fewer wet nappies, sunken fontanelle), refusing feeds, or weight loss
learningPoints:
Infant reflux (GOR) is common and usually self-limiting. **GORD** is diagnosed when reflux causes troublesome symptoms or complications.

First-line management includes:
- **Positioning:** keep baby upright after feeds
- **Feeding adjustments:** smaller, more frequent feeds; upright positioning
- **Gaviscon Infant:** thickens feeds to reduce regurgitation
- **Thickened formula:** either a pre-thickened formula or a thickener like Carobel — *do not use alongside Gaviscon*

If these measures fail, a trial of **omeprazole** (PPI) for 4 weeks is appropriate.

**CMPA** should be considered when reflux is accompanied by: blood or mucus in stools, significant distress, persistent diarrhoea, eczema, or family history of atopy.

title: Uncontrolled Asthma

recentConsultation.notes: Patient booked routine telephone consultation to discuss concerns.

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *"Hi Doctor, I'm a student at university and I feel like my asthma isn't under control at the moment. I'm using my blue inhaler a lot more than I used to."*

You are Alfred Coleman, a 21-year-old university student who has been struggling with asthma symptoms over the last five weeks.

You've been using your blue inhaler (salbutamol) much more frequently than usual – multiple times a day.

You wake up at night coughing at least 3–4 times a week, making it difficult to sleep.

You've noticed chest tightness more often, and sometimes a wheeze when you breathe.

You don't have chest pain, palpitations, dizziness, or other red flag symptoms.

ONLY say this if the doctor asks: You recently moved into university accommodation, and your roommate smokes indoors. You try to avoid it, but the smoke lingers in the room.

**Social history:** Non-smoker, no alcohol or illicit drug use. Studying Mechanical Engineering at university. Lives in a school hostel.

**Ideas:** Your asthma is not well controlled.

**Concerns:** You would like to join the football team at university but are scared that if your asthma is not controlled, they will not permit you.

**Expectations:** You expect the GP to tell you what to do.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about SOB – is it getting worse, better, or the same?
Ask about wheeze
Ask about cough – any phlegm? Colour? Any blood?
Ask about night-time symptoms
Ask how many times patient has asthma symptoms overall in a week / use of SABA / AIR therapy / MART overall in a week (if above 3 times, consider stepping up therapy)
Ask about red flags – chest pain, palpitations, fever, recent viral infection
Ask about triggers – exercise, pets, moulds, rugs/carpets, stress, emotions
Ask about over-the-counter medications – e.g. ibuprofen, aspirin
Ask about personal or family history of atopy (eczema, asthma)
Ask about smoking and whether anyone else is smoking around the patient
Ask about occupation and whether it could be a trigger
Ask about any recent hospital admission or ITU admission for asthma
Find out if he is taking his inhaler as prescribed and if technique has been checked
Ask about peak flow – what is usual reading and what is the current reading
Make a diagnosis of poorly controlled asthma

exampleExplanation:
*Alfred, based on what you've told me, it sounds like your asthma is not well controlled **at the moment**. You're using your blue inhaler too frequently, waking up at night coughing, and experiencing tightness in your chest, which all suggest that your preventer inhaler (**Clenil**) may not be working as effectively as it should.*

*A big factor could be your new living environment, especially with your roommate smoking indoors, as smoke is a known trigger for asthma.*

*Alfred, since your asthma is not well controlled, I think the best approach would be to change your inhaler to a combination inhaler. This will mean you'll have just one inhaler that works to both relieve your symptoms and control your asthma in the long term.*

*The inhaler I'm prescribing is called a Maintenance and Reliever Therapy (MART) inhaler. It contains both a preventer medication (steroid) to reduce inflammation and a long-acting reliever to **open up** your airways. The advantage of this is that it helps keep your asthma under control while also providing quick relief when needed.*
management: Bring in for face to face to examine chest, check weight/height, BP and pulse
Offer MART inhalers as per new asthma guideline (e.g. Symbicort, Fostair)
Advise that smoking from his roommate may be a potential trigger – encourage talking to his roommate or speaking to accommodation services to request a smoke-free environment
Offer referral to asthma nurse for a full asthma review
Asthma nurse will also discuss a personalised asthma plan covering medications, normal peak flow readings, triggers, how to recognise a flare, and what to do when flares occur
Offer vaccinations – influenza, COVID
Safety netting – advise to return if symptoms worsen or if he experiences an acute flare
Follow up in 4 weeks
learningPoints:
**Poorly controlled asthma** is defined by:
- Using reliever (SABA) inhaler 3 or more times per week
- Night-time symptoms 3 or more nights per week
- Daytime symptoms on 3 or more days per week
- Any limitation of activity

For adults with poorly controlled asthma on low-dose ICS, the current NICE/BTS guideline recommends stepping up to a **MART (Maintenance and Reliever Therapy)** inhaler containing a combination ICS and fast-acting LABA (e.g. Symbicort or Fostair). This replaces both the preventer and reliever inhaler.
