*The best course of action now is to contact your recovery team directly **as soon as possible** — they are best placed to advise and provide you with the support you need. If you've been unable to reach them, I can help by trying to contact them on your behalf today.*

*If you do start to feel unwell or begin having withdrawal symptoms — like sweating, shaking, stomach cramps, or feeling restless — it's important not to try and manage this yourself. Please do not use any street drugs to cope, as the risk of overdose is very high, especially if your body is no longer used to heroin or other opioids. Even a small amount could be dangerous or life-threatening.*

*If withdrawal symptoms become severe and you're struggling to manage, the safest thing to do is to go to your local A&E where they can assess you and offer appropriate support.*

*Leah, while we're going through everything today, you mentioned that you smoke. I just wanted to gently bring it up because stopping smoking, even after many years, can really benefit your health and your recovery journey.*

*And because you've got a young child at home and there's been an accidental spill of methadone, I will need to make a referral to our safeguarding team. This isn't about judgement or blame; it's a standard step we take to make sure both children **and parents are supported and safe. It also helps ensure you have the right help around you going forward.*

*We'll do all we can to support you. You're doing the right thing by asking for help — let's take it one step at a time together.*
management: Do not prescribe methadone from the GP practice; avoid being pressured into issuing opioid prescriptions in an unplanned or emergency manner to manage withdrawal symptoms
Explain that methadone must be prescribed by their specialist or drug and alcohol recovery team
Advise patient to contact her recovery team directly as soon as possible if reachable
You can also attempt to contact her named keyworker or local drug and rehabilitation team to help with prescription
Offer smoking cessation advice
If withdrawal symptoms occur, advise not to attempt to self-manage with street drugs or opioids
Warn about risk of overdose if street opioids are used — especially if injected due to loss of tolerance
Advise to go to the nearest A&E or seek urgent medical advice if symptoms become severe (e.g. vomiting, agitation, tremors, or risk of relapse)
Check if patient has received harm reduction education, including dangers of injecting, overdose prevention, naloxone access; if not, offer referral to a keyworker or recovery support worker
Make a child safeguarding referral due to methadone spill in a household with a child present — explain this is standard and supportive, not punitive
Safety net: advise to attend A&E or call 111 if feeling unwell, in withdrawal, or at risk of relapse
learningPoints:
This station highlights the importance of balancing empathy with safety when managing patients on **opioid substitution therapy**. You must empathise with the patient's distress, acknowledge that withdrawal is unpleasant, and offer support — but also understand that prescribing methadone in general practice for acute withdrawal is not appropriate.

Instead, refer to or liaise with the **local drug and alcohol service**, and if withdrawal symptoms become severe, advise the patient to attend A&E for safe management. Use this opportunity to offer harm reduction advice, and do not feel pressured to prescribe — your role is to support safely, not to enable risk.

It's essential to recognise **safeguarding concerns** here, especially when a child lives in a household where a parent misuses or is prescribed controlled drugs. Even accidental spills may raise concerns around supervision, access, and potential neglect.

title: Behavioural Concerns in a Child

recentConsultation.notes: Patient's mother (Tina Carter) booked routine consultation to discuss concerns.

patientStory:
You are Tina, Leo's mum. You have booked a routine appointment because you are concerned that Leo might have ADHD.

He is very hyperactive, always jumping and moving, and says he finds it difficult to sit still at home. His older brother (Lucas, age 9) is not this way and this makes you feel he may have ADHD.

No one else — school, nursery, or family members — has raised any concerns.

If asked: Leo sleeps fine at night, no toileting issues, eats well, has friends and plays well with them. No behavioural concerns from teachers. No significant difficulties with attention, learning, or following rules in structured settings. No history of trauma, safeguarding concerns, or developmental delay.

**Social history:** Lives with you, his dad, and his older brother. All is well at home. No family history of ADHD/Autism.

**Ideas:** You wonder if Leo might have ADHD.

**Concerns:** You worry he may struggle in school or socially if not addressed early.

**Expectations:** Hopes the GP can assess him or refer for a diagnosis and to get medication prescribed.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about nature of behaviour: when it happens, how often, in what settings
Ask for presence of inattention symptoms — does the child appear not to listen, as if his mind is elsewhere without any obvious distraction?
Ask about hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms — e.g. does this child fidget or tap his hands or feet when seated? Does he interrupt or intrude on others?
Ask if patient has friends and if he has issues with interacting with peers
Ask about impact on daily life: sleep, learning, social interactions
Ask if anyone else has noticed or pointed out this child's behaviour — any concerns from teachers?
Ask for family history of ADHD or Autism
Ask about the home environment — communication within household, any difficulties or concerns at home
Ask about PBIND history (Pregnancy, Birth, Immunisation, Nutrition and Development)
Give a diagnosis of a normal energetic male — unlikely ADHD

exampleExplanation:
*Thanks, Tina, for sharing your concerns — it's completely understandable to wonder about ADHD when a child is full of energy, and I really appreciate how closely you're observing Leo's behaviour.*

*From what you've told me, Leo sounds like a bright and lively 6-year-old. It's also reassuring to hear that school hasn't raised any concerns, and that he's getting along well socially and emotionally. When we assess for ADHD, one of the key things we look for is whether the challenges are happening in more than one setting — like both at home and at school — and whether they're having a significant impact on things like learning, relationships, or day-to-day functioning.*

*At the moment, **there's no strong indication of ADHD**, so what I'd suggest is a period of watchful waiting. We'll keep an open mind, and I'd like to review Leo again in around 10 weeks to see how things are progressing.*

*You mentioned that his older brother isn't like this, and I can see why that might make you worry. But it's worth remembering that no two children are the same, even within the same family. Children develop and express themselves differently. Some are naturally more active or excitable, while others are more calm or quiet. That doesn't always mean something is wrong — just that every child has their own temperament and pace.*

*In the meantime, I can give you some helpful resources on child development and behaviour, and we can look at some simple behavioural strategies that may help with managing his energy in a positive way. We can also offer you a referral to a group-based parenting support programme.*

*If anything changes before then — especially if school raises concerns or you notice any difficulties with learning or behaviour becoming more significant — just let us know, and we can look into things further.*
management: Reassure the parent that Leo's current behaviour is within the normal range for his age, especially in the absence of concerns from school or social difficulties
Acknowledge and validate the comparison with his older brother and gently explain that no two children are the same in their development or temperament
Offer a period of watchful waiting — suggest a follow-up review in 10 weeks to reassess if any new concerns have developed
Offer a referral to a group-based parenting support programme (ADHD-focused or positive parenting group) if the parent is interested
Encourage the mother to maintain communication with the school and ask them to report any concerns should they arise
Safety net: Advise the mum to return sooner if concerns escalate, especially if school begins to notice learning difficulties, attention issues, or challenging behaviour
learningPoints:
This station highlights the importance of taking parental concerns seriously while recognising that **not all high-energy behaviour is pathological**.

A diagnosis like ADHD requires that symptoms are **persistent**, occur in **multiple settings** (e.g. home and school), and significantly impact day-to-day functioning — which is not the case here.

It also reminds us to acknowledge comparisons with siblings and gently reassure that every child develops differently.

The GP's role is to offer **reassurance, support, and structured follow-up** through watchful waiting, while encouraging parenting support strategies and maintaining close communication with school. This approach helps avoid premature labelling while still keeping the child under careful review.

title: Sensation of Lump in Throat

recentConsultation.notes: No recent GP consultations recorded. Patient booked routine appointment to discuss concerns.

patientStory:
You are Hailey Davies, a 39-year-old female.

**Opening Statement:** *Hi doctor, I've had a lump in my throat for a few weeks now and I'm really worried about it.*

You've been feeling a persistent lump sensation in your throat for over four weeks. It's not painful, and you're not having any difficulty swallowing. You've not lost any weight, and you haven't noticed any night sweats, nausea, vomiting, or loss of appetite. You don't have heartburn, tummy pain, or any changes in your bowel or bladder habits. You frequently clear your throat and swallow saliva even when you're not eating or drinking anything.

You've been feeling very stressed lately because your boyfriend was recently diagnosed with testicular cancer 5 weeks ago. He's currently awaiting surgery. This news has been emotionally overwhelming, and you're finding it hard to cope at work. You work as an accountant, and due to the stress, you've made two significant mistakes recently. Your employer has issued warnings, and this has added to your anxiety.

**Social History:** You do not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs.

**Ideas:** You suspect that the lump in your throat could be a sign of cancer.

**Concerns:** You're concerned this could be something serious, like cancer, and feel very anxious about it.

**Expectations:** You're hoping the doctor can arrange some tests or scans to rule out anything serious.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask when the patient first noticed the sensation of a lump in the throat
Ask whether the sensation is constant or intermittent (intermittent symptoms are more typical of globus sensation)
Ask if there is any associated throat pain
Ask if she has noticed any lumps or swellings in the neck
Ask if she has any difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) or pain when swallowing (odynophagia)
Ask if she experiences heartburn or a sour taste in the mouth (may suggest acid reflux)
Ask about symptoms of postnasal drip such as a runny nose or mucus dripping down the back of the throat
Ask about any nausea or vomiting, and if present, whether the vomiting has included blood
Ask about red flag symptoms: unintentional weight loss, night sweats, persistent hoarseness, or changes in the voice
Ask if she has noticed any particular triggers (e.g. stress, certain foods, caffeine, time of day)
Ask if she frequently clears her throat or dry-swallows (swallowing saliva without food or liquid)
Ask about any recent emotional stress, including anxiety or difficult life events
Ask about smoking history, alcohol use, and occupational exposures
Give a likely diagnosis of globus sensation

exampleExplanation:
*Hailey, thank you for sharing everything with me today — I can hear how much this has been worrying you, especially with everything going on in your personal life. I understand that you're quite concerned this lump sensation might be something serious, like cancer, and you were hoping for a scan to rule that out.*

*From what you've told **me, and based on the fact that** you've had no weight loss, no difficulty swallowing, no voice changes or other red flag **symptoms, this** doesn't sound concerning **for** cancer at this stage. What you're describing **actually sounds** quite like a condition we call globus **pharyngeus** — have you come across that term before?*

*It's where you feel a lump in the throat, but when we examine the area, there's no actual lump there. That doesn't mean what you're feeling isn't real, far from it, but it usually isn't due to anything harmful. It's a very common symptom, and it can often be brought on or made worse by stress and emotional strain. Given what you've been dealing with recently, especially around your partner's health and the stress at work, it's very possible that this is playing a role.*

*However, I would still like to invite you in for a face-to-face appointment so we can take a proper look at your neck and throat, just to make sure there's nothing we're missing. Would that be okay with you?*

*You mentioned that you would like to have a scan, and I completely understand your concern. At this stage, based on the information you have provided and the absence of any red flag symptoms, a scan or referral is not necessary. However, if anything changes, such as a worsening of your symptoms or if we find anything concerning during the examination, we will certainly take the appropriate next steps.*

*In the meantime, there are a few strategies that may help ease your symptoms — stress management approaches such as mindfulness, CBT, or gentle physical activity like yoga. Some patients also find relaxation apps like Headspace helpful. One simple tip is to sip chilled, fizzy water when the urge to clear your throat arises, as this can help settle the reflex and reduce discomfort.*

*If work has been particularly overwhelming, I can also provide you with a short-term fit note. What do you think?*
management: Offer a face-to-face appointment for further assessment, including examination of the neck and throat
Acknowledge that stress and anxiety may be contributing factors and recommend support strategies such as CBT, mindfulness, yoga, regular exercise, or relaxation apps like Headspace
Provide vocal hygiene advice, including reducing caffeine intake, avoiding habitual throat clearing or dry swallowing, and suggesting sipping chilled carbonated water when the urge arises
Offer a short-term fit note as work-related stress is impacting her health and performance
Reassure the patient that, given the absence of red flag symptoms, a scan or referral is not indicated at this stage
Advise that if symptoms persist, worsen, or if anything concerning is found on examination, further investigation including referral to a specialist may be necessary

Safety-netting: advise the patient to seek urgent medical attention if the throat sensation becomes constant or noticeably worsens, or she develops difficulty swallowing, voice changes, unexplained weight loss, pain, or any visible lumps or swellings
Offer follow-up appointment in 3 to 4 weeks to assess progress and review response to the current management plan
learningPoints:
**Globus sensation** is a subjective feeling of a lump or foreign body in the throat, often described as 'something stuck', even though no actual obstruction is found. It is sometimes referred to as globus pharyngeus.

**Common causes** include gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD), psychological factors such as anxiety and stress, increased upper oesophageal sphincter pressure, pharyngeal irritation or inflammation (e.g. pharyngitis, tonsillitis, postnasal drip from chronic sinusitis), and oesophageal motility disorders (e.g. cricopharyngeal spasm).

Most cases can be effectively managed in primary care through careful history, exclusion of red flag symptoms, and appropriate examination.

However, referral to ENT for urgent flexible nasoendoscopy should be considered if the sensation is persistent and constant, or if associated with: pain on swallowing (odynophagia), difficulty swallowing (dysphagia), unexplained weight loss, night sweats, persistent hoarseness, or history of smoking or significant alcohol use. These features may suggest a more serious underlying pathology such as malignancy and warrant urgent (2-week wait) assessment.

title: Abnormal Cholesterol Results

recentConsultation.seenBy: Dr Daniel Stubbs (Clinical Practitioner) — 3 weeks ago
recentConsultation.notes:
Presenting complaint: Patient booked appointment to request routine blood tests, particularly cholesterol because he did a quick random home testing kit which indicated a raised cholesterol level.

Examination: BP 130/80 mmHg, BMI 31.

Plan: Arrange full lipid profile and routine blood tests. Schedule follow-up consultation to review and discuss results once available.

bloodTestResults.summary: Raised total and LDL cholesterol with elevated total/HDL ratio; QRISK3 4% (low risk). Other bloods normal.

patientStory:
You are here today to discuss the results of your recent cholesterol blood test.

You did a quick home cholesterol test out of curiosity after your brother-in-law sadly died of a heart attack at the age of 40. The result suggested high cholesterol, which prompted you to contact the surgery to request cholesterol tablets, but the GP advised formal lab tests, which have now been completed.

You've been feeling fine, with no chest pain, shortness of breath, or other symptoms.

**Social History and Lifestyle:** You don't exercise much, and your job involves sitting most of the day (you work as a web developer for a tech company). You smoke about 10 cigarettes per day and have been doing so for around 10 years. You don't drink alcohol. You live with your wife. Your diet is unhealthy as you rely on processed and takeaway food.

You were particularly worried after your brother-in-law, who is in his 40s, had a heart attack, and the family said it was because of his cholesterol.

**Family history:** You were adopted as a baby, so you don't know your biological family history.

**Ideas:** You think your cholesterol is probably high because of diet.

**Concerns:** You're worried about a heart attack, especially because of your brother-in-law.

**Expectations:** You would like to be started on cholesterol tablets (statins).

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Clarify why the patient requested the cholesterol test (explore background and motivation)
Ask about symptoms of cardiovascular disease: chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations, dizziness, headaches, and weakness or numbness affecting one side of the body
Ask about lifestyle factors including diet, exercise, and occupation (sedentary work increases CVD risk)
Ask about smoking, alcohol, and substance use
Ask about any personal or family history of cardiovascular disease
Explore understanding of cholesterol and its risks (identify misconceptions)
Explore Ideas, Concerns, and Expectations, especially fear of heart attack and desire for statins
Give a diagnosis of raised cholesterol with low QRISK3 of 4%

exampleExplanation:
*Daniel, thanks for coming in today and for being proactive about your health.*

*I've reviewed your blood results, and they show that your total cholesterol is raised at 6.0, and your LDL cholesterol, which is the 'bad cholesterol', is also raised. These are important findings because raised cholesterol can increase the risk of heart and blood vessel problems over time.*

*To help us understand your overall risk, we use a tool called QRISK3. This **takes into account** your age, blood pressure, smoking status, cholesterol, and other factors to estimate your chance of having a heart attack or stroke over the next 10 years. Your score comes out at 4%, which we consider to be low risk. To put it in perspective, in a group of 100 people with the same risk factors as you, about 4 are likely to have a heart attack or stroke over the next 10 years.*

*That said, even with a low risk, there's still benefit in reducing it further, and that's where lifestyle changes come in. Eating a healthy, balanced diet, cutting down on saturated fat, checking food labels, and including unsaturated fats like olive oil and oily fish are great starts. Aiming for at least 150 minutes of moderate activity per week will also help. And stopping smoking would make a significant difference — smoking not only raises your cholesterol but also significantly increases your risk of heart attacks and strokes.*

*Since you're keen to start cholesterol tablets, we can certainly talk through that. Statins work by lowering the level of cholesterol your body makes. Like all medications, statins can have side effects — some people experience muscle aches, tummy upset, or effects on the liver — but for many people the benefits outweigh the risks. If you're happy to go ahead, we can prescribe the statin today and repeat your blood tests in about 3 months.*
management: Reassure that although cholesterol is raised, QRISK3 score is low (4%), so there is no current mandatory indication for statin per NICE guidelines
Explain that the patient's QRISK3 score of 4% means their estimated risk of having a heart attack or stroke over the next 10 years is 4% — low risk, but worth reducing further
Offer lifestyle advice: smoking cessation referral/support (key modifiable risk), heart-healthy diet advice, encourage regular aerobic exercise (30 mins, 5x/week)

If the patient still wishes to proceed with statin treatment, explain what statins are, their potential benefits in lowering cholesterol and reducing cardiovascular risk, and possible side effects such as muscle aches and tummy upset
If, after a balanced discussion, the patient is well-informed and happy to go ahead, it would be **reasonable to offer statin** therapy

According to NICE guidelines, even when the QRISK3 score is below 10%, **statin treatment can still be considered if lifestyle change alone is ineffective, if the patient expresses an informed preference, or where there is concern that the calculated risk may underestimate their true cardiovascular risk**
Arrange a repeat lipid profile in 3 months, regardless of whether the patient starts statin therapy or opts for lifestyle changes alone
Offer referral to Health and Wellbeing Coach or lifestyle support services
Provide written materials or links to trusted lifestyle and CVD risk resources (e.g. NHS website or British Heart Foundation)
Safety-net: advise to seek urgent medical help if he develops symptoms (e.g. chest pain, breathlessness, palpitations, weakness or numbness affecting one side of the body)
Offer follow-up appointment in 3 months to review progress
learningPoints:
This station explores the management of mildly raised cholesterol in a low-risk patient and highlights the importance of **shared decision-making** in primary prevention of cardiovascular disease (CVD).

NICE recommends offering statin therapy for primary prevention to people with a **10-year QRISK3 score of 10% or more**, people with type 1 diabetes, chronic kidney disease, or familial hypercholesterolaemia, and people aged 85 and over.

However, NICE also makes it clear that if the QRISK3 score is below 10%, statins may still be considered if the patient has an **informed preference for treatment** after a discussion of risks and benefits, or there is concern that the QRISK3 score **underestimates true risk** (e.g. due to unrecorded risk factors such as unknown family history in adopted individuals).

This case also reinforces the importance of supporting **lifestyle changes** — including diet, physical activity, smoking cessation, and weight management — as the first-line approach in low-risk individuals.

Regardless of whether a statin is prescribed, it is essential to arrange a **repeat lipid profile after 3 months**.

title: Methotrexate Request

patientData.name: Thomas Reid
pastMedicalHistory: Rheumatoid arthritis (known to Rheumatology — under shared care agreement)

recentConsultation.seenBy: Mr Rahul Mehra (Pharmacist access role) — 4 months ago
recentConsultation.notes:
Missed last 2 blood test appointments for methotrexate monitoring bloods.

Note entry: Attempted to contact patient by phone three times and sent text regarding missed methotrexate monitoring appointment. No response received.

Plan: Methotrexate withheld as per safety protocol. Notification letter sent to patient's home address.

Previous bloods 7 months ago (filed as satisfactory): FBC, U&Es, LFTs, inflammatory markers all within normal range.

bloodTestResults.summary: Bloods from 7 months ago — all satisfactory. Current bloods outstanding (patient missed monitoring appointments).

patientStory:
You are here today to discuss restarting your methotrexate medication for rheumatoid arthritis (RA), which was stopped a few months ago.

You've noticed increasing pain, stiffness, and swelling in your hands over the past 5 days, which is now affecting your work and daily routine. You're especially struggling to type and manage documents, which is frustrating as your work as a criminal lawyer is very demanding.

Four months ago, you were due for routine blood monitoring for your methotrexate, but you missed the appointment because of a very busy period at work — you had several complex cases and court appearances, and things got overwhelming. You received a letter from the GP saying the methotrexate would be stopped if the bloods weren't done, but you didn't find the time to follow it up.

Your symptoms have gradually worsened, and you now want to restart the methotrexate as it previously kept your RA well controlled. You've been taking paracetamol regularly and only started using ibuprofen yesterday.

**Social history:** Non-smoker, you do not drink alcohol, you live with your wife and 2 kids. You work as a criminal lawyer and your symptoms are impacting your work.

**Ideas:** You think your Rheumatoid arthritis is flaring up because methotrexate was stopped and you now want to restart it as soon as possible.

**Concerns:** You're worried your symptoms will keep getting worse and impact your ability to work effectively.

**Expectations:** You'd like the GP to restart your methotrexate prescription today so your symptoms can be brought back under control.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Clarify the reason for today's call, confirm worsening joint symptoms and impact on function
Ask about symptoms of RA flare: morning stiffness, joint swelling, pain, fatigue
Ask which joints are currently affected and whether any other joints are involved

Ask if the patient is having difficulty moving the affected joint or is unable to move it at all; ask whether the joint is hot or swollen, and enquire about any systemic symptoms such as fever (to rule out septic arthritis)

Ask about extra-articular features of rheumatoid arthritis: eyes (redness or changes in vision), lungs (shortness of breath, cough), heart (chest pain, palpitations), skin (unusual rashes, easy bruising)
Ask about the functional impact on activities of daily living, including ability to work, write or type, and carry out domestic tasks
Confirm last dose of methotrexate, any side effects experienced
Ask if still taking folic acid
Ask about other medications used in the meantime (e.g. NSAIDs)
Explore any symptoms of infection (cough, fever, UTI, sore throat)
Clarify why bloods were missed — explore understanding of monitoring requirements
Ask about social history including occupation, smoking and alcohol history
Explore Ideas, Concerns, Expectations
Give a diagnosis of likely Rheumatoid Arthritis flare due to discontinuation of methotrexate

exampleExplanation:
*Thomas, thank you for getting in touch today and for being so open about what's been going on. I'm **really sorry** to hear how much your symptoms have flared — I can appreciate how difficult that must be, especially given the demands of your work.*

*I agree with you — it does sound like you're experiencing a flare of your rheumatoid arthritis, and the stopping of methotrexate has likely contributed to that. You had good control previously, so it's understandable you're keen to restart it.*

*The challenge is that methotrexate can affect your liver, kidneys, and reduce your blood cells, which can make you more vulnerable to infections. Because of this, national safety guidelines and our shared care agreement with Rheumatology require regular blood tests before we can safely prescribe it. That's why it was stopped when the routine monitoring was missed.*

*I completely understand that work got hectic and that this wasn't intentional. The important thing now is to get a new set of blood tests done — we'll check your full blood count, kidney and liver function. Once we have the results, and everything looks safe, we can then get you restarted on methotrexate without further delay.*

*In the meantime, you mentioned you only just started taking ibuprofen yesterday. Taking it regularly, three times a day with food, can help control the inflammation. Alternatively, we can prescribe naproxen, which is a stronger anti-inflammatory, along with omeprazole to protect your stomach. If those don't give enough relief, we also have the option of short-term steroid tablets to settle the flare, but I'd prefer to hold off unless **really necessary**.*

*I'll also send a message to the rheumatology team today to inform them of your symptoms and ask if they have any additional advice or would like to see you sooner.*

*Going forward, how do you think we can support you in making sure these routine blood tests aren't missed again? One idea might be to set a recurring reminder on your phone or choose a set day well in advance. We can also send you a reminder a month before your next blood test is due.*
management: Acknowledge patient is likely experiencing a flare of rheumatoid arthritis due to methotrexate being withheld
Explain methotrexate cannot be restarted until up-to-date blood tests are done to ensure safety
Arrange urgent blood tests: full blood count, liver function tests, kidney function (U&Es), and CRP
Reinforce importance of regular monitoring for methotrexate due to risk of liver, kidney, and blood-related complications
Prescribe anti-inflammatory treatment for symptom relief: advise taking ibuprofen regularly with food and prescribe omeprazole for stomach protection. Alternatively, offer naproxen with omeprazole
Consider short course of oral steroids if symptoms are severe or not controlled with NSAIDs
Advise that you will send an update to the rheumatology team informing them of current symptoms and your intentions on restarting methotrexate once blood tests are back within reference range
Discuss practical strategies to support future blood test compliance (e.g. setting reminders, booking well in advance)
Offer pneumococcal and annual influenza vaccination to reduce infection risk due to immunosuppressive therapy
Safety-net: advise patient to seek urgent review if symptoms worsen, especially if joint becomes hot, swollen, immobile, or if they develop a fever or feel systemically unwell
Book a follow-up appointment or telephone review once blood results are available
learningPoints:
This case highlights the critical importance of **safety monitoring** in patients prescribed immunosuppressive medications such as methotrexate. As per NICE guidelines and shared care protocols, patients on DMARDs require regular blood tests — typically every **2 to 3 months** — to monitor for potentially serious adverse effects.

These adverse effects may include: **myelosuppression**, **hepatotoxicity**, **renal impairment**, **pulmonary toxicity**, and an **increased risk of infection**.

If a patient misses their monitoring, it is the GP's duty to **withhold methotrexate** until updated blood results confirm it is safe to resume.

In patients presenting with a flare of rheumatoid arthritis, it is important to **liaise with rheumatology or seek specialist advice where possible**. While awaiting specialist review, GPs may consider interim management to alleviate symptoms:

- **NSAIDs** (e.g. ibuprofen or naproxen with gastroprotection)
- **Oral corticosteroids** — a reducing course of glucocorticoids over 2–4 weeks can be started in appropriate cases
- **Intra-articular steroid injections** if a single joint is significantly affected

This scenario also illustrates the value of **practical planning** to help patients avoid missing future blood tests.

title: Struggling with Sex After Past Trauma

recentConsultation.notes: No significant recent consultations. Patient booked a routine video consultation to discuss a personal concern.

patientStory:
You are Priya Kapoor, a 32-year-old woman.

**Opening Statement:** *Hi doctor, I need to talk about something quite personal. I have not been able to have sex with my husband for months now, and I am **really worried**.*

About 8 months ago, you were raped after your drink was spiked at a party. You reported it to the police and an investigation is still ongoing. You had STI screening afterwards and everything was negative.

Since the assault, you have been unable to have penetrative sex. When you try to be intimate with your husband, the muscles around your vagina tighten up automatically, and penetration becomes painful or impossible. You become anxious and tense, even though you love your husband and want to be close to him.

You did not have this problem before the assault. You feel frustrated and embarrassed because you want things to go back to how they were.

You love your husband very much but you have not been able to tell him about the rape, as you feel guilty and keep thinking that if you had stayed home that night, none of this would have happened.

You have not received any counselling or therapy so far.

**Social History:** You live with your husband. You work part-time as an accountant. You do not smoke or drink alcohol. You do not use illicit drugs or any over the counter medications.

**Ideas:** You think the rape has affected your ability to have sex and that your body is reacting against penetration.

**Concerns:** You worry that you may never be able to have sex again and that your marriage might suffer.

**Expectations:** You would like help, support, and guidance on how to overcome this so you can feel normal again.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Acknowledge that the patient has brought a very personal and difficult issue and thank her for trusting you
Show respect and sensitivity by informing her that you will be asking numerous personal questions regarding her sexual history
Ask how long she has been experiencing difficulties with intimacy
Ask what happens during attempted intimacy — fear, anxiety, physical pain, or involuntary tightness (to differentiate emotional trauma response from secondary vaginismus)
Ask if sexual intercourse was comfortable prior to the traumatic event
Ask if she has had any medical review, STI screening, or forensic examination after the incident
Screen for symptoms of PTSD — nightmares, flashbacks, intrusive thoughts, hypervigilance, feeling emotionally numb
Ask about her mood, sleep, appetite, concentration, and general functioning
Ask about suicidal thoughts or self-harm ideation
Ask how her symptoms have impacted her relationship, emotional wellbeing, ability to work, and day-to-day life
Ask about social history, including smoking, alcohol use, and who she lives with
Ask about her ideas, concerns, and expectations
Give a diagnosis of secondary vaginismus, likely triggered by the sexual assault

exampleExplanation:
*Priya, thank you for trusting me with something so personal. I can hear how difficult the last few months have been for you, and I want you to know that everything you are describing is an understandable response to what you went through. No one should ever have to experience that kind of trauma, and none of this is your fault.*

*From what you have told me, it sounds like your body is responding to the trauma by tightening the muscles around the vagina automatically whenever intimacy is attempted. This is something we call **secondary vaginismus**, and it is very common in women who have experienced sexual trauma. It is not something you are choosing or doing deliberately, and the fact that it is happening does not mean you will never be able to be intimate again. With the right support, most women make very good progress.*

*There are a few things we can offer to help you through this. One very effective option is **pelvic floor physiotherapy**. These are specialist physiotherapists who understand vaginismus very well. They will work with you gently, at your own pace, to help you relearn how to relax and control the pelvic floor muscles.*

*Another treatment that many women find helpful is **vaginal dilators**, or vaginal trainers. These are smooth, gradually increasing sizes of devices that help **desensitise** the area and reduce the automatic muscle tightening. You would use them in a very controlled and gentle way, only when you feel ready, and you can buy them over the counter. **The physiotherapist** can also guide you on how to use them.*

*I would also recommend **psychosexual therapy**, ideally with someone experienced in supporting survivors of sexual assault. They can help you work through the emotional and psychological impact of what happened, rebuild confidence, and gradually reduce the fear and anxiety associated with penetration or intimacy.*

*You mentioned that you have not been able to tell your husband yet. I completely understand how hard that must **feel**. There is no pressure to disclose anything before you are ready. However, having his understanding and support often helps couples move forward together.*

*There are also specialist sexual violence support services that offer counselling and emotional support. These services are confidential and tailored to survivors of rape or assault.*

*Before we finish, I want to reassure you that what you are experiencing is treatable, and you are not alone. We will take this step by step, at a pace that feels safe for you.*
management: Acknowledge the trauma and validate the patient's feelings; reassure her that her reactions are understandable and that help is available
Explain that her symptoms are consistent with secondary vaginismus, which can occur after traumatic sexual experiences such as rape
Offer referral to a pelvic floor physiotherapist experienced in vaginismus
Inform her that vaginal dilators (vaginal trainers) are another helpful treatment option — smooth devices in gradually increasing sizes used at her own pace; available over the counter
Offer referral to psychosexual therapy, with a focus on sexual trauma, to address fear, anxiety, and emotional impact

Acknowledge that she may not feel ready to tell her husband, but gently explain that sharing this with him might help him understand and support her — the psychosexual therapy team can help guide and support this discussion when she feels ready
Offer referral to sexual violence victim support charities (e.g. Rape Crisis, local ISVA services) for counselling tailored to survivors of sexual assault
Safety net: advise her to seek urgent help through the GP urgent line or 111 if she develops thoughts of suicide, self-harm, or feels unable to cope
learningPoints:
This case highlights the importance of recognising the psychological and physical consequences of sexual trauma, particularly how it can impact intimacy, emotional wellbeing, and relationships.

**Secondary vaginismus and PTSD** can occur either independently or together following sexual assault. Understanding and distinguishing between them is essential:

**PTSD** is primarily psychological. The individual may experience fear, anxiety, flashbacks, and avoidance behaviours. Management focuses on trauma-focused CBT or EMDR, support from sexual assault or rape crisis services, psychosexual counselling, and possibly SSRIs.

**Secondary vaginismus** involves involuntary physical contraction of pelvic floor muscles, making penetration painful or impossible. Management includes psychosexual counselling and pelvic floor physiotherapy, desensitisation techniques and graded exposure. Medication is not always needed unless co-morbid anxiety or depression is present.

title: Flight Anxiety

patientData.name: James Nolan
pastMedicalHistory: Newly registered at the practice 2 months ago
Flight anxiety (aerophobia) following severe turbulence experience

recentConsultation.notes: No significant recent consultations. Patient booked an urgent telephone appointment to discuss some concerns.

patientStory:
You are James Nolan, a 40-year-old male.

**Opening Statement:** *Hi doctor, I do not want to take up your time, I just need some diazepam for my flight anxiety, if that is okay. I have one tablet left and I am due to run out. I have a couple of flights ahead and would need some more, please.*

You are calling because you're due to fly back to the UK from the Netherlands tomorrow, and you're very anxious about the flight. You have a long-standing fear of flying, and in the past, you've taken diazepam before flying, which was prescribed by your previous GP.

You have one tablet left for the flight home tomorrow. You also have an upcoming long-haul flight to the United States in five days, and you're calling to request a prescription for diazepam for that flight.

Your fear of flying began after experiencing severe turbulence during a flight to Singapore five years ago. During take-off, landing, or when there is turbulence, you start to feel very panicky. Your heart races, you begin to sweat, and you often notice a tingling sensation in your lips and fingers.

You haven't been formally diagnosed with anxiety, and you've never had therapy or counselling. You've tried breathing exercises and listening to calming music on flights, but they don't help much.

**Social History:** You don't smoke or drink, and you're not on any regular medication. You work as an IT consultant. You're currently abroad for a short-term work trip and live in the UK with your wife.

**Ideas:** You believe diazepam helps you fly safely and manage your anxiety. You consider it the only effective solution.

**Concerns:** You are worried that you will panic during the long-haul flight to the US and will be unable to cope without diazepam.

**Expectations:** You would like the doctor to prescribe 2–3 tablets of diazepam (5 mg) for your upcoming flight to the United States. You plan for your wife to collect the medication.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about the onset of flying anxiety, when it started, and whether anything specific triggered it
Ask what typically happens during flights (e.g. panic attacks, inability to board, physical symptoms)
Ask if the patient experiences anxiety in other situations apart from flying
Ask how long he has been using diazepam and where he usually obtains the prescription
Ask about mood, sleep, and appetite
Ask about any history of substance misuse, alcohol intake, and smoking
Ask about his occupation
Clarify current location, return flight date, and detail of the upcoming flight
Ask if he has tried or considered non-drug approaches such as CBT, breathing techniques, or exposure therapy
Ask about his ideas, concerns, and expectations
Give a working diagnosis of flight anxiety

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you for sharing this with me, James. I can hear how difficult flying has been for you and how much you rely on diazepam to manage those feelings of anxiety. I understand you have used it before and felt it helped, so I appreciate this request is important to you.*

*However, current medical guidance no longer supports prescribing diazepam for flight anxiety. The reasons are mainly to do with safety. Diazepam can cause sedation, confusion, and breathing problems, especially at high altitudes. It also increases the risk of blood clots in the legs which can travel to the lungs on long flights and can reduce your ability to respond in an emergency. In addition, it is illegal in some countries, which can pose serious legal risks while travelling. Are you following me so far?*

*Some people find that breathing exercises or using distraction techniques — like listening to music or podcasts, watching a film, reading, or even doing puzzles — can really help keep them calm during a flight. There are also calming apps, such as Headspace, which guide you through relaxation exercises step-by-step.*

*In the longer term, we can work together on finding a more lasting solution. Once you are back in the UK, I would be very happy to arrange a follow-up appointment. We can explore options like talking therapy, and structured fear-of-flying courses offered by airlines like British Airways and EasyJet — these have helped many people feel more confident and in control when flying.*

*How does that sound to you?*
management: Explain that diazepam is no longer prescribed for flight anxiety, as it carries risks including sedation, confusion, increased risk of DVT, respiratory depression, and reduced ability to respond in emergencies
In addition, diazepam is illegal in some countries, creating additional legal and safety risks when flying internationally

Offer safer and evidence-based alternatives for managing flight anxiety: breathing exercises, distraction techniques such as listening to music or podcasts, watching a film, reading, or doing puzzles, and using calming apps like Headspace

If the patient still insists and explains he has already tried breathing and distraction techniques with no improvement, you may offer a very short course of diazepam (for example, two tablets of diazepam 2 mg only). Make it clear this is a one-off prescription and will not be repeated in the future
Explain that long-term options such as talking therapy and structured fear-of-flying courses (like those offered by British Airways or EasyJet) are helpful long-term strategies
Offer a follow-up appointment after his return to the UK to review his symptoms and create a personalised care plan for ongoing anxiety management
learningPoints:
**Flight anxiety** (aerophobia) is common. It can develop after a traumatic incident, such as severe turbulence, or from a fear of losing control — on a plane, a person cannot choose to get off at any point.

Diazepam is **no longer recommended** for managing flight anxiety due to its safety risks, including sedation, impaired reaction in emergencies, increased risk of DVT, paradoxical agitation, and legal issues in certain countries.

Instead, safer and evidence-based approaches should be encouraged:
- **Structured breathing exercises**
- **Distraction techniques** (music, films, reading)
- **Mindfulness apps** like Headspace
- **Airline-run fear-of-flying courses** (e.g. British Airways or easyJet programmes)

title: Abnormal HbA1c Result

recentConsultation.notes: Recall for routine NHS Health Check (aged 40+). Blood pressure: 130/80 mmHg. BMI: 30. Blood samples taken as requested. U&Es, eGFR, FBC, LFTs, TFTs, CRP all reviewed and filed as normal by Dr Andrew Ashburn. HbA1c, cholesterol, and QRISK3 results still awaiting review.

bloodTestResults.summary: Pre-diabetes and raised cholesterol with low QRISK3 score of 5.5%. BMI elevated at 30.

patientStory:
You are Alan Gregory, a 40-year-old male. You are attending this telephone consultation to discuss the results of a recent blood test, which was arranged as part of a routine NHS Health Check.

**Opening Statement:** *"Hi Doctor, I had a blood test a few days ago as part of my NHS check-up, and I got a message asking me to book this appointment."*

If asked further: You are not experiencing any symptoms. You had the test because it was offered as part of the NHS health check for people 40 and over.

**Family History:** Your father has type 2 diabetes.

**Social History:** You work as an IT professional and mostly work from home. Your job involves sitting for long hours. You do not currently exercise, and your diet includes a lot of fast food and snacks. You live alone.

**Ideas:** You are not sure what the results will show.

**Concerns:** You have no specific concerns.

**Expectations:** You would like to go through your results.

**Question for the doctor:** If the doctor explains that you are at risk of developing diabetes or fall within the pre-diabetic range, ask whether there is any medication that could help reduce your risk of progressing to type 2 diabetes.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Confirm the reason for having the blood test
Ask about symptoms to rule out undiagnosed diabetes: blurred vision, increased thirst, frequent urination, increased appetite, weight loss or gain, non-healing wounds, tingling in hands or legs
Ask about any chest pain or shortness of breath (cardiovascular complications of diabetes)
Ask about social and lifestyle factors including smoking, alcohol, diet, weight, physical activity level, and occupation
Ask about family history of diabetes or other medical conditions
Explore the patient's ideas, concerns, and expectations (ICE)
Explain that the blood test shows pre-diabetes and raised cholesterol, but with a low QRISK3 score. Also inform the patient of his raised BMI

exampleExplanation:
*Thanks for coming in to discuss your blood test results, Alan. Your kidney function, liver function, thyroid levels, full blood count, and inflammation markers all came back within the normal range — that's great news.*

*However, your blood sugar level sits in a range we call 'pre-diabetes.' This means your blood sugar is higher than normal, but not high enough to be classed as diabetes. Diabetes is a condition where the body struggles to keep blood sugar levels within a healthy range.*

*We also checked your cholesterol levels, and they came back a little higher than the healthy range. Your BMI is also a bit above the recommended range, and that might be playing a role in the higher cholesterol and blood sugar levels we're seeing.*

*That said, when we put all your results into a risk calculator called a QRISK3 score, your overall risk of having a heart attack or stroke in the next ten years is still low, at 5.5%.*

*We know from lots of research that increasing physical activity can really help reduce blood sugar levels, lower cholesterol, and improve overall health. Simple things like walking more, cycling, or choosing the stairs instead of the lift can make a big difference over time. We also have a programme called the **NHS National Diabetes Prevention Programme**. It is designed for people just like you, whose blood sugar is in the pre-diabetic range. It is a supportive, evidence-based course that helps you make long-term lifestyle changes, and I would really recommend it.*

*Regarding medication — in most cases like yours, we start by focusing on lifestyle changes first. Things like improving your diet, increasing physical activity, and working towards a healthy weight can be very effective in bringing blood sugar and cholesterol levels down. We will monitor your progress with regular check-ups.*
management: Offer lifestyle advice, including adopting a healthy diet by reducing saturated fat intake, increasing dietary fibre, and improving physical activity levels
Encourage at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise per week, such as brisk walking or cycling
Reassure the patient that medication is not routinely recommended for pre-diabetes, as most people can reverse it with lifestyle changes
Refer to the NHS National Diabetes Prevention Programme — a nine-month, evidence-based lifestyle intervention available digitally, face-to-face, individually, or in a group
Inform the patient that HbA1c will be monitored annually to track long-term progress
Arrange a follow-up in 3 months to review lifestyle changes and assess whether additional interventions, such as weight management support or medication for obesity (e.g. orlistat), are required
Advise the patient to seek medical review if he develops symptoms suggestive of diabetes, such as increased thirst, frequent urination, unexplained weight loss, or persistent fatigue
learningPoints:
**Pre-diabetes** and raised cholesterol are common incidental findings during routine NHS Health Checks and can often be managed effectively in primary care. As primary care clinicians, it is important to promote **prevention and early intervention**.

When discussing sensitive topics such as weight, diet, or physical activity, communication should always be **patient-centred and non-judgemental**. Patients should be reassured that pre-diabetes is often reversible through sustained lifestyle changes.

The combination of pre-diabetes, raised BMI, and elevated cholesterol may raise suspicion of **metabolic syndrome**, a cluster of conditions that increase the risk of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes. In practice, the emphasis should remain on **individual cardiovascular risk reduction** through proactive lifestyle management and appropriate monitoring.
