title: Joint Pain After Recent Diarrhoeal Illness

patientData.name: Oscar Hughes
pastMedicalHistory: Campylobacter enteritis — 4 weeks ago (returned from Thailand, stool culture confirmed)

recentConsultation.seenBy: Dr Aaron Cosgrove (Clinical Practitioner) — 4 weeks ago
recentConsultation.notes:
Presenting Complaint: Diarrhoea and crampy abdominal pain ongoing for 7 days after returning from holiday in Thailand where he ate street food. Passing 4–5 episodes per day. Reported some episodes with blood.

Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender. BP 120/70 mmHg, pulse 82 bpm, temperature 36.3°C. PR examination performed: no masses felt, no blood on examination glove.

Plan: Stool culture sent; hygiene advice given.

Stool Culture: Campylobacter species isolated (likely Campylobacter jejuni). Salmonella, Shigella, E. coli O157 not isolated. C. difficile toxin not detected.

Comment: Campylobacter enteritis is usually self-limiting. Antimicrobial therapy not routinely indicated. Public Health notification completed.

bloodTestResults.summary: No recent blood tests. FBC, ESR, CRP, rheumatoid factor, ANA, HLA-B27 to be arranged.

patientStory:
You are Oscar Hughes, a 28-year-old male.

**Opening Statement:** *"Hi doctor, my joints have become swollen and painful, and it is really starting to affect me."*

If asked to explain further: You have noticed generalised joint pain, mainly affecting your right knee and ankle. They become stiff, swollen, and painful, especially in the mornings, and sometimes improve as the day goes on. This started about 6 days ago.

Your symptoms have been getting worse, as the pain has now progressed to involve your back. Two days ago, you developed pain in your back and left buttock. You are not completely sure what is happening, but it has begun to interfere with your work as a builder. Your back and buttocks feel very stiff in the mornings and only start to ease by lunchtime. Because of this, you have had to miss work for the past 2 days.

You have not had any fever or trauma to your joints. You had diarrhoea about 4 weeks ago after returning from Thailand, but this has now completely settled, and you currently feel well otherwise.

**Social History:** You are a non-smoker, you do not drink alcohol, and you live with your long-term partner of 3 years.

**Ideas:** You are not sure what might be happening.

**Concerns:** You are worried because this is affecting your work, and as a self-employed builder you do not get paid when you are unable to work.

**Expectations:** You would like the GP to prescribe something to help with your symptoms.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about onset of symptoms
Ask which joints are affected — reactive arthritis typically presents as asymmetrical oligoarthritis, most often involving lower limb joints
Ask about redness, swelling, or stiffness of joints
Ask about swelling of fingers or toes (dactylitis)
Ask if he is able to move the affected joints and whether he can comfortably bear weight
Ask about the diarrhoea episodes from 4 weeks ago and whether symptoms are still present
Ask if anything makes the symptoms better or worse
Ask about constitutional symptoms such as fatigue, fever, and malaise
Ask about other features of Reiter's triad: conjunctivitis (red or itchy eyes) and urethritis (burning sensation when passing urine or discharge)
Ask about painful, red eyes to rule out uveitis (requires same-day ophthalmology referral if present)
Ask about skin rash or nail changes (to rule out psoriatic arthritis)
Ask about mouth ulcers
Ask about social history including occupation, smoking, and alcohol
Ask how the symptoms are affecting his daily activities and work
Explore ideas, concerns, and expectations
Make a diagnosis of reactive arthritis

exampleExplanation:
*Oscar, thank you for explaining everything to me. From what you have told me, and looking back at your records, it seems that your joint pain and stiffness started a few weeks after you had that tummy upset when you came back from Thailand. This fits with something we call **reactive arthritis**. Have you ever heard of that before?*

*Reactive arthritis is a condition that causes pain, redness and swelling in different parts of the joints after an infection. In your case, this happened after your stomach bug. Normally your body's **defence** system fights the infection and then settles down, but sometimes it overreacts **and also** affects healthy tissue. That is what has caused **the stiffness** and pain in your joints now. Does that make sense?*

*I understand you are worried because you are self-employed, and missing work has financial consequences. Our aim is to help you feel better and get you back to work as soon as possible.*

*I can prescribe you a medicine called naproxen, which reduces swelling and stiffness, plus omeprazole to protect your stomach. I would also like to bring you in today to examine your joints and arrange some blood tests to confirm what is happening. The good news is that this condition usually settles on its own within three to six months.*

*I can also refer you to a social prescriber, who can talk through financial or practical support that may help you while you are off work — for example, Employment and Support Allowance, or the Access to Work scheme, which offers grants to help pay for practical support, equipment or adjustments that make it easier to continue your job.*
management: Offer a face-to-face consultation to assess and examine the affected joints
Arrange blood tests including FBC, ESR, CRP, rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibodies, and HLA-B27
Offer non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) together with a proton pump inhibitor (PPI). If NSAIDs are not tolerated, offer paracetamol with or without codeine
Offer referral to physiotherapy. Explain that this can be helpful as physiotherapists can teach exercises to improve symptoms and aid early return to work
Offer referral to a social prescriber who can provide information about support and benefits, such as Employment and Support Allowance (ESA) or Access to Work
Reassure the patient that reactive arthritis is usually self-limiting, with symptoms resolving in 3–6 months
If symptoms have not resolved after three months, consider referral to Rheumatology, as this may indicate progression to chronic reactive arthritis
Arrange follow-up in 4 weeks to review progress
Safety net: Advise the patient to seek urgent medical attention if symptoms worsen, if he is unable to move the joint, or if he develops a fever
learningPoints:
**Reactive arthritis** is a type of seronegative spondyloarthritis that typically develops **1 to 6 weeks after a gastrointestinal or urogenital infection**.

Reactive arthritis most commonly presents with **asymmetrical oligoarthritis** (2–4 joints affected, on different sides). Other characteristic features include **inflammatory back pain**, **dactylitis** (swelling of entire digits), and **enthesitis** (inflammation at tendon insertion sites such as the Achilles tendon).

Common triggering infections:
- **Post-enteric:** Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella
- **Post-venereal:** Chlamydia trachomatis, HIV

**Management:** NSAIDs as first-line treatment. If symptoms last for **more than three months**, refer to rheumatology for further assessment and consideration of DMARDs.

title: Chronic Widespread Pain

patientData.name: Claire Sutton
pastMedicalHistory: Childhood sexual abuse (disclosed during previous consultation)

recentConsultation.notes:
Patient attended complaining of widespread pain for the past 8 months. States the pain affects multiple areas including her neck, shoulders, back, hips, and legs. Described as deep, aching, and burning. No red flag features identified. No joint swelling, systemic symptoms, or neurological signs.

FBC, ESR, CRP, TFTs, rheumatoid factor and ANA all within normal limits. Blood results filed as normal.

Plan: Consider fibromyalgia. Referred to rheumatology for specialist review. Analgesia (paracetamol PRN) prescribed. Advised to return if symptoms worsen. Follow-up appointment arranged.

bloodTestResults.summary: All routine bloods normal — no inflammatory markers, thyroid or rheumatological cause identified.

patientStory:
You are Claire Sutton, a 34-year-old woman. You have been struggling with widespread pain for about 8 months.

**Opening Statement:** *"Doctor, I just feel like nobody's listening to me. The pain is everywhere, and I'm exhausted all the time."*

If asked to elaborate: Your pain is widespread, affecting your neck, shoulders, back, hips, and legs. It's described as deep, aching, and burning. It's constant, around a 7 out of 10 most days. Sometimes it gets worse, especially after physical activity or if you haven't slept well. You have very poor sleep. You often feel exhausted even after a full night's sleep and feel like your brain is foggy.

You struggle to concentrate at work and take longer to complete tasks than you used to. You feel anxious and stressed most of the time and feel low in mood. You feel like your quality of life has significantly diminished.

You are waiting for a rheumatology appointment but have not been seen yet.

If asked about your childhood history: You disclosed during a previous consultation that you experienced sexual abuse as a child, but you have never received any therapy or support for this.

**Social History:** You live with your husband and two young children. You work as a primary school teacher. You do not smoke, drink occasionally on weekends, and are not on any other medication.

**Ideas:** You think something serious might be wrong, as the paracetamol isn't helping at all.

**Concerns:** You're worried this could be something more serious that's being missed.

**Expectations:** You want the doctor to actually listen to you and offer more effective treatment.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Acknowledge her opening statement and let her know that you hear her and want to understand fully what she has been going through
Ask about the nature of her pain (location, character, severity), and whether any specific areas are more affected than others
Ask about factors that make the pain better or worse
Ask if there are any symptoms that might suggest an alternative diagnosis: joint swelling or redness, skin rashes or lesions, eye problems, oral or genital ulcers, or any bowel or bladder symptoms
Ask about fatigue: how often does she feel tired, does she feel refreshed after sleep, and does her sleep quality affect her pain levels
Ask about cognitive symptoms such as brain fog, poor concentration, or memory problems
Ask about symptoms of depression and anxiety, and conduct a depression screen using PHQ-2 or PHQ-9
Ask if she has had any therapy or support in relation to the previous trauma she disclosed
Ask about work and how her symptoms are affecting her ability to manage at work and at home
Ask about her social history including smoking, alcohol, and relationships at home
Ask about her ideas, concerns, and expectations
Confirm a working diagnosis of fibromyalgia

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you for coming back today, Claire, and for being so open with me. I want to start by saying — I hear you. What you're going through sounds genuinely difficult, and I'm sorry that you have felt unheard. That's not how we want you to feel here.*

*Looking at your blood test results from three weeks ago, I'm pleased to tell you that everything came back normal — no signs of inflammation, thyroid problems, rheumatoid arthritis, or lupus. I know that might feel frustrating when you're still in pain, but it's actually really useful information because it means we're not dealing with those conditions.*

*Based on what you've told me today and what we know from the previous consultation, I think what you have is called **fibromyalgia**. Have you come across that term before? It's a real condition — not something in your head — that causes widespread pain, fatigue, and often poor sleep. We don't fully understand all the causes, but we do know it can be linked to difficult life experiences, stress, or trauma, and it can have a big impact on day-to-day life, just as you've been describing.*

*There are several things we can do to help. Firstly, I'd like to refer you to a pain management programme — it's a specialist service that brings together different approaches, including physiotherapy, psychological support, and practical strategies for managing pain in daily life.*

*I'd also like to offer you some talking therapy, specifically CBT, which we know can be really helpful for both pain and mood. Given that you mentioned having experienced trauma in your childhood and that you've never had any support around that — I just want to gently acknowledge that, and let you know that trauma-focused therapy, such as EMDR, is available if you'd like to explore that when you feel ready.*

*In terms of medications, there are some that are better suited to fibromyalgia than paracetamol. These include amitriptyline, duloxetine, and pregabalin — they won't cure the condition, but they can help reduce pain and improve sleep. Before I prescribe any of these, I'll need to check a few things with you.*

*I'd also like to point you towards some resources, such as the Fibromyalgia Association UK, which offers information and peer support that many people find really helpful.*
management: Acknowledge and validate her experience; clearly state that her pain is real and not 'in her head'
Explain the diagnosis of fibromyalgia and provide a clear, non-judgemental explanation of the condition
Explain that all blood tests have come back normal, ruling out inflammatory arthritis, thyroid disease, lupus, and other systemic causes
Refer to a pain management programme (multi-disciplinary approach including physiotherapy, psychology, and occupational therapy)
Offer cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) to help with both pain and mood
Gently acknowledge the childhood trauma and offer referral to trauma-focused therapy such as EMDR when patient is ready

Consider prescribing low-dose amitriptyline at night to improve sleep and reduce pain. Duloxetine or pregabalin may also be considered. Explain that these are not antidepressants in the traditional sense and that they are used here specifically for pain management
Advise that paracetamol alone is unlikely to provide adequate relief for fibromyalgia
Encourage gentle aerobic exercise, explaining that pacing and gradual increases in activity are important
Encourage good sleep hygiene practices
Refer to the Fibromyalgia Association UK for information and peer support
Conduct a brief depression screen (PHQ-9) and manage accordingly if positive
Arrange a follow-up appointment in 4 weeks to review progress and response to treatment
Safety-net: advise patient to return if new symptoms develop, particularly any joint swelling, rashes, eye changes, or new neurological symptoms that might suggest an alternative diagnosis
learningPoints:
**Fibromyalgia** is a chronic condition characterised by widespread musculoskeletal pain, fatigue, sleep disturbance, and cognitive difficulties ('fibro fog'). It is more common in women and may be associated with **adverse childhood experiences**, **emotional trauma**, or co-existing anxiety and depression.

Diagnosis is **clinical**: widespread pain lasting >3 months, affecting all four quadrants, with no identifiable organic cause after appropriate investigation.

**Management is multidisciplinary:** regular exercise (particularly aerobic), CBT, sleep hygiene, patient education, and social support. Pharmacological options include low-dose **amitriptyline**, **duloxetine**, and **pregabalin**.

The link between **childhood trauma and chronic pain** is well established; trauma-focused therapy such as EMDR may be beneficial. **Avoid opioids** as evidence for efficacy in fibromyalgia is poor, and they carry a risk of dependence.

title: Requesting a Sick Note

patientData.name: Kwame Asante
drugHistory: Ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily PRN (prescribed 6 weeks ago)

recentConsultation.seenBy: Dr Elena Voss (Clinical Practitioner) — 6 weeks ago
recentConsultation.notes: Presenting complaint: Patient presented with low back pain and worsening work stress. Prescribed ibuprofen. Issued 2-week fit note for both conditions. Signposted to self-help resources for low back pain.

patientStory:
You are Kwame Asante, a 41-year-old male.

**Opening Statement:** *"Doctor, I need a sick note. I have been unable to go to work for the last few weeks."*

If asked to elaborate: You have been signed off work for two weeks and then returned to work, but things haven't improved. Your back pain is still present and makes sitting for long periods difficult. Work has been very stressful, and you are finding it increasingly hard to cope.

You work as a data entry operative, which requires prolonged sitting. You have not been able to concentrate at work, and your productivity has dropped. Your manager has made comments about your performance, which has made things worse.

You feel persistently low in mood and are not sleeping well. You feel like your confidence has taken a hit and you dread going to work each morning. You have not been eating well.

**Social History:** You live alone. You are divorced, and your two teenage children live with your ex-wife. You do not smoke. You drink about 15 units of alcohol per week. You do not use recreational drugs.

**Ideas:** You think you need more time off work to recover.

**Concerns:** You are worried that if things don't improve, you may lose your job.

**Expectations:** You would like a sick note and would also like some help to feel better.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about the nature of the current symptoms and how they have changed since the previous consultation
Explore the back pain: ask about current severity, any radiation, and whether red flag features are present
Ask about what makes the pain better or worse (e.g. sitting, moving, heat)
Ask about specific work-related stressors and explore how long this has been an ongoing issue
Screen for depression using PHQ-2 or PHQ-9 (low mood, anhedonia, appetite change, sleep disturbance, concentration difficulties)
Ask about thoughts of self-harm or suicide
Ask about alcohol use and quantify intake; sensitively ask about recreational drug use
Ask about how he has been coping at home, and assess his social support
Ask about occupation and explore the impact of prolonged sitting on symptoms
Ask about his expectations regarding the sick note (duration) and any other help he may want
Diagnose work-related stress and low back pain, with possible depressive features

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you for coming back to see me, Kwame. I can hear that things have been really tough since you went back to work.*

*I want to make sure I understand what's going on fully, so I'd like to ask you a few questions to help me help you.*

*Can you tell me a bit more about how you've been feeling in yourself — not just the back, but in your mood? Have you been feeling low, down, or hopeless at any point? Have there been days when you've struggled to find enjoyment in things you normally like?*

*How has your sleep been, and how have you been managing at home on your own?*

*I'd also like to gently ask — you mentioned things have been difficult. Have you ever had any thoughts of harming yourself or not wanting to be here?*

*Based on everything you've described — the low mood, the difficulty concentrating, changes in sleep and appetite, and the back pain — it sounds like you're going through a really difficult period, and you're right to seek some support.*

*I'm happy to provide you with a sick note for the next four weeks, which should give you some time to start feeling better without the added pressure of work. I would also like to refer you to IAPT — that's our free NHS talking therapy service — because it can really help with stress, low mood, and the psychological impact of what you're going through.*

*I'd also like to check in with you in about two weeks to see how you're getting on. And if things feel worse before then, or you feel unsafe at any point, please don't wait for that appointment — contact us straight away.*
management: Issue a fit note for 4 weeks covering both conditions: work-related stress and low back pain
Perform a formal depression screen using PHQ-9 and manage accordingly
If PHQ-9 indicates moderate to severe depression, discuss starting an SSRI antidepressant such as sertraline
Offer referral to IAPT (Improving Access to Psychological Therapies) for CBT or talking therapy
Gently acknowledge alcohol intake of 15 units per week; provide brief alcohol advice. Alcohol can worsen both mood and back pain
Ask about risk of self-harm or suicidality and safety-net appropriately
Advise gentle physical activity such as walking and provide back pain self-management advice
Advise patient that physiotherapy referral can be arranged if back pain persists
Encourage him to stay connected with friends or family, as social isolation can worsen low mood
Signpost to useful resources such as Mind.org.uk or the NHS Every Mind Matters website
Arrange follow-up in 2 weeks to review mood, symptoms, and whether IAPT referral has been processed
learningPoints:
A fit note (Statement of Fitness for Work) can be issued by a GP for various conditions, including mental health problems and musculoskeletal pain. From **December 2022**, a fit note can also be completed and signed by a wider range of healthcare professionals including nurses, occupational therapists, physiotherapists, and pharmacists — it is no longer restricted to doctors.

A fit note can state that a patient is either **'not fit for work'** or **'may be fit for work'** with adjustments, such as reduced hours or altered duties. GPs are not required to examine patients before issuing a fit note if the clinical history supports the reason for absence.

Important: for the first **7 days of illness**, employees can self-certify. A fit note is only required after 7 days of absence. GPs need to be aware of this to avoid unnecessary consultations.

title: Psoriasis

recentConsultation.notes: No significant recent consultations. Patient booked routine video consultation to discuss concerns.

patientStory:
You are Matthew Grayson, a 28-year-old male.

**Opening Statement:** *"Hi doctor, I've got this rash and I want to know what it is and what I can do about it."*

If asked to elaborate: You have noticed a rash on your scalp, elbows, and knees for around 6 weeks. It is red with silver, flaky patches. It is very itchy at times. The flaking is embarrassing, especially at work, where you are a customer-facing employee at a bank. You have tried moisturising creams without much improvement. The itching keeps you awake at night sometimes.

There is no discharge from the rash, no blisters, and it has not spread to your face or genital area. No recent illnesses, foreign travel, or contacts with similar rashes. You have not had this before.

**Social History:** You live with your girlfriend. You drink about 14 units of alcohol per week. You smoke about 5 cigarettes a day. You do not use recreational drugs. Your work is stressful.

**Family History:** Your mum had a similar rash but you don't know what it was.

**Ideas:** You are not sure what it is.

**Concerns:** You are embarrassed about the flaking skin, especially at work.

**Expectations:** You want to know what it is and how to get rid of it.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about onset and duration of the rash
Ask about location of the rash: scalp, body, flexures, palms, soles, nails, genitals
Ask about character of the rash: colour, texture, scaling, itching, pain, any discharge or blistering
Ask if there is nail involvement: pitting, thickening, discolouration, or separation from nail bed (onycholysis)
Ask about joint symptoms: stiffness, swelling, or pain in multiple joints (to screen for psoriatic arthritis)
Ask if the patient has had this before, and whether there is any relevant family history of a similar skin condition
Ask about triggers such as stress, infections, medications (e.g. lithium, beta-blockers), smoking, and alcohol
Ask about impact on quality of life including work, sleep, and self-confidence
Explore ideas, concerns, and expectations
Make a clinical diagnosis of psoriasis

exampleExplanation:
*Matthew, thank you for sharing this today. From what you have described — the red, silvery, flaky patches on your scalp, elbows, and knees — this is likely a skin condition called psoriasis. Have you heard of it before?*

*Psoriasis is a long-term condition where skin cells replace themselves much more quickly than normal, which leads to the build-up of those scaly, flaky patches. It can run in families — you mentioned your mum had a similar rash — and it is often triggered or worsened by things like stress, smoking, and alcohol, which are all things you mentioned.*

*I want to be honest with you — psoriasis is a chronic condition, which means it tends to come and go over time. It cannot always be fully cured, but it can definitely be well managed, and many people live comfortably with it.*

*For your scalp, I can prescribe a medicated shampoo and a topical steroid solution to help with the itching and flaking. For the patches on your elbows and knees, the first step is to use a **potent topical corticosteroid** cream. I can prescribe you something like betamethasone, which is a strong anti-inflammatory cream. It is important to apply it carefully — you should use it for the prescribed period and avoid using it on thin-skinned areas like the face without specific guidance.*

*I can also add a vitamin D cream like calcipotriol. Using the steroid and the vitamin D cream together has been shown to be more effective than either alone.*

*Moisturising regularly with an emollient is also really important — it helps to keep the skin hydrated and reduce scaling. It's especially helpful to apply before your steroid cream to help it absorb better.*

*I'll arrange a face-to-face appointment so I can examine the rash properly, and we can also assess whether your nails or joints have been affected.*

*If things don't improve with these treatments, or if the psoriasis becomes more widespread, we can refer you to a dermatologist who can consider light therapy or other specialist options.*
management: Diagnose psoriasis based on clinical description (red plaques with silver scales in typical distribution)
Offer face-to-face review to examine rash, nails, and assess for features of psoriatic arthritis
Prescribe a potent topical corticosteroid (e.g. betamethasone valerate 0.1%) for body and limb plaques
Consider adding a vitamin D analogue (e.g. calcipotriol) to the corticosteroid for enhanced effect
Prescribe a topical steroid solution or medicated shampoo (e.g. containing coal tar or ketoconazole) for scalp involvement
Recommend regular use of emollients to moisturise and reduce scaling
Advise on known triggers: stress reduction, smoking cessation support, reducing alcohol intake
Advise the patient to avoid picking or scratching the plaques
If treatment with topical agents fails or the disease is extensive, refer to dermatology for consideration of phototherapy (UVB), systemic agents (e.g. methotrexate), or biologics
Signpost to the Psoriasis Association for patient information and peer support
Arrange follow-up in 6–8 weeks to assess response to treatment
learningPoints:
**Psoriasis** is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory skin condition characterised by well-defined, erythematous plaques with silvery-white scales, most commonly found on the scalp, elbows, knees, and sacral areas.

Key associations: **HLA-Cw6** genetic link, family history, and multiple triggers including **stress**, **smoking**, **alcohol**, **infections** (especially streptococcal), and certain medications (lithium, beta-blockers, antimalarials).

Ask about **joint symptoms** in every psoriasis consultation — up to **30% of patients** develop **psoriatic arthritis**, and early identification is important to prevent joint damage.

First-line treatment: **combined topical calcipotriol + betamethasone**. Scalp: medicated shampoos (ketoconazole, coal tar, selenium sulfide) and topical steroid solutions or lotions. If extensive or refractory, refer for phototherapy, systemic agents (methotrexate, ciclosporin), or biologics.

title: Potential Drug Interaction

patientData.name: Sandra Walsh
pastMedicalHistory: Recurrent chest infections (3 episodes in the past year)

recentConsultation.seenBy: Dr Trevor Banfield (Clinical Practitioner) — 3 days ago
recentConsultation.notes:
Presenting complaint: Ongoing productive cough with green sputum, fever, and malaise for 5 days. Examination: Temperature 38.2°C. Chest auscultation: reduced air entry at the right base. BP 128/72 mmHg. Sats 97%.

Impression: Likely community-acquired pneumonia.

Plan: Prescribed clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily for 5 days. Safety-netted. Patient booked urgent telephone consultation to discuss concerns.

patientStory:
You are Sandra Walsh, a 47-year-old woman.

**Opening Statement:** *"Hi doctor, I was given antibiotics 3 days ago, but when I looked them up online I read that they can interact badly with my antidepressants. I'm quite worried. I've not taken the antibiotics yet because of this."*

If asked to elaborate: You were seen by a doctor 3 days ago and prescribed clarithromycin for a chest infection. You haven't started taking it because after reading online, you found that clarithromycin can interact with sertraline, and you're now worried about starting the antibiotics.

You still have a cough, but you are generally feeling a little better than you were. You're not feeling more breathless, you don't have chest pain, and you haven't coughed up blood.

You haven't taken the antibiotics yet and are concerned about whether it's safe to do so.

**Social History:** You do not smoke or drink alcohol. You live with your husband. You work as an NHS administrator and are currently signed off sick.

**Ideas:** You think the antibiotics might react dangerously with your sertraline.

**Concerns:** You are worried about taking both medications together because of the risk of serotonin syndrome.

**Expectations:** You would like the GP to clarify whether it is safe to take the clarithromycin, or whether an alternative antibiotic should be prescribed.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about her current symptoms and whether they have improved, worsened, or remained the same since the previous appointment
Ask specifically about respiratory symptoms: cough, sputum (colour and amount), breathlessness, chest pain, and haemoptysis
Ask about systemic symptoms such as fever, chills, fatigue, or reduced appetite
Establish whether she has taken any doses of clarithromycin yet
Ask about her concerns regarding the drug interaction and what she has read online
Ask how the current symptoms are affecting her daily life and ability to function
Confirm current medication history and any other medications she may be taking, including over-the-counter and herbal remedies
Explore her ideas, concerns, and expectations
Identify the potential drug interaction: clarithromycin + sertraline = risk of QT prolongation and serotonin syndrome

exampleExplanation:
*Sandra, thank you for being so proactive and for flagging this up. It's really important that you checked, and I can completely understand why you were worried.*

*You are right that there is a potential interaction between clarithromycin and sertraline. Both medications can affect the heart's electrical activity — specifically something called the QT interval — and when taken together, they can increase the risk of abnormal heart rhythms. There is also a small risk of something called serotonin syndrome, where too much serotonin builds up in the body.*

*Now, in many cases, this combination can still be used carefully, but I'd prefer to switch you to a different antibiotic to avoid that risk altogether, especially since we have safe alternatives available.*

*I'm going to prescribe you amoxicillin instead. This is commonly used for chest infections and is safe to take alongside your sertraline. I'll send the prescription to your pharmacy today.*

*You mentioned that you're feeling slightly better, which is a good sign. However, it's important to complete the full course of antibiotics to make sure the infection clears fully.*

*Please watch out for any worsening breathlessness, chest pain, coughing up blood, or a high temperature above 38.5°C — these would be signs that you need to be seen urgently. If at any point you feel you're getting significantly worse, please call 111 or go to A&E.*
management: Acknowledge and validate the patient's concern about the drug interaction — her vigilance was appropriate
Explain that clarithromycin can interact with sertraline: both can prolong the QT interval, and there is also a risk of serotonin syndrome
Switch to a safer antibiotic: prescribe **amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days** as first-line for community-acquired pneumonia in primary care
If the patient has a penicillin allergy, doxycycline 200 mg on day one then 100 mg once daily would be an appropriate alternative
Advise the patient to complete the full antibiotic course
Advise on rest, good hydration, and paracetamol for fever and discomfort
Safety-net: advise the patient to seek urgent review or call 999 if she develops worsening breathlessness, chest pain, coughing up blood, high fever (>38.5°C), confusion, or signs of deterioration
Arrange follow-up in 48–72 hours to confirm clinical improvement
learningPoints:
This case highlights the importance of recognising and managing **drug interactions** in primary care. GPs must be aware of common interactions, particularly those that can cause serious harm.

**Clarithromycin + SSRIs (e.g. sertraline):** both can prolong the **QT interval** and increase the risk of serious arrhythmias such as Torsades de Pointes. There is also an increased risk of **serotonin syndrome** due to additive serotonergic effects.

**Serotonin syndrome** features include agitation, confusion, hyperthermia, hypertonia, clonus, diaphoresis, and tachycardia — in severe cases, it can be life-threatening.

For community-acquired pneumonia in primary care, first-line treatment is **amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 5 days**. In penicillin allergy, doxycycline or clarithromycin are alternatives — but if clarithromycin cannot be used safely, doxycycline is preferred.

title: GP Returning to Practice After Burnout

patientData.name: Dr Oliver Hartley
pastMedicalHistory: Work-related burnout and depression — signed off work 5 months ago
Returned to work as GP 2 weeks ago under phased return programme

recentConsultation.seenBy: Dr Greta Fischer (GP and Occupational Health Physician) — 1 month ago
recentConsultation.notes: Review of fitness to return to work. Patient commenced phased return with restricted hours and no on-call duties as agreed with the practice. Ongoing follow-up arranged.

patientStory:
You are Dr Oliver Hartley, a 38-year-old GP.

**Opening Statement:** *"Hi, I'm Oliver Hartley, a GP. I'm here for a follow-up appointment after returning to work two weeks ago. I haven't been well and things haven't been going well since I came back."*

If asked to elaborate: You were signed off work five months ago with burnout and depression. Since starting your phased return two weeks ago, things have not been as smooth as you hoped. You are finding the consultations incredibly difficult — you feel an overwhelming amount of responsibility for each patient and worry you might miss something. A few days ago, you asked a nurse colleague to take over one of your consultations because you felt unable to continue.

You have been snapping at colleagues and feel irritable, which is unlike you. You notice your concentration is not what it was. You went home and had a cry after one particularly difficult consultation — a terminally ill patient who reminded you of your father.

You are worried about yourself, but you're even more worried about your patients. You have not made any clinical errors, but you feel unsafe.

**Social history:** You are married with two young children. Your wife is very supportive. You do not smoke. You drink a small glass of wine in the evenings to unwind — roughly 7 units per week. You do not use recreational drugs.

**Ideas:** You're not sure if you're ready to be back at work.

**Concerns:** You're worried about patient safety and about being seen as incompetent by colleagues.

**Expectations:** You would like the doctor's opinion on whether you should remain at work or take further time off.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask how he has been feeling since returning to work — explore mood, energy, concentration, and general wellbeing
Ask about specific episodes at work, including the consultation he handed over to the nurse
Explore his feelings about returning: what is going well, what is not going well
Screen for depression using PHQ-9 and screen for anxiety using GAD-7
Ask about intrusive thoughts, flashbacks, or hypervigilance (to assess for burnout or possible PTSD symptoms)
Ask whether he has thoughts of self-harm, suicide, or harming others
Ask about alcohol use and quantify his intake — he mentions drinking to unwind
Explore his current support systems at home and at work
Ask if he has been in contact with occupational health, his GP, or his revalidation appraiser recently
Ask whether he is registered with a GP (as healthcare professionals sometimes avoid registering with their own practice or nearby colleagues)
Ask if the patient has disclosed his return to work and current difficulties to his GMC-registered GP and occupational health
Explore his ideas, concerns, and expectations

exampleExplanation:
*Dr Hartley — Oliver — thank you for coming today and for being so honest. I can hear how much you're carrying right now, and I want you to know this is a safe space.*

*From everything you've described — the difficulty concentrating, the emotional intensity at work, handing over a consultation, snapping at colleagues, and feeling unsafe with your patients — it sounds like you may not yet be in a position where it is safe for you to continue practising in your current capacity.*

*I want to be clear: this is not a reflection of your ability as a doctor. Burnout and depression are serious conditions, and recovery takes time. The fact that you are here, raising these concerns, shows real insight and courage. But both patient safety and your own wellbeing have to come first.*

*I think the most appropriate step now is to sign you off work again, at least temporarily, and to get a more structured review in place with occupational health. I would also strongly recommend contacting the BMA Doctors for Doctors service, which offers confidential support specifically for healthcare professionals.*

*I'd also like to ensure you are registered with a GP who is not a colleague at your practice, if that's not already the case, so that your own care remains confidential and independent.*

*I will issue an updated fit note today. I'll also contact your occupational health team to ensure they're aware of what has happened since your return, and we can work together to plan a safer, more supported phased return when the time is right.*
management: Take the concerns seriously — validate and acknowledge the difficulty of his situation
Conduct a PHQ-9 and GAD-7 assessment to formally evaluate his current mental state
Assess for suicidal ideation and any risks to patient safety
Issue a new fit note to sign him off work — he has expressed concern about patient safety, which must be prioritised
Ask if he is registered with an independent GP and encourage him to do so if not already the case
Advise him to self-refer to or contact the BMA Doctors for Doctors confidential support line
Refer back to occupational health to inform them of the deterioration since his return and to reconsider the phased return plan
Ask whether his clinical supervisor or the practice is aware of the difficulties he has been experiencing
Discuss whether the GMC's Confidential Support Line or NHS Practitioner Health may be appropriate
Arrange a follow-up appointment in 2 weeks to review mental state and assess readiness for a future structured return to work
learningPoints:
This station highlights the importance of supporting healthcare professionals who are themselves patients. GPs must provide the same standard of care to doctor-patients as to any other patient, while being mindful of the additional complexities involved — including professional stigma, confidentiality, and fitness to practise concerns.

Key resources for healthcare professionals in difficulty include: **BMA Doctors for Doctors** (confidential support line), **NHS Practitioner Health** (for GP wellbeing), and the **GMC Confidential Support Line**.

When a clinician expresses uncertainty about their fitness to practise or patient safety concerns, the GP has a **duty of candour and a duty to patient safety**. Returning a doctor to work before they are ready can result in serious harm — both to patients and to the clinician.

title: Unexplained Weight Gain

recentConsultation.notes: No significant recent consultations. Patient booked routine video consultation to discuss concerns.

patientStory:
You are Ananya Krishnan, a 31-year-old woman.

**Opening Statement:** *"Hi Doctor, I've been putting on weight over the last few months and I'm not sure why. I haven't really changed what I eat."*

If asked to elaborate: Over the past three months, you have gained around 6 kg without intentionally changing your diet. You have been feeling increasingly tired, especially in the mornings, and have noticed that your skin seems drier than usual. Your hair has been falling out more than normal, and you have noticed your eyebrows thinning at the outer edges.

Your periods have been more irregular than usual and have become heavier over the past few months. You occasionally feel cold, even when others around you are warm. You have been constipated recently, which is not normal for you.

You have been feeling a bit low in your mood, and your concentration is not as sharp as it usually is.

**Social History:** You live with your husband. You work as a marketing manager and occasionally work long hours. You do not smoke. You drink about 5 units of alcohol per week. You do not use recreational drugs.

**Family History:** Your mother has an underactive thyroid.

**Ideas:** You wonder whether it could be thyroid-related as your mother has thyroid problems.

**Concerns:** You're worried about unexplained weight gain and feel self-conscious about it.

**Expectations:** You would like the GP to run some blood tests.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask how long she has been gaining weight and how much she has gained
Ask about changes to diet, appetite, or activity levels
Ask about symptoms of hypothyroidism: fatigue, cold intolerance, dry skin, hair loss, constipation, and mood changes

Ask about symptoms of other conditions: polycystic ovarian syndrome (irregular periods, acne, hirsutism), Cushing's syndrome (weight gain mainly around the abdomen, easy bruising, stretch marks, facial rounding)
Ask about menstrual cycle: regularity, flow, duration, and any recent changes
Ask whether she is sexually active and whether pregnancy is possible
Ask about fatigue: how severe, when it occurs, whether sleep quality is good
Ask about mood, concentration, and memory changes
Ask about family history of thyroid conditions
Ask about social history including diet, physical activity, alcohol, smoking, and stress
Ask about any neck swellings or discomfort when swallowing
Explore ideas, concerns, and expectations
Give a working diagnosis of likely hypothyroidism

exampleExplanation:
*Ananya, thank you for coming in today. From everything you've told me — the weight gain, the tiredness, the dry skin, the hair loss, the constipation, the heavier and more irregular periods, and feeling cold — these are really classic signs of a condition called hypothyroidism, or an underactive thyroid. And with your mum having a thyroid condition too, it does raise our suspicion further.*

*The thyroid is a small gland in your neck that produces hormones to regulate your metabolism — basically how fast your body burns energy. When it doesn't produce enough hormones, everything slows down, which explains the symptoms you're experiencing.*

*I'm going to arrange blood tests today to check your thyroid function. I'll also check your full blood count and iron levels, as sometimes there can be anaemia contributing to fatigue as well.*

*If the blood tests confirm your thyroid is underactive, we'll start you on a medication called levothyroxine. It's a tablet you'd take once a day, and most people feel quite a bit better once their levels stabilise. We'd check the levels regularly and adjust the dose as needed.*

*I'll also arrange for you to come in face-to-face so I can examine your neck and check your thyroid gland. The blood test results should be back within a few days, and I'll contact you once they're in.*
management: Offer blood tests: TFTs (TSH and free T4), FBC, ferritin, iron studies
Arrange a face-to-face appointment to examine the thyroid gland (for goitre or nodules) and assess other clinical features of hypothyroidism
If bloods confirm hypothyroidism, start levothyroxine at a starting dose of 25–50 micrograms once daily, reviewed every 4–6 weeks with repeat TFTs until stable
Offer lifestyle advice regarding diet and gentle exercise regardless of results
If blood tests are normal, consider further investigation for other causes of weight gain such as PCOS, Cushing's syndrome, or depression
If pregnancy is suspected, do a urine pregnancy test before initiating any investigations or treatment
Arrange follow-up once blood results are available, within 5–7 days
learningPoints:
**Hypothyroidism** is a common endocrine disorder, more prevalent in women and associated with a strong familial tendency. Classic features include weight gain, fatigue, cold intolerance, dry skin, hair loss (particularly lateral eyebrow thinning), constipation, bradycardia, and menstrual irregularities.

Diagnosis is confirmed with **elevated TSH and low free T4**. Treatment is with **levothyroxine**, starting at 25–50 micrograms daily, with dose adjustments every 4–6 weeks based on TSH levels. The target TSH should be in the lower half of the normal range (0.5–2.5 mIU/L for most patients).

Hypothyroidism can mimic depression and must be considered and excluded when a patient presents with low mood, fatigue, or unexplained weight gain.

title: Recurrent Urinary Tract Infections in Women

patientData.name: Joanna Fitzgerald
pastMedicalHistory: Recurrent UTIs (3+ episodes in the past 12 months)
drugHistory: Trimethoprim 100 mg nocte (prophylactic — prescribed 6 months ago)

recentConsultation.notes:
Presenting complaint: Burning and stinging when passing urine, urinary frequency, lower abdominal pain for 2 days, no fever, no haematuria, no loin pain. Dipstick: Nitrites +, Leucocytes ++, Blood trace.

Plan: Urine MC&S sent. Given the ongoing prophylaxis with trimethoprim and this breakthrough infection, prescribed cefalexin 500 mg twice daily for 3 days pending culture results. Patient booked urgent telephone appointment to discuss concerns.

bloodTestResults.summary: No recent blood tests. Urine MC&S pending.

patientStory:
You are Joanna Fitzgerald, a 43-year-old woman.

**Opening Statement:** *"Doctor, I've had another UTI and I'm really fed up. This is the fourth one in less than a year. I want to know what can be done about this long-term."*

If asked to elaborate: You're already taking trimethoprim at night to prevent infections but you've still had this breakthrough UTI. You're tired of it and want a longer-term solution. You are sexually active and have noticed the infections often come after sex. You drink coffee frequently throughout the day. You feel you have tried most things people advise and want real solutions.

**Social History:** You do not smoke. You drink about 10 units of alcohol per week. You work as a teacher and have had to take several days off due to UTIs this year. You live with your husband.

**Gynae History:** Menstrual cycle is regular; not currently pregnant. Not going through menopause.

**Ideas:** You know that antibiotics help but are frustrated they keep coming back.

**Concerns:** You are worried about being on so many antibiotics and the long-term effects. You read something about antibiotic resistance.

**Expectations:** You want a longer-term strategy beyond just more antibiotics.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Acknowledge the patient's frustration about recurrent UTIs and validate her concerns
Ask about the relationship between sexual intercourse and the onset of UTIs
Ask about contraceptive methods (diaphragm and spermicide use are associated with UTIs)
Ask whether urinary symptoms are present between infections (to rule out interstitial cystitis)
Ask about fluid intake and types of drinks consumed — caffeine and carbonated drinks can irritate the bladder
Ask about toilet habits — wiping technique, urinating after sex
Ask about menopausal status and any vaginal dryness or atrophy
Ask about urinary incontinence or incomplete bladder emptying
Ask about any previous investigations, e.g. urine cultures, renal imaging, or referrals
Ask about previous antibiotic use and whether cultures have been done to identify the causative organism
Ask about any structural abnormalities of the urinary tract or history of kidney stones
Explore ideas, concerns, and expectations

exampleExplanation:
*Joanna, I completely understand your frustration — four UTIs in under a year is exhausting, and it's clear this is having a real impact on your quality of life and your work.*

*Let me explain what we can do differently going forward to try and break this cycle.*

*First, we should review your current prophylaxis. The fact that you've had a breakthrough UTI while on trimethoprim suggests it may not be working as well as we hoped, either because of resistance or simply because the dose or timing isn't quite right for you. Depending on what the urine culture shows, we might consider switching to a different prophylactic antibiotic.*

*Because some of your infections seem to occur after sex, it might also be worth trying **post-coital prophylaxis** — this means taking a single antibiotic tablet within two hours of intercourse, rather than every night. Some women find this approach more effective when infections are clearly linked to sex.*

*There's also a non-antibiotic option called **Hiprex**, which is an antiseptic tablet taken twice daily. It doesn't contribute to antibiotic resistance and can reduce UTI frequency in some women.*

*Another option that has good evidence — and no antibiotics involved — is **D-mannose**, a natural sugar supplement that can help prevent bacteria from sticking to the bladder wall. Cranberry extract also has some evidence, but the research is not as strong.*

*There are also some lifestyle changes that can help: drinking more water (aim for 1.5–2 litres a day), reducing caffeine and fizzy drinks, emptying your bladder after sex, and making sure you wipe front to back.*

*Finally, I would like to refer you to urology for further investigation — they can check that there's no structural issue contributing to the recurrence, and offer additional management options.*
management: Acknowledge the patient's frustration and the significant impact on her quality of life and work
Review and potentially switch the prophylactic antibiotic to one based on the urine culture and sensitivity result
Discuss post-coital antibiotic prophylaxis (a single dose within 2 hours of intercourse) as the infection pattern appears related to sexual intercourse
Consider Hiprex (methenamine hippurate) as a non-antibiotic prophylactic option, taken twice daily, that reduces antibiotic resistance concerns
Advise on non-pharmacological strategies: increasing fluid intake (1.5–2 litres/day), reducing caffeine and carbonated drinks, urinating after intercourse, and ensuring front-to-back wiping
Discuss D-mannose and cranberry supplements as adjunctive options, acknowledging their limited but emerging evidence base
Advise about antibiotic resistance in response to her concerns and explain that reducing unnecessary antibiotic use is part of the plan
Refer to urology for investigation of recurrent UTIs, to exclude structural abnormalities, bladder dysfunction, or other contributing factors
Arrange a follow-up once urine culture results are back to review antibiotic choice and reassess the management plan
Safety-net: advise patient to seek urgent review if she develops loin pain, fever, rigors, nausea, or vomiting, which may indicate upper urinary tract involvement
learningPoints:
**Recurrent UTI** is defined as two or more culture-proven UTIs within six months, or three or more within twelve months. It is significantly more common in women.

Key management strategies include: **review of prophylactic antibiotics** (consider switching based on sensitivities), **post-coital prophylaxis** for those whose infections are clearly triggered by intercourse, **Hiprex (methenamine hippurate)** as a non-antibiotic antimicrobial, **D-mannose** (emerging evidence), behavioural and lifestyle modifications (hydration, post-coital voiding, wiping technique), and **urology referral** for structural assessment if recurrence continues despite primary care measures.

For postmenopausal women, **topical vaginal oestrogen** (e.g. vaginal oestradiol cream or pessaries) can significantly reduce UTI frequency by improving urogenital tissue integrity.

title: Palliative Care: Patient With Cancer

patientData.name: Eileen Foster
pastMedicalHistory: Ovarian cancer — stage 4, metastatic (diagnosed 8 months ago)
drugHistory: Oramorph (morphine sulphate) oral solution 10 mg/5 mL — 5 mg every 4 hours and 5 mg as needed PRN
MST Continus (modified-release morphine sulphate) 20 mg twice daily

recentConsultation.seenBy: Dr Harriet Ogden (Palliative Care Specialist Nurse) — 2 weeks ago
recentConsultation.notes:
Patient has stage 4 ovarian cancer. Now in the palliative phase of care. Chemotherapy completed 3 months ago with no further active treatment planned.

Pain currently managed with modified-release morphine, with immediate-release oramorph for breakthrough. However, the patient reports inadequate breakthrough pain relief. Appetite and bowel function also reviewed.

Patient declined resuscitation in writing — DNACPR in place. Patient has expressed wish to die at home. Preferred priorities of care document completed. Anticipatory medications: not yet prescribed — team deferred to GP to prescribe via Palliative Care Hub.

Patient booked urgent video consultation to discuss concerns.

patientStory:
You are Eileen Foster, a 68-year-old woman.

**Opening Statement:** *"Doctor, I just want to feel comfortable. The pain has been really bad lately, and I'm having to use my extra morphine quite often."*

If asked to elaborate: The pain is mainly in your abdomen and lower back. It has been getting worse over the past two weeks despite the regular morphine. You are using your breakthrough oramorph doses 4 to 5 times a day. You feel the breakthrough dose is not quite doing enough, and you sometimes have to wait a while for it to kick in. You have also been feeling very nauseous lately, and you find it difficult to eat.

Your bowels have been sluggish, despite taking the macrogol laxatives. You feel bloated. You are sleeping poorly because the pain wakes you up at night.

You are not frightened of death but you are frightened of pain. You feel anxious about what the future holds. You have shared your wish to die at home with your family, and they are fully supportive.

**Social History:** You are a widow. You have two daughters who take turns staying with you. You used to enjoy gardening but no longer can. You do not smoke. You drink occasionally.

**Ideas:** You feel the breakthrough morphine is helping a little but not enough.

**Concerns:** You are scared of dying in pain.

**Expectations:** You want to feel comfortable and to stay at home until the end.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about the nature and location of pain and how it has changed over recent weeks
Ask how many breakthrough doses she is using in 24 hours
Ask if the breakthrough oramorph provides adequate relief, and how long it takes to work
Ask about other symptoms: nausea, vomiting, appetite, constipation or diarrhoea, fatigue, breathlessness
Ask about sleep and whether pain is waking her at night
Ask about mood and anxiety; screen for depression or emotional distress
Ask about her current support system at home
Confirm DNACPR status, preferred place of care, and advance care plan
Ask whether anticipatory medications have been prescribed or are available at home
Explore her ideas, concerns, and expectations sensitively

exampleExplanation:
*Eileen, thank you for being so open with me today. I want to make sure you are as comfortable as possible — that is our absolute priority.*

*From what you have told me, it sounds like your current pain relief is not quite meeting your needs, and I want to address that today. Using four or five breakthrough doses a day is a sign that we need to increase your regular morphine. We can do that by increasing your MST — the long-acting morphine you take twice a day — and adjusting the breakthrough dose accordingly.*

*We'll also make sure your anticipatory medications are prescribed and ready at home. These are a small set of medications — usually for pain, nausea, agitation, and secretions — that a district nurse can administer if you need them urgently and the pharmacy or surgery is not quickly available.*

*For the nausea, I can add a medication called haloperidol or levomepromazine, both of which are commonly used to help manage nausea in palliative care.*

*You mentioned your bowels have been sluggish even with macrogol. We may need to increase the laxative dose or add another type of laxative to help things move along.*

*I can also arrange for a district nurse to visit you regularly, and for the palliative care team to stay closely in touch. You mentioned you want to stay at home, and we will do everything we can to support that.*

*I understand you are worried about pain at the end of life, and I want to reassure you — managing that pain is exactly what we are here for.*
management: Acknowledge the inadequate pain control and increase the regular modified-release morphine (MST Continus) dose
The breakthrough Oramorph dose should be recalculated as one-sixth of the total daily morphine dose
Prescribe anticipatory medications for home use to cover pain, nausea, agitation, and respiratory secretions — these allow district nurses to administer them without waiting for a new prescription
Add an antiemetic such as haloperidol or levomepromazine for nausea, either orally or for inclusion in a syringe driver if needed
Review and optimise laxative regime: increase macrogol dose or add a stimulant laxative such as senna; consider bisacodyl suppositories if oral laxatives are insufficient
Consider stopping non-essential medications such as metformin and amlodipine, as they are unlikely to provide benefit in the palliative phase and may cause unnecessary side effects
Confirm and document DNACPR status, advance care plan, and preferred place of care
Arrange regular district nurse visits to support symptom management and carer support
Ensure the palliative care team and out-of-hours services are made aware of the patient's needs and preferences
Safety-net: provide carers with a direct contact number for the palliative care team and out-of-hours GP service in case of urgent symptom deterioration
learningPoints:
In **palliative care**, the focus shifts entirely to **symptom control and quality of life**. As GPs, we play a vital role in supporting patients who wish to die at home.

When breakthrough opioid doses are being used **more than 3 times in 24 hours**, this signals that the regular (background) dose needs to be increased. The rule of thumb is: **the breakthrough dose = one-sixth of the total 24-hour oral morphine dose**.

**Anticipatory prescribing** is essential for patients approaching the end of life. It involves prescribing medications in advance (usually subcutaneous injections) that district nurses can administer if symptoms suddenly worsen — preventing unnecessary hospital admissions and ensuring comfort at home.

**Deprescribing** is equally important: non-essential medications should be reviewed and stopped where appropriate, reducing pill burden and side effects in patients approaching the end of life.
