title: Potential Testicular Cancer

recentConsultation.notes: No significant recent consultations. Patient booked routine video consultation to discuss concerns.

patientStory:
You are Liam Shaughnessy, a 26-year-old male.

**Opening Statement:** *"Hi doctor, I've noticed a lump on my testicle and I'm a bit worried about it."*

If asked to elaborate: You noticed a hard, painless lump on your right testicle about 2 weeks ago when you were in the shower. It has not changed in size. The lump is on the testis itself, not on the skin or in the area above the testicle. You have not had any trauma to the groin.

You have a dull ache in the lower abdomen, which comes and goes. You haven't noticed any swelling around the groin or elsewhere. You feel generally well with no fatigue, weight loss, or night sweats. There is no nipple tenderness or breast swelling.

**Social History:** You live with your girlfriend. You work as a secondary school teacher. You do not smoke or drink alcohol.

**Ideas:** You are not sure if it is something serious.

**Concerns:** You are worried it could be cancer. Your uncle had testicular cancer and you have been told that your history of an undescended testicle is a risk factor.

**Expectations:** You would like the doctor to examine you and advise on next steps.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about onset, duration, and whether the lump has changed in size or character
Ask if the lump is painful or if he has any pain in the testicle or groin
Ask about the nature of the lump — hard or soft, smooth or irregular
Ask whether he has noticed any other lumps in the groin, abdomen, or neck (lymphadenopathy)
Ask about gynecomastia (breast swelling or tenderness)
Ask about constitutional symptoms: weight loss, fatigue, night sweats
Ask about urinary symptoms or any changes in urine colour (haematuria)
Ask about any history of trauma to the groin or testicle
Ask about sexual health history: any history of sexually transmitted infections
Ask about family history of testicular cancer or any cancer
Ask about history of undescended testis (already documented) and orchidopexy
Explore ideas, concerns, and expectations
Make a clinical diagnosis of suspected testicular cancer — urgent referral warranted

exampleExplanation:
*Liam, thank you for coming to see me, and I'm glad you noticed this and got in touch. I can hear that you're worried, and I want to be straightforward with you.*

*I'd like to arrange an urgent in-person examination. Based on what you've described — a hard, painless lump on the testicle itself, along with your history of an undescended testicle — I want to make sure we investigate this promptly. To do this, I will refer you today under a two-week-wait pathway, which means you should be seen within two weeks by a urology specialist.*

*They will arrange an ultrasound scan of the testicle, which is the best way to look at lumps in this area. They may also do some blood tests called tumour markers — these are substances that can sometimes be raised when certain types of testicular cancer are present.*

*I want to be honest with you: I cannot tell you at this stage whether this is cancer or not — only further tests can confirm that. What I can tell you is that even if it is, testicular cancer is one of the most treatable cancers there is, especially when caught early. The outcomes are excellent.*

*In the meantime, please try not to examine the lump repeatedly as this can cause discomfort. If you notice any rapid increase in size, sudden pain, or feel generally unwell, please contact us straightaway.*
management: Arrange an urgent face-to-face appointment to examine the testicle and check for groin lymphadenopathy
Refer urgently via the 2-week-wait pathway to urology for suspected testicular cancer
Inform the patient that the urologist will arrange a scrotal ultrasound and tumour marker blood tests (AFP, β-hCG, LDH)
Avoid fine-needle aspiration biopsy — this is contraindicated in suspected testicular cancer due to risk of seeding
Provide reassurance that testicular cancer, when detected early, has an excellent prognosis with high cure rates
Advise the patient not to repeatedly examine the lump
Safety-net: advise to seek urgent review if there is sudden increase in swelling, severe pain, or general deterioration
learningPoints:
**Testicular cancer** is the most common malignancy in men aged 15 to 45 and should be suspected in any young man presenting with a painless, hard testicular lump. Risk factors include **undescended testis (cryptorchidism)**, **family history**, and **contralateral testicular cancer**.

Key clinical features: painless hard testicular lump (most common), dull ache in lower abdomen or scrotum, backache or abdominal mass (lymph node metastases), and rarely, gynaecomastia (due to β-hCG secretion by tumour).

All patients with suspected testicular cancer must be referred urgently via the **2-week-wait pathway** to urology. **Do not perform fine-needle aspiration** as this risks tumour seeding. The investigation of choice is a **scrotal ultrasound**, supported by serum tumour markers: AFP, β-hCG, and LDH.

title: Requesting Antibiotics for a Cold

recentConsultation.notes: Patient booked routine telephone consultation to discuss concerns.

bloodTestResults.summary: eGFR 42 mL/min/1.73m² (CKD Stage 3). HbA1c and other bloods reviewed 3 months ago — within acceptable range.

patientStory:
You are Patricia Howells, a 59-year-old woman.

**Opening Statement:** *"Hi doctor, I've had a cold for the past few days and I'd really like some antibiotics to clear it up."*

If asked to elaborate: You have had a runny nose, nasal congestion, a sore throat, and a mild cough for the past 3 days. You feel tired and had some headache yesterday, but it has mostly resolved. No high temperature. No breathlessness or chest tightness. You are eating and drinking normally. No ear pain or discharge.

You have had colds before and noticed that antibiotics seemed to help 'speed up' your recovery in the past. Your daughter bought you some elderflower tea and zinc lozenges, but you feel they are not helping much.

**Social History:** You do not smoke. You drink about 4 units of alcohol a week. You live alone since your husband passed away 2 years ago. You enjoy gardening.

**Ideas:** You believe antibiotics will help you recover faster.

**Concerns:** You're concerned because of your diabetes and kidney condition, and you worry about getting seriously ill.

**Expectations:** You would like antibiotics to speed up your recovery.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about the onset and duration of symptoms
Ask about any fever, rigors, or feeling very unwell
Ask about throat pain, difficulty swallowing, or any pus visible at the back of the throat
Ask about ear pain or discharge
Ask about breathlessness, chest pain, or tight chest
Ask about the nature of the cough — is it productive? Is there any coloured sputum?
Ask about any symptoms of urinary tract infection — burning, frequency
Ask whether symptoms have been worsening or improving
Ask about diabetes management — has she been monitoring blood sugars?
Ask about how her symptoms are affecting daily life
Ask about previous antibiotic use and whether she was prescribed them for similar symptoms
Explore ideas, concerns, and expectations
Give a working diagnosis of viral upper respiratory tract infection (URTI)

exampleExplanation:
*Patricia, thank you for calling and for letting me know how you have been feeling. I completely understand why you want to feel better as quickly as possible, especially as you have your diabetes and kidney condition to think about.*

*From what you have described — a runny nose, sore throat, mild cough, and fatigue for 3 days, without a high fever or significant breathlessness — this really does sound like a viral cold. Antibiotics only work against bacteria, not viruses. So unfortunately, they will not help here, and they can actually cause side effects such as nausea, diarrhoea, or even thrush. What is more, using antibiotics when they are not needed can lead to antibiotic resistance, which is a growing problem for everyone.*

*I know that in the past, antibiotics may have seemed to help, but it is likely that you were recovering from the virus naturally at the same time and the antibiotics were not the cause of your improvement.*

*The best thing for a viral cold is rest, fluids, and simple painkillers like paracetamol. You can also use a saline nasal rinse or over-the-counter decongestant spray to help with the congestion. These are safe with your current medications.*

*I would like to reassure you that most people with a cold feel significantly better within 7 to 10 days. However, given your diabetes and kidney condition, if your symptoms worsen, if you develop a high fever, shortness of breath, or chest pain, please do not wait — contact us or call 111 straightaway.*
management: Reassure that the symptoms are consistent with a viral upper respiratory tract infection and that antibiotics are not indicated
Explain clearly why antibiotics are not prescribed: they treat bacteria, not viruses; they will not speed up recovery; they carry risks of side effects and antibiotic resistance
Advise self-care: adequate rest, increased oral fluid intake, paracetamol for discomfort or fever, saline nasal rinse, and over-the-counter decongestants if needed
Advise patient to monitor blood glucose levels, as infections can cause blood sugar to rise in diabetic patients
Advise the patient to temporarily hold her metformin if she stops eating or drinking properly, as it can accumulate in the setting of dehydration and CKD, increasing the risk of lactic acidosis
Signpost to NHS 111 online for self-care advice

Safety-net: advise the patient to seek urgent review if she develops a high fever, increasing breathlessness, chest pain, changes in urine output or colour, or feels significantly worse after day 7 of illness
learningPoints:
This case highlights the importance of **antimicrobial stewardship** — prescribing antibiotics only when clinically indicated, to reduce side effects, drug resistance, and unnecessary healthcare costs.

Upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs) are caused by viruses in the vast majority of cases and do not require antibiotics. GPs can use tools like the **FeverPAIN** or **Centor** criteria to assess the likelihood of bacterial tonsillitis when sore throat is a predominant feature.

A key prescribing safety point in this patient: **metformin should be withheld in patients with CKD who become unwell, dehydrated, or stop eating and drinking properly**, due to the risk of lactic acidosis. This is especially important when eGFR is already borderline, as in this case.

title: Perimenopause

patientData.name: Deborah Cartwright
drugHistory: Sumatriptan 50 mg — as needed for migraines

recentConsultation.notes: Patient booked routine telephone appointment to discuss concerns.

patientStory:
You are Deborah Cartwright, a 46-year-old female.

**Opening Statement:** *"Hi doctor, I've been having some hot flushes, and my periods have been a bit all over the place. I'm wondering if I'm going through the menopause?"*

If asked to elaborate: You have been experiencing hot flushes and night sweats for about three months. You sometimes wake up drenched in sweat at night. Your periods, which used to be regular (every 28 days), have become irregular over the past 6 months. They sometimes come every 3 weeks and sometimes every 6–7 weeks. The flow is heavier on some cycles.

You are sleeping very poorly and feel tired and irritable most days. Your mood has been quite low, and your concentration at work is suffering. You are also experiencing vaginal dryness and some discomfort during sex, which is affecting your relationship. Your memory feels worse than usual and you've been more forgetful.

**Social History:** You live with your partner. You have two adult children. You work as a HR manager. You do not smoke, drink about 6 units of alcohol per week. You exercise 3 times a week.

**Family History:** Your mother had a heart attack at age 62 and had osteoporosis.

**Ideas:** You think this might be the menopause or approaching it.

**Concerns:** You have heard that HRT increases the risk of cancer and would like to discuss whether it is safe for you.

**Expectations:** You want advice on whether HRT is appropriate and whether it is safe given your health history.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about vasomotor symptoms: hot flushes, frequency, severity, and whether they occur at night (night sweats)
Ask about menstrual cycle changes: frequency, flow, and whether periods have stopped
Ask about genitourinary symptoms: vaginal dryness, discomfort during sex, urinary symptoms
Ask about mood, anxiety, and cognitive symptoms (brain fog, memory changes, irritability)
Ask about sleep quality and impact on daily life
Ask about joint or muscle aches
Ask about cardiovascular risk factors: smoking, hypertension, diabetes, high cholesterol, or family history
Ask about bone health and risk factors for osteoporosis (family history, steroid use, low BMI)
Ask about history of migraines — type (with or without aura) and frequency
Ask about personal or family history of breast cancer or blood clots
Ask about contraception needs
Explore ideas, concerns, and expectations, especially anxiety about HRT
Make a clinical diagnosis of perimenopause

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you for sharing all of this, Deborah. From what you've described — the irregular periods, hot flushes, night sweats, sleep problems, mood changes, vaginal dryness, and memory difficulties — it does sound very much like you are going through the **perimenopause**. This is the transition phase leading up to the menopause, which is when your oestrogen levels are beginning to decline.*

*I know you have concerns about HRT, and I really appreciate that you have brought this up. The evidence around HRT has changed a lot in recent years, and the risk is much smaller than people have previously been led to believe.*

*Now, you mentioned you have migraines with aura. This is an important consideration because **combined HRT patches** — the type that contain both oestrogen and progestogen — can sometimes increase the risk of stroke in women with migraines with aura. For this reason, there is actually a safer way to give you HRT.*

*We can use a **transdermal oestrogen patch or gel** — oestrogen absorbed through the skin — which avoids the increased clot risk associated with oral oestrogen tablets. This is the preferred route for women with migraines with aura. You will also need a progestogen alongside it to protect the lining of the womb, and we would use a progesterone-only coil (Mirena) or oral micronised progesterone such as Utrogestan, as these are associated with a lower risk.*

*For the vaginal dryness and discomfort during sex, we can also prescribe local vaginal oestrogen in the form of a cream, gel, or pessary, which works locally and has very little absorption into the bloodstream.*

*Would it be helpful if I arranged a face-to-face appointment so we can go through everything more carefully, check your blood pressure, and start the right treatment for you?*
management: Diagnose perimenopause based on age and clinical history — investigations such as FSH are not routinely required in this age group
Offer HRT, explaining that it is the most effective treatment for perimenopausal symptoms and that risks are lower than often perceived
For this patient with migraines with aura, prescribe **transdermal oestrogen** (patch or gel) rather than oral oestrogen, to minimise stroke and VTE risk
Combine with either **Mirena IUS** (levonorgestrel-releasing coil) or **oral micronised progesterone (Utrogestan)** rather than synthetic progestogens, as these carry a lower breast cancer risk
Advise that local vaginal oestrogen (cream, pessary, or ring) can be prescribed for genitourinary symptoms and is safe even in women who cannot take systemic HRT
Discuss the risks and benefits of HRT individualised to her history: family history of cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis risk, migraines with aura
Advise on lifestyle measures: regular weight-bearing exercise, calcium-rich diet, vitamin D supplementation, limiting alcohol, and smoking cessation
Discuss contraceptive needs — women in perimenopause still require contraception until 2 years after the last period (under 50) or 1 year after the last period (over 50)
Arrange a face-to-face appointment for blood pressure check, BMI, and to initiate prescribing with informed consent
Offer follow-up in 3 months to review symptom control and tolerability of HRT
learningPoints:
**Perimenopause** is the transitional phase before menopause, characterised by hormonal fluctuations and irregular periods. Diagnosis is clinical in women over 45 — FSH testing is not routinely required.

For women with **migraines with aura**, combined oral HRT is associated with increased stroke risk and should be avoided. Instead, **transdermal oestrogen** (patch or gel) is preferred, as it bypasses first-pass hepatic metabolism and does not increase clotting risk.

For the progestogen component, **Mirena IUS** or **oral micronised progesterone (Utrogestan)** are associated with a lower breast cancer risk compared to older synthetic progestogens and are preferred in evidence-based practice.

**Local vaginal oestrogen** is safe, highly effective for genitourinary symptoms, and can be used even in women who cannot take systemic HRT.

title: New Diagnosis of Parkinson's Disease

patientData.name: Gerald Watkins
pastMedicalHistory: Parkinson's disease — newly diagnosed by neurology
drugHistory: Ropinirole 0.25 mg three times daily (newly initiated by neurology)

recentConsultation.notes:
Thank you for referring Mr Watkins. Having reviewed this gentleman, the clinical picture and examination are consistent with a diagnosis of Parkinson's disease. He demonstrates the classical triad of resting tremor, bradykinesia, and cogwheel rigidity, most notably on the right side.

I have commenced ropinirole (dopamine agonist) at a low dose (0.25 mg three times daily) with a plan to gradually titrate upward as tolerated.

Please note that this medication may be associated with impulse control disorders. Mr Watkins was counselled at our review.

I have arranged follow-up in four months. Should there be any concern regarding his driving, the DVLA should be notified. The patient was also signposted to Parkinson's UK.

Patient booked routine video consultation to discuss concerns.

patientStory:
You are Gerald Watkins, a 67-year-old man.

**Opening Statement:** *"Doctor, I've just been told I have Parkinson's disease and I don't fully understand what that means for my future."*

If asked to elaborate: You were recently seen by a neurologist and have been told you have Parkinson's disease. You have been started on a new medication called ropinirole. You feel overwhelmed by the diagnosis. You have noticed your hand trembling when you are at rest, and you have been feeling stiff and slow when getting up in the morning.

You are worried about how this will affect your independence, particularly as you still drive and have an active social life. You are retired but enjoy socialising, and you walk your dog twice a day.

You haven't told your wife yet because you don't want to worry her.

**Social History:** You are retired (former accountant). You live with your wife. You do not smoke or drink alcohol. You have a son who lives nearby.

**Ideas:** You are not sure what Parkinson's means long term.

**Concerns:** You are worried about losing your independence, especially your driving. You are also worried about becoming a burden to your family.

**Expectations:** You want the doctor to explain what Parkinson's is, what to expect, and how to manage day to day.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask how long he has been experiencing symptoms and what changes he has noticed
Ask about the main symptoms he is aware of: tremor, stiffness, slowness of movement
Ask about falls or balance problems
Ask about speech changes — softer voice or slurred speech
Ask about sleep problems, such as vivid dreams or acting out dreams (REM sleep behaviour disorder)
Ask about cognitive symptoms: memory, concentration
Ask about mood — depression and anxiety are common in Parkinson's
Ask about any urinary or bowel problems
Ask about how symptoms affect activities of daily living: dressing, eating, walking
Ask about driving — whether symptoms have affected his driving, and whether he is aware of the DVLA notification requirement
Ask about social and emotional support at home
Ask about his understanding of ropinirole and any side effects he may have noticed
Explore ideas, concerns, and expectations

exampleExplanation:
*Gerald, thank you for coming in today and for sharing how you've been feeling. I can only imagine how overwhelming it must feel to receive this news, and I want to make sure you leave today feeling better informed and supported.*

*Parkinson's disease is a long-term condition that affects parts of the brain involved in controlling movement. It tends to progress slowly, and many people live well with it for years, especially with the right treatment and support. The tremor, stiffness, and slowness you've noticed are the classic early signs.*

*The medication you've been started on, ropinirole, is a type called a dopamine agonist. It helps replace some of the dopamine that your brain is no longer producing as much of. It is started at a low dose and increased gradually. I want to make sure you're aware of a potential side effect, which the neurologist will have mentioned — this medication can occasionally cause what we call impulse control disorders. This might look like an unusual urge to gamble, shop, eat, or increased sexual interest. These are uncommon, but important to flag if they arise, as we can adjust the medication.*

*On the subject of driving — I know this is important to you. You do need to inform the DVLA that you have been diagnosed with Parkinson's. This doesn't necessarily mean you have to stop driving — the DVLA will review your case and may ask for a medical report. In the meantime, as long as your symptoms are not affecting your ability to drive safely, you can continue.*

*I would strongly encourage you to tell your wife. I understand you are trying to protect her, but a diagnosis like this is easier to manage with the support of those closest to you. We can also offer you both a referral to the Parkinson's nurse specialist and to Parkinson's UK, which is an excellent source of information and support.*

*Exercise — like the dog walking you already do — is really helpful in Parkinson's. Physiotherapy and speech and language therapy can also be beneficial as things progress.*
management: Explain Parkinson's disease in clear, accessible language — emphasise that it is manageable and that many people live well with it
Reinforce the neurologist's explanation of ropinirole: mechanism (dopamine agonist), titration plan, and importance of taking it regularly
Warn about impulse control disorders as a side effect of dopamine agonists and advise the patient and family to report any unusual behaviours
Advise the patient to **notify the DVLA** of his Parkinson's diagnosis — he may continue driving if safe to do so, but the DVLA must make a formal assessment
Encourage him to disclose the diagnosis to his wife and family, explaining that support from loved ones is vital
Offer referral to a **Parkinson's Disease Nurse Specialist** for ongoing support, monitoring, and medication management
Offer referral to **physiotherapy** to support mobility, balance, and exercise planning
Offer referral to **speech and language therapy** if speech, voice, or swallowing concerns develop
Signpost to **Parkinson's UK** for patient information, peer support groups, and helpline
Screen for depression — depression is common in Parkinson's; use PHQ-9 if indicated
Arrange a follow-up appointment in 4 weeks or sooner if new symptoms arise
learningPoints:
**Parkinson's disease (PD)** is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by dopaminergic neuron loss in the substantia nigra. Classical features include **resting tremor**, **bradykinesia**, and **rigidity**, often with **postural instability** in later stages.

**Management in primary care** involves: medication review and monitoring (ropinirole, levodopa, or other agents initiated by neurology), monitoring for side effects — particularly **impulse control disorders** with dopamine agonists, signposting to Parkinson's UK and specialist nursing, and multidisciplinary input (physiotherapy, SALT, OT).

**DVLA notification** is mandatory. Patients must inform the DVLA of any diagnosis of Parkinson's disease. The DVLA will then assess fitness to drive — this does not automatically mean driving must stop, but failure to notify is illegal.

title: Domestic Abuse

patientData.name: Samira Rashid
pastMedicalHistory: Recurrent abdominal pain and headaches (multiple consultations, no organic cause found)

recentConsultation.seenBy: Dr Georgina Lambert (Clinical Practitioner) — 3 weeks ago
recentConsultation.notes: Patient attended for headaches and lower abdominal pain. Physical examination was unremarkable. Full blood count, CRP, TFTs all normal. Urine dipstick: normal. Advised to return if symptoms persist.

bloodTestResults.summary: FBC, CRP, TFTs all normal. No blood tests outstanding.

patientStory:
You are Samira Rashid, a 29-year-old woman.

**Opening Statement:** *"Hi doctor, I've been having these headaches and stomach pains again. I know I came in last time for the same thing."*

If asked: You feel stressed and tense most of the time. Things at home have not been great. You are married and have a 3-year-old son together.

If the doctor is sensitive and builds rapport and asks directly about your home situation or safety: Your husband has been controlling and aggressive lately. He monitors your phone, controls where you go, and shouts at you in front of your son. Last week, he shoved you against the wall during an argument, and you hit your shoulder. You have not told anyone until now.

You are scared. You are worried about your son. You do not know what to do or where to go. You do not want to be separated from your son.

If asked if you feel safe at home: Hesitate and say "I'm not sure". If the doctor gently presses or offers a safe space to talk, disclose that you do not feel safe.

**Social History:** You moved to the UK 3 years ago from Pakistan when you got married. You live with your husband and son. You have no family in the UK. You are not working. You do not smoke or drink alcohol.

**Ideas:** You think your pain is from stress.

**Concerns:** You are afraid of what your husband might do if he finds out you have spoken to a doctor about him.

**Expectations:** You would like some help with the pain, but you are also quietly hoping someone will notice that something else is wrong.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about the headaches and abdominal pain — onset, severity, and any associated symptoms
Explore psychosocial factors — how things are at home and how the patient is feeling in herself
Create a safe, non-judgemental environment before asking about the relationship
Use a direct, sensitive question to ask about safety at home, e.g. 'Sometimes symptoms like these can be related to stress or difficult situations at home — how are things at home for you?'
If domestic abuse is disclosed, ask how long it has been happening and what form it takes (physical, emotional, financial, coercive control)
Ask about any physical injuries — when and how they occurred
Ask about the child — whether the child has been harmed, witnessed the violence, or is otherwise affected
Ask about her support network — does she have family or friends nearby?
Ask about immigration status and whether she has leave to remain
Ask about her safety now — is she safe at home today?
Ask about her wishes — what does she want to happen?
Document everything carefully

exampleExplanation:
*Samira, I want to thank you for trusting me with this today. It takes real courage to speak up, and I want you to know that everything you share with me here is confidential, unless we have serious concerns about your safety or your son's safety.*

*What you've described — your husband pushing you against a wall, controlling your phone and movements, shouting at you and your son — is domestic abuse. This is not your fault, and you do not deserve this.*

*You are not alone, and there is support available to you. I would like to refer you to IRIS, which is a specialist domestic abuse service that works closely with GP practices like ours. They can provide confidential advice, support, and safety planning, and they work with interpreters if needed.*

*I am also going to document what you have told me today in your medical records. This is important because if you ever need evidence in the future — whether for a legal case or to support an application for housing or benefits — this documentation can help.*

*I also need to ask you about your son. You mentioned he has witnessed some of what has happened. I want to be honest with you — because there is a child involved, we have a responsibility to think about his safety as well. I would like to consider making a safeguarding referral to children's social care, and I want to talk through what that means so it doesn't come as a surprise.*

*Most importantly, Samira, your safety comes first. If you are ever in immediate danger, please call 999. The national domestic abuse helpline number is 0808 2000 247, and it is free and available 24 hours a day.*

*Would it be okay if we met again in person very soon — within the next few days — so we can talk more and put a plan together?*
management: Acknowledge and validate the patient's experience; make it clear that what she is experiencing is domestic abuse and that it is not her fault
Ask directly about safety at home — use the CAADA-DASH risk assessment tool if trained to do so
Refer to the IRIS (Identification and Referral to Improve Safety) programme, or equivalent local domestic violence service
Provide the national domestic abuse helpline number: 0808 2000 247 (free, 24 hours)
Make a safeguarding referral to children's social care given that a 3-year-old child is in the household and witnessing abuse
Document all disclosures accurately and sensitively in the medical records, as this may be used as evidence in future legal proceedings
Explore any concerns around immigration status and signpost to relevant legal support services if appropriate
Advise that if she is in immediate danger, she should call 999
Offer a face-to-face appointment within a few days to continue the conversation, complete a safety plan, and provide ongoing support
Do not contact the perpetrator or disclose information to him under any circumstances
learningPoints:
**Domestic abuse** is a pattern of controlling, coercive, threatening, or violent behaviour by an intimate partner. It includes physical, emotional, sexual, financial, and psychological abuse. It is estimated that 1 in 4 women will experience domestic abuse in their lifetime.

GPs play a crucial role in **identifying domestic abuse** — often the only healthcare professional patients see. Key clinical features include: **recurrent unexplained physical symptoms**, frequent attendance with no clear diagnosis, depression and anxiety, and inconsistency in explanations of injuries.

Ask directly but sensitively. Use simple, open-ended questions such as: *"Sometimes when people are feeling stressed, there can be difficulties at home — is that something you'd be comfortable talking about?"* Creating a safe, private environment is essential.

**Safeguarding children** is a mandatory consideration when children are present in an abusive household. Even if the child has not been directly harmed, witnessing abuse is harmful and constitutes a safeguarding concern.

title: Post-Operative Complications

patientData.name: Nigel Cromwell
pastMedicalHistory: Right inguinal hernia repair (open mesh repair, 5 days ago)
drugHistory: Co-codamol 30/500 mg — 1–2 tablets up to four times a day for post-operative pain
Lactulose 15 mL twice daily — to prevent opioid-induced constipation

recentConsultation.seenBy: Mr Stuart Walsh (Consultant General Surgeon) — 5 days ago (discharge from day surgery)
recentConsultation.notes: Discharge from Day Surgery Unit after right inguinal hernia repair (open mesh technique) performed under general anaesthesia. Procedure was uneventful. Post-operatively stable. Discharged with analgesia and wound care instructions. Follow-up: 4–6 weeks post-op in outpatient clinic. Patient booked urgent telephone appointment to discuss post-op concerns.

patientStory:
You are Nigel Cromwell, a 52-year-old male.

**Opening Statement:** *"Hi doctor, I had a hernia repair 5 days ago and I'm getting quite worried. There's some swelling and it feels quite warm and tender around the wound area."*

If asked to elaborate: The swelling started around the wound yesterday. The area feels warm to touch, and when you pressed on it this morning, there was a small amount of yellowish discharge. You have had a temperature (you felt hot and shivery last night). You are still in pain around the wound, which has not improved much from when you left hospital.

You are walking short distances but struggle with anything more than that. You have not had any problems with your waterworks or bowels. You had your first bowel movement today (soft stool). You are eating and drinking. You do not have any chest pain or breathlessness.

**Social History:** You live with your wife, who has been caring for you since the operation. You work as a site manager. You do not smoke. You drink about 15 units of alcohol per week.

**Ideas:** You think the wound might be infected.

**Concerns:** You are worried about needing to go back to hospital.

**Expectations:** You would like advice on what to do next.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about the nature of the symptoms: swelling, redness, warmth, pain, and any discharge
Ask about any change in the character or colour of the discharge (clear, yellow, green, or bloody)
Ask about fever, chills, and general feeling of being unwell
Ask about whether the wound has changed in appearance since discharge (opened up, increased in size)
Ask about pain management — is the analgesia controlling the pain adequately?
Ask about bowel function — any constipation, diarrhoea, or pain on defecation
Ask about urinary symptoms
Ask about whether there is any hardening, bulge, or lump near the wound or groin area (to rule out haematoma or recurrence)
Ask about any breathlessness or leg pain (to screen for pulmonary embolism or DVT after surgery)
Ask about mobility and activity since discharge
Ask about alcohol consumption — this is relevant as it can impair wound healing
Explore his ideas, concerns, and expectations

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you for calling, Nigel, and I'm glad you got in touch. From what you've described — redness, warmth, discharge, and a fever following your hernia repair — I'm concerned that your wound may be showing signs of infection. This is something we do need to review in person today.*

*I'd like you to come in this afternoon so I can examine the wound properly. Depending on what I find, you may need a course of antibiotics, and in some cases where there is a collection of fluid or pus, the wound may need to be opened and cleaned. If I have any concerns about how serious this looks, I would contact the surgical team.*

*In the meantime, try to keep the wound clean and dry. If you have any wound dressings, leave them in place until we see you. If you feel significantly worse before the appointment — for example, you develop a high fever above 38.5°C, the wound becomes more swollen or very painful, or you feel very unwell — please call 999 or go directly to A&E.*

*I also want to gently mention — alcohol can interfere with wound healing and with how your medications work, so it would be wise to avoid it completely while you are recovering.*
management: Arrange a face-to-face appointment today to examine the wound and assess for signs of infection (redness, warmth, discharge, pus, wound dehiscence)
If wound infection is confirmed, prescribe antibiotics based on local guidelines (e.g. co-amoxiclav or flucloxacillin as first line for post-operative wound infections)
If a collection or abscess is suspected, refer back to the surgical team for incision and drainage
If there is wound dehiscence or other serious post-operative complication, arrange urgent surgical review
Advise to continue with co-codamol and ensure adequate analgesia at home
Review laxative management — constipation post-operatively and on opioid analgesia is common; ensure he has adequate laxative cover
Advise on wound care: keep clean and dry, no baths until healed
Advise on avoiding heavy lifting and strenuous activity until cleared by the surgeon at follow-up
Gently advise on reducing alcohol intake to support wound healing and medication effectiveness
Safety-net: advise to attend A&E if he develops high fever, significant wound opening, or systemic deterioration
learningPoints:
This case highlights the importance of recognising **post-operative wound infection**, one of the most common surgical complications managed in primary care. Signs of wound infection include localised erythema, warmth, oedema, purulent discharge, and fever.

Risk factors for wound infection include: obesity, diabetes, smoking, poor nutritional status, prolonged surgery, and use of mesh (as in hernia repair).

Post-operative DVT and PE should always be considered following any surgical procedure. Screen for leg pain, swelling, or breathlessness and refer urgently if suspected.

Nurse-led wound clinics in primary care play an important role in managing post-operative wound care and identifying early complications.

title: Eating Disorders

recentConsultation.notes: No significant previous consultations. Patient booked routine video consultation to discuss concerns.

patientStory:
You are Holly Marshall, a 17-year-old female.

**Opening Statement:** *"Doctor, I've not been eating properly for quite a few months now and I'm worried about my health."*

If asked to elaborate: Over the past seven months, you have been restricting what you eat very significantly. You skip meals, count calories obsessively, and avoid anything high in fat or sugar. You eat as little as possible most days — sometimes only a handful of crackers and some plain yoghurt in the whole day. You feel very anxious after eating, even small amounts, and feel like you have failed if you eat anything 'bad'. You currently weigh 45 kg and are 165 cm tall (BMI approximately 16.5 kg/m²).

You have not had a period for 5 months. You feel exhausted all the time, cold, dizzy when you stand up, and sometimes your heart feels like it's racing.

You are terrified of gaining weight. Even though people around you say you look thin, you still feel fat when you look in the mirror. You have not told your parents because you don't want to worry them. You have been trying to handle this yourself but feel that you are losing control.

**Social History:** You live with your parents and younger brother. You are in Year 12. You work hard at school and are very academically focused. You have friends but spend less time with them recently. You do not smoke, drink alcohol, or use drugs.

**Ideas:** You know something is wrong but feel scared about admitting it and scared of treatment.

**Concerns:** You're worried about your health but terrified of being told to eat more or gain weight.

**Expectations:** You want to understand what is happening to your body but are ambivalent about treatment.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about the onset and duration of changes in eating behaviour
Ask what her typical daily diet currently looks like
Ask about food avoidance, calorie counting, or fear of certain foods
Ask about compensatory behaviours: purging (induced vomiting), laxative use, excessive exercise
Ask about menstrual history — including when her periods stopped
Ask about physical symptoms related to malnutrition: fatigue, dizziness or fainting, cold intolerance, palpitations, hair loss, dental problems
Ask about body image: how she sees herself in the mirror versus how others see her
Ask about mood, anxiety levels, and any history of self-harm or suicidal ideation
Ask if she has told anyone about this — parents, school, friends
Ask about school performance and social life
Ask about her understanding of what is happening and her thoughts about treatment
Explore ideas, concerns, and expectations
Make a working diagnosis of anorexia nervosa

exampleExplanation:
*Holly, thank you for having the courage to speak up today. I can hear how much you've been carrying alone, and I'm really glad you reached out.*

*From what you've told me, I'm concerned that what you're experiencing is an eating disorder called **anorexia nervosa**. I want to explain that carefully, because I know the word 'eating disorder' can feel frightening or feel like a label. What it means is that your thoughts about food and your body have become very distressing and are now having a serious impact on your health.*

*Your body is showing signs that it isn't getting enough energy and nutrition — the dizziness, the missed periods, the cold, the tiredness, and the palpitations are all signals that your body is under strain. These are things we need to take seriously.*

*I understand that you're scared of gaining weight, and that the idea of eating more feels overwhelming. Those feelings are a part of the condition — it's not a personality flaw or a choice. It's something we can treat, and many young people do recover with the right support.*

*I would like to involve your parents in this — not to get you in trouble, but because you deserve to have people around you who know what's happening and can support you. I would also like to refer you urgently to our specialist CAMHS eating disorder team, who are experienced in exactly this kind of situation.*

*In the meantime, I'd like to see you in person today or tomorrow to check your weight, blood pressure, heart, and do some blood tests to make sure you are safe from a medical point of view.*
management: Acknowledge the patient's courage in seeking help and validate that this is hard to talk about
Explain the diagnosis of likely anorexia nervosa in a sensitive and non-judgemental way
Arrange an urgent face-to-face appointment to assess physical safety: weight, BP (including lying and standing for postural hypotension), heart rate, peripheral temperature, and hydration
Arrange blood tests to assess for medical complications: FBC, U&Es (hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia), glucose, LFTs, TFTs, magnesium, phosphate, albumin, and ECG if indicated
Refer urgently to CAMHS (Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services) eating disorder team
Consider involving parents — as a 17-year-old, she is Gillick competent and can consent to or refuse treatment, but parental support is strongly encouraged and generally beneficial
Explain that while the CAMHS team will guide treatment, the GP should remain closely involved in monitoring physical health

Safety-net: if she develops signs of serious medical instability (fainting, severe electrolyte abnormalities, dangerous bradycardia, BMI below 13, or refeeding syndrome risk), she must be admitted to hospital
Offer follow-up within the week to review results and ensure the CAMHS referral is progressing
learningPoints:
**Anorexia nervosa** carries the highest mortality rate of any psychiatric condition, making **early identification and urgent referral** critical. GPs must be vigilant for warning signs including amenorrhoea, weight loss, food restriction, and distorted body image.

Physical complications include **electrolyte disturbances (hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, hypophosphataemia)**, bradycardia, prolonged QT interval, renal impairment, and bone loss.

**Refeeding syndrome** is a dangerous complication when nutrition is reintroduced too quickly after starvation. It causes dangerous electrolyte shifts (especially hypophosphataemia) and can be life-threatening.

For under-18s, refer to **CAMHS** eating disorder team. For adults, refer to adult eating disorder services. For patients aged 16–18 with capacity, NICE guidance emphasises the importance of **collaborative working** with the young person and, where appropriate, their families.

title: Safeguarding an Elderly Patient (Neglect)

patientData.name: Gertrude Blackwell (caller: Gary Blackwell, her son)
pastMedicalHistory: Previous left hip fracture — surgical repair 2 years ago
drugHistory: Calcichew D3 500 mg/200 IU once daily

recentConsultation.notes: Home visit for routine dressing change (pressure sore, left heel). Wound healing slowly. Patient appears unkempt and environment noted to be unclean. Carer (paid carer who attends twice daily) has been inconsistent with attendance according to neighbour report. Raised concerns informally with GP but no formal action taken.

bloodTestResults.summary: HbA1c 63 mmol/mol (suboptimal glycaemic control). Vitamin D 28 nmol/L (insufficient).

rows.referenceRange: Target <53 mmol/mol in older adults with dementia

patientStory:
You are Gary Blackwell, the son of Gertrude Blackwell. You live 2 hours away and visit every couple of months.

**Opening Statement:** *"Hi doctor, I went to visit my mum last weekend and I'm really worried about what I found."*

If asked to elaborate: When you arrived at your mother's home, you found her sitting in a chair in soiled clothing. She had not been washed. The fridge was mostly empty. There were no clean dishes. She was confused and did not recognise you at first.

You discovered that the paid carer, who is supposed to come twice a day, has apparently only been coming once or sometimes not at all. A neighbour told you this. You are also worried because you have noticed bruising on her left upper arm that you cannot explain.

Your mum was confused and could not tell you what had happened. She did say she had been lonely and scared at night.

**Social History:** She lives alone in a council flat. She has not left the flat independently for several months. She has no other family besides you.

**Ideas:** You are concerned something is wrong with her care.

**Concerns:** You are worried she is being neglected, and possibly harmed, by the carer.

**Expectations:** You want the doctor to take action to ensure your mother is safe.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask the son to describe exactly what he found when he arrived — condition of the home, patient's hygiene, and food availability
Ask about the bruising: location, size, how it was noticed, and whether the patient was able to explain it
Ask about the current care package: how many times per day the carer is supposed to come, and how often they have actually been attending
Ask how long these concerns have been building and whether the son has raised them before
Ask whether there has been a formal assessment of his mother's care needs recently
Ask if there is any known family conflict or financial concerns around his mother's assets
Ask about the patient's mental capacity: does she have dementia, and is she able to make decisions for herself?
Ask if there is a formal Power of Attorney in place
Ask whether the district nurse or any other professional has raised concerns previously
Explore ideas, concerns, and expectations

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you for calling today, Gary, and for being so open about what you found. I can hear how worried you are, and I want you to know that you have done absolutely the right thing by contacting us. What you are describing raises very serious concerns about your mother's safety and welfare, and we need to act on these today.*

*What you have described — finding your mother in soiled clothing, without food in the house, with an unexplained bruise, and a carer who is not consistently attending — are serious indicators of neglect and possible physical abuse. This is a safeguarding situation.*

*I will be raising this with our safeguarding team and making an urgent referral to Adult Social Care. They will arrange an emergency assessment of your mother's needs and safety, which may include arranging alternative care, reviewing the care package, and potentially suspending or investigating the current carer.*

*The unexplained bruising is particularly concerning, and as part of the safeguarding process, this will be reported to the police as well, so that they can investigate whether a crime has taken place. You are not being asked to do this yourself — we will handle the referral.*

*I would also like to arrange a home visit from the GP or district nurse as soon as possible to assess your mum's physical condition, including the bruise, her pressure sore, and her general health.*

*Gary, in the meantime, if you are able to stay with your mother or arrange for someone to be with her until the emergency team can respond, that would be very helpful.*
management: Acknowledge the son's concerns and validate them as a serious safeguarding matter
Raise an urgent safeguarding alert and make a referral to Adult Social Care for an emergency welfare assessment
Report the unexplained bruising to the police as it may constitute elder abuse
Arrange an urgent home visit by the GP or district nurse to assess Gertrude's physical condition, including examination of the bruise, pressure sore, nutrition, hydration, and mental state
Review and update the care package as a matter of urgency, in collaboration with Adult Social Care
Consider whether an emergency placement or alternative care arrangement is needed while the situation is investigated
Involve the safeguarding lead at the GP practice and document all actions, concerns, and decisions clearly
Review medication appropriateness in the context of her current condition and cognitive decline
Ensure Advance Care Planning and DNACPR discussions are updated where appropriate
Advise Gary to stay with his mother or ensure someone is present with her until emergency care arrangements are in place
learningPoints:
This station highlights the importance of recognising and acting on **elder abuse and neglect**. Types of elder abuse include physical, emotional, financial, and sexual abuse, as well as neglect — intentional or unintentional failure to provide basic needs.

Any concern about an adult at risk of abuse or neglect must trigger a **safeguarding alert** to the local authority Adult Safeguarding team. This applies even when the patient cannot consent to the referral (e.g. due to dementia), as the duty to safeguard overrides confidentiality in these circumstances.

**Signs of elder neglect** include poor hygiene, malnourishment, dehydration, untreated medical conditions, and unsafe living conditions. Unexplained bruises must always raise suspicion of physical abuse and should prompt referral to both Adult Social Care and the police.

title: Chronic Fatigue Syndrome

patientData.name: Rachel Summers
pastMedicalHistory: Anxiety (previously managed with CBT, no current medication)

recentConsultation.seenBy: Dr Priya Malhotra (Clinical Practitioner) — 4 weeks ago
recentConsultation.notes: Patient attended reporting persistent fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive difficulties, and post-exertional malaise lasting more than 6 months following glandular fever. Bloods reviewed: FBC, U&Es, LFTs, TFTs, HbA1c, ferritin, vitamin D, B12 — all normal. Referred to ME/CFS specialist service. Patient booked follow-up video consultation to discuss current management and concerns.

bloodTestResults.summary: All routine bloods normal — no organic cause identified.

patientStory:
You are Rachel Summers, a 35-year-old woman.

**Opening Statement:** *"Doctor, I'm still exhausted all the time. It's been over 6 months now. I'm not getting any better and I don't know what to do."*

If asked to elaborate: You had glandular fever 6 months ago and have never fully recovered. You feel exhausted even after a full night's sleep. The fatigue is not relieved by rest. Your sleep is unrefreshing — you go to bed tired and wake up just as tired.

You have significant brain fog: you struggle to remember words mid-sentence, cannot concentrate for more than 20 minutes, and feel mentally drained by the end of even a simple task. After any physical or mental activity — even short walks or a phone call — you feel dramatically worse for 1–3 days. This is the worst part for you, as it means you have to be very careful about doing anything.

You have had to reduce your working hours from full-time to 2 days a week and even that is a struggle. You were previously very active — you used to run regularly — but any attempt at exercise now causes a crash. Your social life has become almost non-existent. You feel very isolated and low in mood at times, but you do not feel depressed in the classic sense — you still enjoy things when you have enough energy.

**Social History:** You live with your partner, who is supportive. You work as a graphic designer. You do not smoke or drink alcohol.

**Ideas:** You believe you have ME/CFS and have been reading extensively about it.

**Concerns:** You are worried about being told to push through or exercise harder, as this makes you significantly worse.

**Expectations:** You want to be validated in your diagnosis and understand what support is available.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about the onset and course of fatigue — did it begin following an infection?
Ask about the nature of fatigue — constant, worse after activity, unrefreshing sleep
Ask specifically about post-exertional malaise (PEM) — worsening of symptoms after physical or mental exertion, lasting 12–72 hours or longer
Ask about cognitive symptoms: brain fog, difficulty concentrating, memory problems
Ask about sleep quality — whether sleep is restorative or unrefreshing
Ask about autonomic symptoms: dizziness on standing, palpitations (to assess for postural tachycardia syndrome, which can co-exist with ME/CFS)
Ask about pain: headaches, muscle or joint pain
Ask about mood and whether she has depressive symptoms or anxiety
Ask about how symptoms are affecting work, social life, and daily activities
Ask if she has noticed any triggers or patterns in when symptoms are worse
Ask about any prior treatments attempted and whether they have helped or worsened symptoms
Explore ideas, concerns, and expectations
Confirm a working diagnosis of ME/CFS

exampleExplanation:
*Rachel, thank you for coming back and for explaining everything so clearly. I want to start by saying — I believe you. What you are describing is real, and it has a name: Myalgic Encephalomyelitis, also known as ME, or Chronic Fatigue Syndrome.*

*ME/CFS is a recognised medical condition — not something that is 'just in your head'. It can follow an infection like glandular fever, as it has done in your case, and it causes exactly the symptoms you have described: debilitating fatigue that is not relieved by rest, unrefreshing sleep, brain fog, and post-exertional malaise — that crash you experience after any kind of effort. You were absolutely right to highlight that, and I want to reassure you: **we do not recommend pushing through or graded exercise therapy (GET)**. That approach is no longer recommended for ME/CFS, because evidence shows it can cause harm by worsening PEM.*

*What we do recommend is something called **pacing** — learning to work within your available energy limits, avoiding doing too much on good days, and building in rest before you reach exhaustion. Many people find it helpful to keep a diary of activities and symptoms to identify patterns.*

*I have already referred you to the ME/CFS specialist service, and I hope to hear back from them soon. In the meantime, we can support you here in general practice. I would like to refer you to our social prescriber, who can help explore any financial support you may be entitled to given your reduced hours, and also look at what community support groups might be available.*

*For the brain fog and difficulty concentrating, some people find occupational therapy input helpful — they can advise on pacing, activity management, and adjustments at work.*

*If your mood becomes more of a concern at any point, we can also explore support for that separately.*

*I know how isolating this condition can feel. Please know that we are here to support you, and I would like to check in with you again in 4 weeks.*
management: Validate the diagnosis of ME/CFS; explain that it is a recognised medical condition and not a psychological or fabricated illness
Clarify that **graded exercise therapy (GET) is no longer recommended** for ME/CFS — it is not on the current NICE guideline and can worsen post-exertional malaise
Explain pacing as the cornerstone of self-management: staying within energy limits, building in rest, and avoiding the boom-bust cycle
Confirm that referral to the ME/CFS specialist service has been made; follow up if not yet received an appointment
Offer referral to occupational therapy for pacing, energy management, and work adjustments
Offer referral to a social prescriber for support with financial entitlements (e.g. PIP, ESA) and community resources
Signpost to the ME Association and Action for ME for peer support and self-management resources
Screen for depression and anxiety; treat if indicated, but do not conflate ME/CFS with a purely psychological condition
Offer symptomatic treatment where appropriate (e.g. paracetamol for pain, sleep hygiene advice for unrefreshing sleep)
Arrange follow-up in 4 weeks to review progress and ensure specialist service contact has been made
learningPoints:
**ME/CFS (Myalgic Encephalomyelitis / Chronic Fatigue Syndrome)** is a complex, multisystem condition characterised by: profound fatigue not relieved by rest, **post-exertional malaise (PEM)** — worsening of symptoms after physical or cognitive exertion, unrefreshing sleep, and cognitive difficulties ('brain fog').

The **2021 NICE guideline** on ME/CFS made significant changes to recommended care. Most notably, **graded exercise therapy (GET) is no longer recommended**, as it can exacerbate symptoms. The focus is now on **energy management and pacing**.

**Post-exertional malaise** is the hallmark feature of ME/CFS and must be carefully explained to patients. Any activity — physical or cognitive — can trigger a significant worsening of symptoms lasting days or weeks. Patients must learn to stay within their 'energy envelope' to avoid repeated crashes.

title: Medication Overuse Headache

patientData.name: Wendy Charlton
drugHistory: Sumatriptan 50 mg — as needed for migraines (using frequently)
Ibuprofen 400 mg — as needed for headaches (using frequently)

recentConsultation.seenBy: Dr Susan Flanagan (Clinical Practitioner) — 3 months ago
recentConsultation.notes: Migraine review. Patient taking sumatriptan and ibuprofen frequently. Headache diary not maintained. No neurological symptoms or red flags. BP 132/84 mmHg. Plan: Continue current medications. Offered headache diary. Follow-up in 3 months.

bloodTestResults.summary: No blood tests outstanding. BP 132/84 mmHg at last review.

patientStory:
You are Wendy Charlton, a 44-year-old woman.

**Opening Statement:** *"Doctor, my headaches have become almost daily over the past 3 months. Nothing seems to work anymore. I've been taking tablets practically every day."*

If asked to elaborate: You have had migraines since your twenties, but they used to come about once a fortnight. Over the past 3 months, your headaches have become almost daily. They are different from your usual migraines — less severe, more like a dull, constant ache that is always there. When you take ibuprofen or sumatriptan they give temporary relief, but the headache comes back within a few hours. You have been taking sumatriptan or ibuprofen, or both, almost every day.

You have no new neurological symptoms — no weakness, no vision changes (other than your usual aura), no sudden onset thunderclap headache. The headaches are not worse in the morning or when you cough. You feel generally well.

**Social History:** You work as a secondary school librarian. You live with your husband and teenage son. You do not smoke. You drink about 8 units of alcohol per week. You have recently been under stress at work due to redundancies.

**Ideas:** You think your migraine medication has stopped working.

**Concerns:** You are worried something more serious is causing the daily headaches.

**Expectations:** You would like stronger medication to control the headaches.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about the frequency, character, and severity of the headaches
Ask how many days per week she is taking analgesics or triptans
Clarify whether the headaches feel different from her usual migraines
Ask about associated symptoms: nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, visual aura

Ask about red flag symptoms: sudden onset (thunderclap), associated neurological symptoms (weakness, speech problems, double vision), worsening with coughing or bending, new onset in patient over 50, or change in pattern
Ask about morning headaches or those worse on waking (to screen for raised intracranial pressure)
Ask about sleep quality and any recent changes in stress levels
Ask about caffeine intake (coffee, tea, energy drinks)
Ask about alcohol and smoking
Ask about menstrual cycle and whether headaches have any pattern around her periods
Review all current analgesic and triptan use — frequency and quantity
Explore ideas, concerns, and expectations
Make a working diagnosis of medication overuse headache

exampleExplanation:
*Wendy, thank you for explaining this so clearly. From what you've described — daily headaches, a change in the character from your usual migraines, and using painkillers or sumatriptan almost every day — I think I know what is happening, and I want to explain it to you.*

*This is something we call **medication overuse headache**, sometimes known as a rebound headache. It is actually quite a common condition, especially in people with migraine. What happens is that when pain relief is taken on more than around 10 to 15 days a month, it actually begins to change how the brain processes pain signals. Over time, instead of preventing headaches, the medications start causing a new type of daily headache — and then taking more medication gives brief relief but triggers the cycle again.*

*I know this is frustrating, especially as you've been taking the medication because you've been in pain. The most important step to breaking this cycle is to gradually stop or significantly reduce the overused medication.*

*I would suggest we start by stopping the ibuprofen first. I know that might feel daunting. Over the first 2 to 4 weeks, the headaches will likely get worse before they get better — this is the withdrawal phase. But for most people, within 4 to 8 weeks they see a significant improvement. I'd like to support you closely during this time.*

*Once we have withdrawn the overused medications, we can then look at proper migraine prevention — there are effective tablets we can prescribe to reduce how often your migraines occur in the first place.*

*I would also recommend keeping a headache diary from today, noting when headaches occur, what you took, and what helped or did not. This will really help us plan the best treatment going forward.*
management: Explain the diagnosis of medication overuse headache clearly and non-judgementally
Educate the patient that the overuse of analgesia and triptans is perpetuating and worsening the headache cycle
Advise withdrawal of the overused medications — starting with ibuprofen, then addressing sumatriptan
Warn the patient that headaches may initially worsen during the withdrawal period (typically 2–4 weeks) before improving
For sumatriptan withdrawal specifically, advise abrupt or gradual cessation; consider short-course naproxen or prednisolone during withdrawal to ease symptoms
Once medication overuse headache has resolved, initiate prophylactic migraine treatment — first-line options include propranolol, topiramate, or amitriptyline
Advise on keeping a detailed headache diary to track triggers, frequency, and response to treatment
Discuss non-pharmacological strategies to reduce headache frequency: good sleep hygiene, hydration, stress management, limiting caffeine
Offer follow-up in 4–6 weeks to assess progress during withdrawal and plan for preventative therapy
Safety-net: advise the patient to seek urgent review if she develops a sudden severe 'thunderclap' headache, new neurological symptoms, or headaches worsening on lying down
learningPoints:
**Medication overuse headache (MOH)**, also known as rebound headache, occurs when analgesics or triptans are used on **10 or more days per month for more than 3 months**. It is one of the most common causes of chronic daily headache and is often missed in primary care.

Key diagnostic features: background of a primary headache disorder (e.g. migraine), increasing frequency of headaches over time, headache present on most days, and improvement with analgesic use but recurrence within hours.

**Management** involves: educating the patient, planned withdrawal of the overused medication (the most important step), supporting them through the withdrawal period (headaches may temporarily worsen), and then initiating **preventive migraine therapy** once the overuse cycle is broken.

First-line preventive treatments for migraine include: **propranolol**, **topiramate** (avoided in pregnancy and those planning pregnancy), and **amitriptyline** (particularly if poor sleep is also an issue).

title: Opioid-Induced Constipation

patientData.name: Charles West
pastMedicalHistory: Meniscal tear – right knee (sustained during football, managed conservatively)
drugHistory: Co-codamol 30/500 mg, 1–2 tablets every 6 hours as required (maximum 8 tablets per day)
