title: Flare of Ankylosing Spondylitis

patientData.name: Jack Ramsay
pastMedicalHistory: Ankylosing spondylitis (diagnosed 5 years ago, HLA-B27 positive, previously well controlled on ibuprofen)
drugHistory: Not currently on any regular medication

recentConsultation.notes:
**Dear GP,**

Thank you for referring Mr Jack Ramsay, whom I reviewed recently in the rheumatology clinic.

Mr Ramsay presented with a history of chronic lower back pain and stiffness, particularly worse in the mornings and improving with activity. Following a thorough clinical assessment, including review of his symptoms, examination findings, and HLA-B27 positivity, a diagnosis of ankylosing spondylitis has been confirmed.

His symptoms are currently well controlled with regular ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily as required. No additional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) are indicated at this stage.

Mr Ramsay has been referred to the local physiotherapy service for ongoing support.

In view of the stability of his condition and good response to conservative management, Mr Ramsay is now discharged from our Rheumatology Clinic.

**Dr Sarah Whitcombe, MBBS, MRCP (Rheumatology) – Consultant Rheumatologist**

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *Hello doctor, I need some help with my back pain because it has not been improving despite taking ibuprofen and paracetamol.*

If asked to explain further: You developed lower back pain two weeks ago, which came on gradually and feels like a dull ache. It is worse in the early morning and associated with stiffness, but moving around for a while helps to reduce the pain. You have been taking paracetamol and ibuprofen, but they are not improving or adequately controlling your symptoms.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:

You have not had any recent trauma or falls. You do not have any tingling, numbness, or weakness in your legs. You have no bladder or bowel symptoms.

If asked about physiotherapy, explain that you did not attend the physiotherapy appointment because your symptoms improved with ibuprofen at the time and you did not feel it was necessary.

**Social History:** You do not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. You live with your girlfriend. You work as a self-employed barber. Your symptoms are affecting your work, as your job involves prolonged standing.

**Ideas:** You think this may be a flare-up of your ankylosing spondylitis.

**Concerns:** You are concerned because the pain is affecting your work and may reduce your income.

**Expectations:** You would like the GP to help manage your symptoms and provide treatment to improve your pain and function.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about the onset of pain and whether it developed gradually or suddenly
Ask about the nature of the pain, including location, severity, and whether it improves with movement or worsens with rest
Ask about associated symptoms, including early morning stiffness, which is characteristic of ankylosing spondylitis
Ask about neurological symptoms, including tingling, numbness, or weakness in the legs

Ask about red flag symptoms, including recent trauma (which may indicate a fracture), saddle paraesthesia, loss of bowel or bladder control, and bilateral radicular pain or lower limb weakness (which may suggest cauda equina syndrome), as well as unexplained weight loss, fever, or night pain

Ask about extra-articular features of ankylosing spondylitis, including anterior uveitis (red, painful eyes with blurred vision or photophobia), enthesitis, skin changes suggestive of psoriasis, and gastrointestinal symptoms
Ask about social history, including occupation, smoking status, and alcohol use
Assess the impact of symptoms on daily activities, work, and functional ability
Ask what treatments he has tried for pain relief and whether he has engaged with physiotherapy
Explore the patient's ideas, concerns, and expectations
Make a working diagnosis of a flare of ankylosing spondylitis

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you, Jack, for explaining all that. From what you have told me, this sounds like a flare of your ankylosing spondylitis. It is reassuring that you do not have any red flag symptoms **at the moment**, such as numbness, weakness, or problems with your bladder or bowels.*

*Ankylosing spondylitis is a long-term condition that affects the spine and can cause stiffness and pain, especially in the lower back. It tends to flare up from time to time, and these flares can last for days or weeks before settling again.*

*Right now, I think it would be helpful to see you in person, so I can examine your back and check your nerves, just to make sure nothing else is going on.*

*For the pain, I would recommend trying a stronger anti-inflammatory called naproxen, which you would take regularly for a few days. I would also give you a medication to protect your stomach while using it.*

*Physiotherapy is also **really important** in ankylosing spondylitis. It can help with your pain, movement, and posture, and may make it easier to cope at work. I would like to refer you back to physiotherapy. I can also get in touch with the rheumatology team who saw you before, just to ask their advice.*

*I understand you are self-employed and this is affecting your ability to earn. If you would like, I can refer you to a social prescriber, who can explore any financial or practical support that may be available to you.*

*If you develop any new symptoms, such as weakness in your legs, numbness around the back passage, or loss of control over your bladder or bowels, or if the pain suddenly becomes severe, you should seek urgent medical help – that would mean calling 999 or going straight to A&E.*
management: Offer a face-to-face appointment to examine the back and perform a full neurological examination
Offer an alternative NSAID like naproxen for pain relief, alongside a proton pump inhibitor for gastroprotection
Offer referral to physiotherapy and explain that physiotherapy can help improve pain, mobility, and overall function
Offer to seek advice and discuss his current flare with the rheumatology team to determine whether any additional or alternative treatments may be appropriate
Provide advice on workplace adjustments, including regular breaks from prolonged standing and stretching during the working day
Offer referral to a social prescriber, who can discuss any support or financial aid he may be entitled to

Provide safety-netting advice to seek urgent medical attention by calling 999 or attending A&E if red flag symptoms develop, including weakness in the lower limbs, loss of bowel or bladder control, numbness around the back passage, or sudden severe back pain
Arrange follow-up in 2–4 weeks to review symptoms, or earlier if new advice is received from rheumatology
learningPoints:
Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a chronic inflammatory condition that primarily affects the spine and sacroiliac joints. It typically presents with inflammatory back pain, which develops gradually, is worse in the early morning with stiffness lasting more than 30 minutes, and improves with movement rather than rest. Patients with AS often experience intermittent flares.

People with ankylosing spondylitis are at **increased risk of osteoporosis and spinal fractures** due to long-standing inflammation. The combination of spinal rigidity and osteoporosis increases the chance of fractures, with up to 10% of people with axial spondyloarthritis experiencing a spinal fracture. These fractures may happen with minimal or no trauma.

Clinicians should also be alert to **red flag symptoms** including inability to control bladder or bowels, numbness in the saddle area, and new lower limb weakness, which may indicate **cauda equina syndrome** and require urgent escalation.

Extra-articular features of AS include uveitis, enthesitis, psoriasis, and gastrointestinal symptoms pointing towards inflammatory bowel disease.

title: Recurrent Axillary Lumps

patientData.name: Rebecca Falkner
drugHistory: Not currently on any regular medication

recentConsultation.seenBy: Dr Kelechi Phillips (Clinical Practitioner Access Role) – 6 months ago
recentConsultation.notes:
**Presenting Complaint**: Patient reported ongoing episodes of multiple painful boils in her right armpit. She was treated with co-amoxiclav one month ago for a similar episode, but the symptoms did not fully resolve.

**On examination**: Multiple erythematous, tender nodules measuring 1–2 cm in diameter, clustered in the intertriginous folds of right axilla. Two nodules show central fluctuance, consistent with early abscess formation. No evidence of sinus tract formation.

**Impression**: Recurrent axillary boils.

**Plan**: Commenced on clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily for 7 days. Blood tests including HbA1c requested to rule out diabetes.

HbA1c: 38 mmol/mol (Normal). FBC, ferritin, LFTs, TFTs, U&E – all within normal limits.

bloodTestResults.summary: HbA1c and routine bloods normal six months ago.

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *Hi doctor, I have got another painful lump under my arm and now I have one in my groin too. I am a bit worried it is starting to spread.*

If Asked to Explain Further: You first noticed a painful lump in your right armpit about two weeks ago, and over the past five days it has become increasingly red and sore. Two days ago, you also noticed a similar lump in your left armpit and another in your left groin.

ONLY say below if asked:

At the moment, you have around three painful red lumps in the right armpit and one lump in the left armpit and groin which are not painful. None of the lumps are discharging pus. You feel well in yourself and have not had any fever. You have been taking paracetamol to help with the pain.

You have had two previous episodes affecting the right armpit and were prescribed antibiotics on both occasions.

**Social History:** You work as a healthcare assistant in a nursing home and live with your partner. You smoke 10 cigarettes per day and have done so for the past 10 years. You do not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. You try to eat healthily.

**Ideas:** You are wondering whether this might be related to your PCOS.

**Concerns:** You are worried that the lumps are starting to spread, since they have now appeared in more than one area.

**Expectations:** You would like something to treat the pain and help reduce the lumps.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about the onset and progression of the lumps seen in the image
Ask whether similar lumps are present elsewhere, including the other armpit, groin, or perineal area
Ask about associated features such as redness, pain, itchiness, discharge of pus, fever, or generalised malaise
Ask whether she has noticed any scarring or skin changes in the armpits or groin
Ask about possible triggers or aggravating factors, including shaving, use of deodorants, stress, tight clothing, sweating, friction, and hormonal influences such as menstrual cycle related flares
Ask about previous episodes, including what treatments were given and how effective they were
Ask whether the symptoms are affecting daily activities, sleep, or ability to work
Ask whether the symptoms have had any psychological impact, such as low mood, anxiety, or reduced self-esteem
Ask about red flag symptoms to exclude malignancy, including unintentional weight loss, night sweats, or loss of appetite
Ask about family history of similar skin conditions
Ask about social history, including smoking status, alcohol intake, diet, and level of physical activity
Explore the patient's ideas, concerns, and expectations
Make a working diagnosis of hidradenitis suppurativa

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you, Rebecca, for explaining all that. I can understand why this has been worrying for you, especially as the lumps have now appeared in more than one area.*

*From what you have told me and from the pattern of these painful lumps in areas such as the armpits and groin, this is most consistent with a condition called hidradenitis suppurativa. Is this something you have heard of before?*

*Hidradenitis suppurativa is a long-term skin condition that tends to flare from time to time and affects areas where skin rubs together, such as the armpits and groin, causing repeated painful lumps. Does that make sense so far?*

*You mentioned you were worried the lumps are spreading. What is actually happening is that the condition can affect more than one area, rather than spreading from one lump to another.*

*Firstly, would it be okay if I arranged a face-to-face appointment so I can examine the areas properly and rule out any other possible causes?*

*In terms of treatment, because the lumps are currently painful and red, I would like to offer a short course of antibiotics to help settle this. For pain, you can continue using simple pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen. I would also recommend using an antiseptic wash, such as **Octenisan** or chlorhexidine, which can help reduce future flares.*

*You were also wondering whether this could be linked to your PCOS. Hormonal factors do play a role in hidradenitis suppurativa, and people with PCOS are at a higher risk of developing this condition, so you are right to think about that.*

*Another important thing I wanted to discuss with you is smoking. Stopping smoking is **really important**, not just for your overall health, but because smoking is known to make this condition worse. We have a lot of support available and can help you with this if you would like.*

*If you notice the lumps becoming much more painful, spreading redness, a lot of pus, fever, or if you start to feel unwell, please seek urgent medical advice.*
management: Offer a face-to-face appointment to examine the lesions in the armpits and groin to assess severity and exclude any other abnormalities

As there are features suggestive of **acute infection**, including redness and pain, offer treatment with either **oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily** for 5 to 7 days or **clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily** for 5 to 7 days depending on suitability and tolerance
Advise regular **simple analgesia**, such as paracetamol or ibuprofen, to help manage pain
Offer the use of **topical antiseptic washes**, such as Octenisan antimicrobial wash or a 4% chlorhexidine solution, to be used regularly as this can help reduce flares
Advise the patient to keep a **symptom diary** to help identify possible triggers such as periods of stress, certain foods, hormonal changes, or other factors occurring around flare episodes
Acknowledge the patient's ideas and explain that hormonal factors are linked to hidradenitis suppurativa and that people with PCOS are at increased risk
Reassure the patient that hidradenitis suppurativa is not caused by poor hygiene
Encourage gradual increases in physical activity where possible, as this can support weight reduction and help reduce flares
**Offer smoking cessation advice** and explain that stopping smoking can improve overall health and help reduce the frequency of flares
Advise the patient to **avoid tight clothing and tight underwear**, as tight clothing can increase friction and irritation and may trigger flares
Advise against squeezing or manipulating the lumps, as this can worsen inflammation and increase the risk of scarring

Safety-net by advising her to seek urgent medical review if the lesions become increasingly painful, develop spreading redness, start discharging significant pus, are associated with fever, or if she feels unwell
Arrange follow-up in five days to assess whether the symptoms have improved
learningPoints:
**Hidradenitis suppurativa** is a chronic inflammatory skin condition affecting apocrine gland bearing areas, most commonly the axillae, groin, perineum, buttocks, and under the breast.

It is **more common in women** and in people of **Afro Caribbean ethnicity**. Risk factors include obesity, cigarette smoking, a positive family history, hormonal influences, polycystic ovary syndrome, and stress.

If there are features suggestive of acute infection, offer oral antibiotics. Prescribe flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for 5 to 7 days, or clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily for 5 to 7 days if the patient is penicillin allergic.

If there are **no features suggestive of acute infection**, or **once an acute infection has resolved and inflammation persists**, offer **topical clindamycin 2%** applied twice daily for three months for **mild disease**. If disease is **more widespread**, consider an **oral antibiotic for three months**. Options include **lymecycline 408 mg once daily**, **tetracycline 500 mg twice daily**, **doxycycline 100 mg once daily**, or **erythromycin 500 mg twice daily**.

**Refer the patient to a dermatologist** if there is severe psychological impact, no improvement despite adequate first-line treatment, severe disease at presentation, diagnostic uncertainty, pregnancy, or significant scarring or sinus tract formation.

title: Request for Contraception for a Young Person with Down's Syndrome

patientData.name: Charlotte Barratt
drugHistory: Not currently on any regular medication

recentConsultation.notes: Patient's mother, Julie Barratt, booked a routine telephone consultation to discuss concerns about contraception for her 15-year-old daughter Charlotte, who has Down's syndrome and has recently started a new relationship.

patientStory:
**Opening Statement (Mother's brief):** *Hello doctor, I am calling on behalf of my daughter. I would like her to be started on contraception and wanted to discuss what the best option would be for her.*

If Asked to Explain Further: Charlotte has recently started a new relationship with a boyfriend, and you are worried that she could become pregnant. You feel it is important to put contraception in place.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:

Her boyfriend is also 15 years old and has Down's syndrome. They met through a learning disability group. Charlotte has not had sex with him yet. You know this because Charlotte always confides in you. You or another responsible adult is always present when they are together. Charlotte does not know you are discussing contraception on her behalf. Her menstrual cycle is regular, every 28 days, and her last period started three days ago.

**Social History:** Charlotte attends secondary school, Year 11, doing well academically. She does not smoke or drink. She lives at home with you, her father, and her older brother.

**Ideas:** You understand that if Charlotte were to have sex without contraception, she could become pregnant.

**Concerns:** You are worried that pregnancy would be very difficult for Charlotte to cope with at her current age.

**Expectations:** You would like to discuss the most suitable form of contraception for Charlotte and would like her to be started on it.

If the doctor explains the different contraceptive options, say that you would prefer the injectable method for her, as she may forget to take a daily pill.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask where Charlotte is at the moment and whether she is aware of the call or conversation
Ask why the mother is requesting contraception for Charlotte
Ask whether Charlotte is sexually active or considering sexual activity

Ask about the partner, including where Charlotte met him, his age, and whether Charlotte feels safe in the relationship, and ask whether the mother is aware of any coercion, pressure, or force from the boyfriend in relation to sexual activity
Ask whether the mother believes Charlotte understands the implications of sex and the use of contraception
Ask about menstrual history, including the date of her last menstrual period, the length of her cycle, whether her periods are regular, and if there are any menstrual problems
Ask about any medical contraindications to contraception, including migraines, personal or family history of thromboembolism, and personal or family history of breast cancer
Ask whether Charlotte is taking any regular or over-the-counter medications not listed in her records and confirm no known drug allergies
Ask about lifestyle factors, including smoking, alcohol use, and illicit drug use
Ask about social history, including who Charlotte lives with, whether she is currently attending school, and whether there are any concerns at school
Explore the mother's ideas, concerns, and expectations regarding contraception and Charlotte's wellbeing

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you, Julie, for taking the time to explain your concerns and for being so thoughtful about Charlotte's wellbeing. It is clear that you are trying to do the right thing for her.*

*I think it is important to say first that it is completely appropriate to raise contraception at this stage, especially as Charlotte is in a relationship. We can certainly talk through the options today at a general level. However, I do need to be clear that we cannot start any contraception without seeing and speaking to Charlotte directly, as she is the patient. Her understanding, views, and consent are central to this decision. Does that make sense so far?*

*There are several different forms of contraception available. One option is the pill, which needs to be taken every day. There is also the contraceptive patch, applied once a week for three weeks, and the vaginal ring, changed every three weeks.*

*We also have long-acting reversible options, such as the coil, which is placed inside the womb and can provide contraception for between five and ten years. Another option is the contraceptive injection, given every twelve weeks, and the implant, placed under the skin of the arm and lasting for up to three years.*

*What I will do is send you an information leaflet that explains these options clearly. It would be helpful if you could go through it with Charlotte so she can start thinking about what might suit her.*

*It is also important to be aware that these methods do not protect against sexually transmitted infections, so condoms should also be used.*

*The next step would be to arrange another appointment with Charlotte present, ideally face to face. During that consultation, I would speak with her directly, assess her understanding and capacity to make decisions about contraception, and talk through the options in simple, clear language.*

*Young people are usually encouraged to involve their parents in these discussions, but it is important to be clear that the decision to involve you ultimately rests with Charlotte unless she is assessed as lacking capacity.*
management: Thank the mother for raising her concerns and for the support she provides in looking after Charlotte
Provide a brief overview of the different types of contraception, including their main advantages and disadvantages, and offer an information leaflet to read through together with Charlotte
Explain that only condoms protect against sexually transmitted infections and that sexual health screening is recommended for anyone who is sexually active
Explain clearly that contraception cannot be prescribed without seeing and speaking to Charlotte directly, as she is the patient and her understanding, views, and consent must be assessed
Offer to arrange a separate face-to-face or telephone consultation with Charlotte present, ideally without a parent in the room initially, to allow a confidential discussion
Explain that during this consultation, Charlotte's capacity and competence to make decisions about contraception will be assessed, including her understanding of sex, pregnancy, and contraception

Reassure the mother that young people are usually encouraged to involve their parents in these discussions, but that this decision ultimately rests with Charlotte unless she is assessed as lacking capacity
Explain that if Charlotte is found not to have capacity, any decision would need to be made in her best interests, with appropriate involvement of parents and relevant professionals
Arrange a follow-up appointment within one to two weeks with Charlotte present to complete the assessment. In the meantime, if sexual activity were to occur, advise that condoms should be used
learningPoints:
This station highlights the importance of capacity, consent, and confidentiality when discussing contraception in young people. Having Down's syndrome or being under the age of 16 does not automatically mean that a young person lacks capacity. Children under 16 can consent to their own treatment if they have sufficient understanding, intelligence, and maturity to fully appreciate what the treatment involves. This is referred to as **Gillick competence**.

Parental concerns should always be acknowledged and respected; however, contraception cannot be prescribed without directly involving the young person, as their views, understanding, and consent are central to the decision-making process.

title: Poorly Controlled Type 2 Diabetes with Hypertension

recentConsultation.notes:
**Presenting complaint:** Patient attended for a routine diabetic review. He reported no symptoms or concerns.

**Examination:** Blood pressure 150/100 mmHg. Pulse 76 bpm. BMI: 32.5 kg/m². Diabetic foot examination satisfactory. Urinalysis negative for all parameters.

**Plan:** Blood samples taken for routine HbA1c and renal function. Patient provided with a urine specimen bottle to return a sample for urine albumin to creatinine ratio (ACR) testing.

bloodTestResults.summary: HbA1c worsened to 64 mmol/mol. eGFR mildly reduced at 59. Urine ACR raised at 7 mg/mmol, suggesting early diabetic nephropathy.

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *Doctor, I booked this appointment to discuss my blood test results and my urine test from my routine diabetes check.*

If Asked to Explain Further: You have type 2 diabetes and usually have blood tests every three months to monitor your blood sugar levels.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:
You do not have any symptoms. You struggle to take your afternoon dose of metformin because of your work. You work as a truck driver and are very busy during the afternoons, which means you often forget the lunchtime dose and usually only take the morning and evening doses.

**Social History:** You do not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. You work as a truck driver. You live at home with your wife and two children. You are aware that your diet is not ideal, as you tend to eat a lot of carbohydrate-based meals and snack frequently due to the nature of your job.

**Ideas:** You suspect that your blood sugar results may be high because you often forget to take your afternoon dose of medication.

**Concerns:** You want to get your diabetes under better control but find it difficult to remember your afternoon medication because of work commitments.

**Expectations:** You would like the GP to advise you on what you can do to better control your blood sugar levels.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Start by acknowledging that he has attended to discuss the results of his recent blood and urine tests from his routine diabetes review

Ask about symptoms suggestive of diabetic complications, including blurred vision (diabetic retinopathy), excessive thirst and frequent urination (osmotic symptoms), chest pain, shortness of breath, or palpitations (cardiovascular complications), pins and needles or numbness in the hands or feet (diabetic neuropathy), blood in the urine, reduced urine output, or leg swelling (diabetic kidney disease), and non-healing ulcers or wounds on the legs or feet (diabetic foot disease)
Ask about adherence to his prescribed medications
Ask whether he experiences any side effects from his medications, for example metformin, which can cause gastrointestinal side effects like diarrhoea, abdominal pain, or vomiting
Ask about social history and lifestyle factors, including smoking status, alcohol intake, occupation, diet, and physical activity levels
Explore his ideas, concerns, and expectations regarding diabetes control and treatment
Make a working diagnosis of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, uncontrolled hypertension, and suspected early chronic kidney disease

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you, Azad, for explaining all that.*

*Looking at your results, your blood sugar levels are higher than we would like, which fits with what you mentioned about sometimes missing your afternoon dose because of work. **To make things easier, I would suggest starting you on a type of metformin that you only need to take once a day** to help with compliance. It is called modified release metformin, 1 g once daily. How does that sound?*

*We will also add another medication called dapagliflozin once daily. This helps to control your blood sugar **and also** protects your kidneys and heart. We would not start both medications at the same time. We will begin with metformin first, and if you are tolerating it well, we will then introduce dapagliflozin.*

*Your blood pressure is also higher than it should be, despite you taking ramipril regularly. For that reason, I would recommend adding another blood pressure tablet called amlodipine, starting at 5 mg once daily.*

*Your blood and urine tests suggest that your kidneys are not working quite as well as we would expect, and there is a small amount of protein leaking into your urine. This can happen in people with diabetes and high blood pressure. We will repeat these tests in three months to look at the overall pattern.*

*Because diabetes, high blood pressure, and kidney problems increase the risk of heart attack and stroke, I would also like to check your cholesterol levels and calculate your heart risk score.*

*Alongside medication, lifestyle changes are **really important**. I can refer you to a dietitian who can help tailor advice to your routine, and I would encourage you to aim for around 30 minutes of walking each day.*

*If at any point you become unwell, for example if you develop tummy pain, vomiting, excessive thirst, or confusion, please seek urgent medical advice.*
management: Offer modified release metformin 1 g daily and add dapagliflozin 10 mg once daily
Explain that modified release metformin will be started first, and after approximately two weeks, once it is confirmed that he is tolerating it well, dapagliflozin will then be introduced

Inform him of side effects: metformin can cause gastrointestinal upset including diarrhoea and nausea; dapagliflozin can increase the risk of urinary tract infections and, in rare cases, Fournier's gangrene

Explain sick day rules for both medications: if he develops vomiting or diarrhoea, he should temporarily stop these medications and restart them 24 to 48 hours after he is able to eat and drink normally again
Advise adding amlodipine 5 mg daily to improve blood pressure control; inform him about possible side effects including ankle swelling and dizziness

Inform him that the blood tests show his kidney function is not within the expected range and that the urine test has detected some protein leakage; explain that these tests will need to be repeated in three months to confirm whether this is a one-off finding or a persistent issue
Offer further blood tests to check cholesterol levels and calculate his QRISK score
Provide lifestyle advice, including increasing physical activity, eating healthily, and aiming for gradual weight loss
Offer vaccinations including influenza, pneumococcal, and COVID vaccination
Advise him to attend his annual diabetic eye screening
Provide safety-netting advice to seek urgent medical attention if he becomes unwell or develops symptoms such as abdominal pain, vomiting, excessive thirst, or confusion
Offer follow-up in 3 months with repeat HbA1c, renal function tests, and urine ACR
learningPoints:
This station highlights the importance of **holistic management** of type 2 diabetes in primary care. Poor medication adherence, uncontrolled blood pressure, and lifestyle factors can lead to **worsening blood sugar control**, **early kidney disease**, and **increased cardiovascular risk**.

The station also reinforces the correct approach to diagnosing **chronic kidney disease**. A single abnormal result is not sufficient. NICE recommends that **eGFR or urine ACR abnormalities must be confirmed on repeat testing at least three months apart**. In this case, there is only one raised urine ACR and one eGFR reading below 60 mL/min, so repeat testing is required before confirming a diagnosis of CKD.

Once a diagnosis of hypertension has been established, **clinic blood pressure readings** are used to monitor the response to lifestyle changes or medication. **Ambulatory or home blood pressure monitoring is not routinely required** after diagnosis has been established, unless white coat hypertension is suspected or a fourth antihypertensive medication is being considered.

title: Hypoglycaemia on Insulin and Sulfonylurea in Chronic Kidney Disease

patientData.name: Heather Brady
pastMedicalHistory: Chronic Kidney Disease Stage 4 (eGFR 23 mL/min/1.73 m², urine ACR 72 mg/mmol)
drugHistory: Lantus SoloStar (insulin glargine) 100 units/mL pre-filled pen, 6 units subcutaneously once daily at night

recentConsultation.notes:
**Dear GP,**

I reviewed Heather in the renal outpatient clinic today for follow-up of her chronic kidney disease (CKD stage G4, A3).

Recent bloods confirm an eGFR of 23 ml/min/1.73 m² (previously similar trend), with a urine ACR of 72 mg/mmol. Using the four-variable Kidney Failure Risk Equation (KFRE), her estimated risk of progression to kidney replacement therapy is 10.8% at 2 years and 33.6% at 5 years.

Her most recent HbA1c is 69 mmol/mol, indicating suboptimal glycaemic control.

In view of her renal function, I have advised discontinuation of metformin due to the increased risk of lactic acidosis. To maintain glycaemic control, I have initiated insulin glargine (Lantus) at a dose of 6 units subcutaneously once daily at night.

I have also started atorvastatin 20 mg once daily for cardiovascular risk reduction. She should continue ramipril 10 mg once daily.

**Dr Anna Rutherford, MBChB, MRCP (UK), PhD, FRCP – Consultant Nephrologist**

bloodTestResults.summary: eGFR 23 mL/min/1.73 m², HbA1c 69 mmol/mol, urine ACR 72 mg/mmol (stage G4 A3 CKD).

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *Hello doctor. I would like to stop the insulin as it is making me feel giddy every morning.*

If Asked to Explain Further: You were prescribed insulin four weeks ago by the kidney doctors because your metformin was stopped. Since starting insulin, you wake up most mornings feeling giddy — meaning light-headed, with difficulty concentrating and headaches. When this happens, you usually need to take something sugary to feel better.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:

Your other symptoms include excessive sweating and shaking of your hands. You have a glucometer and your morning readings are often low, usually between 3.0 and 3.2 mmol/L. You take your gliclazide in the morning after breakfast and your insulin at night. You have never needed help from anyone during these episodes. You check your blood pressure at home; it was 120/75 mmHg this morning.

**Social History:** You do not smoke, and you do not drink alcohol. You work as a cashier in a food store. You drive, but you avoid driving when you feel dizzy or light-headed. You live with your husband.

**Ideas:** You think you are experiencing episodes of low blood sugar caused by the insulin.

**Concerns:** You are worried about these symptoms as they are affecting your ability to get to work on time. You are also concerned about having to keep checking your blood sugars frequently.

**Expectations:** You would like the GP to stop the insulin and discuss alternative ways to manage your blood sugar safely.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask why the patient wants to stop insulin
Ask if there are specific times the symptoms occur and how frequent they are
Ask about other symptoms of hypoglycaemia including sweating, tremor, palpitations, confusion, headache, or visual disturbance
Ask about red flag or severe features of hypoglycaemia including loss of consciousness, seizures, falls, or injuries related to hypoglycaemia
Ask whether she checks her blood glucose levels during these episodes and what the recorded readings are
Ask whether she is aware of early warning symptoms of hypoglycaemia and what actions she takes to relieve symptoms. Also ask if she has ever needed help from someone during hypoglycaemic episodes
Ask whether insulin is taken alongside gliclazide and confirm the timing of gliclazide dosing, as taking them together can cause early-morning hypoglycaemia
Ask about missed meals, reduced appetite, or reduced evening food intake
Ask if the patient was taught how to use her insulin and check if she has any injection site problems such as lipohypertrophy
Ask whether she monitors her blood pressure at home and when it was last checked
Ask about lifestyle and social history including occupation, alcohol use, smoking, and prolonged exercise
Ask how the symptoms have affected the patient
Ask about her home situation and whether she has any support
Ask about the patient's ideas, concerns, and expectations
Make a working diagnosis of medication-induced hypoglycaemia, most likely due to insulin and sulfonylurea use in the context of advanced chronic kidney disease

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you Heather for explaining all that so clearly. From what you have told me, the giddy feelings you are getting in the mornings are most likely due to low blood sugar levels. This has happened because you are currently on both insulin and gliclazide, and together they can push your blood sugar too low. This effect is stronger because your kidney function is reduced, which means your body is not able to recover from low blood sugars as easily as it normally would. Does that make sense so far?*

*The good news is that insulin itself is not a bad treatment. What we need to do is adjust the treatment so that it works well for you without causing these low sugar episodes.*

*If you are happy to continue with insulin, I would strongly recommend that we stop gliclazide, as this tablet is well known to cause low blood sugars in people with more advanced kidney problems. Removing it should significantly reduce your risk.*

*Once gliclazide has been stopped, we can add another tablet called **Dapagliflozin**. This medication does not usually cause low blood sugars and can work alongside insulin to help keep your blood sugar levels under control.*

*I would also like to offer you a blood sugar monitoring system called **Libre**. This uses a small, wearable sensor on the arm to measure your sugar levels and sends real-time readings to a reader or smartphone app without regular finger-prick testing.*

*I will also refer you to the diabetes specialist nurses, who will help monitor and safely adjust your insulin dose. Because you will be continuing insulin, you do need to inform the DVLA.*

*Always carry a fast-acting sugary drink, such as fruit juice or a fizzy drink that is not sugar-free, and take this immediately if you feel symptoms starting. If you ever become very confused, collapse, have a seizure, or symptoms do not improve after sugary drinks, you or your family should call 999 immediately.*
management: Explain to the patient that the combination of insulin and gliclazide is causing recurrent hypoglycaemia and that in advanced chronic kidney disease the body's counter-regulatory response to low blood sugar is impaired
Offer a continuous glucose monitoring device such as **FreeStyle Libre** to reduce the need for finger-prick testing and help identify patterns of low blood sugar

**If she agrees to continue insulin:** Stop gliclazide. Advise a consistent evening meal and a bedtime snack. Refer urgently to the diabetes specialist nurse for close monitoring and insulin dose titration. Offer SGLT2 inhibitors such as dapagliflozin or DPP-4 inhibitors such as linagliptin in addition to insulin

**If she refuses to continue insulin:** Stop insulin and stop gliclazide. Offer SGLT2 inhibitors and DPP-4 inhibitors. **Note that** when eGFR is less than 45 mL/min/1.73 m², SGLT2 inhibitors lose their effectiveness in controlling blood sugar, so they are not suitable as monotherapy and an additional agent is often required

Advise that she must not drive if she develops impaired hypoglycaemia awareness or experiences severe hypoglycaemia requiring help from another person, and that she would need to inform the DVLA. If she decides to continue insulin, advise that she **needs to inform the DVLA**
Advise keeping fast-acting carbohydrates readily available (150–200 mL of fresh juice or fizzy drink, not sugar-free); advise avoiding biscuits or chocolate due to high fat but low sugar content
Encourage informing and educating close family members about her hypoglycaemia risk

Safety-net clearly and advise her to call 999 if she develops severe hypoglycaemia including confusion, blackouts, or seizures, or if mild to moderate symptoms do not improve after taking sugary drinks
Arrange follow-up with the diabetes specialist nurses
learningPoints:
Hypoglycaemia is a recognised adverse effect of insulin therapy and sulfonylureas such as gliclazide. Chronic kidney disease is an independent risk factor for hypoglycaemia, and the risk is significantly increased when insulin is combined with sulfonylureas.

According to ABCD clinical practice guidelines, **sulfonylureas should be avoided alongside insulin in people with an eGFR below 45 mL/min/1.73 m², unless there is clear evidence of the absence of hypoglycaemia.**

Gliclazide is the preferred sulfonylurea in renal impairment because it is primarily metabolised in the liver, is shorter acting, and carries a lower risk of hypoglycaemia compared with other sulfonylureas. However, caution is still required in patients with reduced kidney function.

**Metformin** is **contraindicated** in patients with an eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m².

**SGLT2 inhibitors** can be initiated in patients with an eGFR between 15 and 29 mL/min/1.73 m² primarily for renal and cardiovascular protection, but have minimal glucose-lowering effect when eGFR is below 45 mL/min/1.73 m².

**DPP-4 inhibitors (e.g. linagliptin)** can be used in patients with an eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m² and provide a safe and effective treatment option. **Note:** DPP-4 inhibitors should not be used alongside GLP-1 receptor agonists as they work on the same pathway.

title: Widespread Pain in a Military Veteran

patientData.name: Peter Clarkson
pastMedicalHistory: Military veteran, previously served in the British Army
drugHistory: Not currently on any regular medication

recentConsultation.seenBy: Dr Tina Fury (Clinical Practitioner Access Role) – 1 week ago
recentConsultation.notes:
**Presenting Complaint:** Patient reports generalised body pain, particularly across the back and shoulders, ongoing for nine months with no improvement. No red flag symptoms were reported.

**Examination:** Mild tenderness across both shoulders and across all segments of the spine. No lumps or swellings identified. Range of movement was full, with no restriction. Normal neurological examination.

**Impression:** Suspected rheumatoid arthritis, rule out polymyositis.

**Plan:** Blood tests arranged including inflammatory markers and autoimmune screen. Follow-up with blood test results.

**Blood Test Results:** FBC, TFTs, LFTs, U&E, bone profile, coeliac screen, HbA1c, vitamin B12, folate, calcium, vitamin D, CRP, ESR, creatine kinase – all normal. Rheumatoid factor: negative. Anti-CCP: negative. ANA: negative. Anti-Jo-1: negative.

bloodTestResults.summary: All blood tests including inflammatory markers, autoimmune screen, and metabolic panel are normal.

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *Hello doctor. I would like to discuss my blood test results if that is okay.*

If Asked to Explain Further: You had these blood tests done because you have been experiencing pain throughout your body, mainly affecting your shoulders and back. The pain has been present for about nine months.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:
The pain is a dull, constant ache. You have taken ibuprofen and paracetamol, but these have not helped much. You feel tired most of the time, and even small tasks make you feel very tired. Even when you sleep well, you still wake up feeling tired. You do not experience joint stiffness. Your sleep and mood are not low.

**Social History:** You do not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. You live with your wife and son. You are currently unemployed and looking for work. You previously served in the British Army, but you were laid off because of this ongoing pain.

**Ideas:** You think this could be rheumatoid arthritis because your friend from the military was recently diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis and had pain in both shoulders.

**Concerns:** The pain has affected your ability to work. You were laid off from the British Army and are currently unemployed due to the pain. You are worried that if this is not resolved, you may struggle to find another job.

**Expectations:** You would like the GP to explain the blood test results and advise you on what to do next.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Clarify with the patient why the blood tests were performed
Ask about the onset, duration, nature, location, and exact distribution of the pain
Ask if there are any relieving or aggravating factors

Ask about morning stiffness. Note that in fibromyalgia, stiffness is usually brief and lasts less than 30 minutes, whereas in ankylosing spondylitis and other inflammatory joint conditions, stiffness typically lasts longer than 30 minutes
Ask if there is any swelling in any of the joints
Ask if there is associated fatigue or feeling tired all the time
If tiredness is present, ask whether it is disproportionate to the level of activity
Ask about other symptoms related to fibromyalgia including headaches, paraesthesia, and impaired memory or concentration
Ask about red flag symptoms including unexplained weight loss, night sweats, fevers, weakness in the lower limbs, or bowel or bladder dysfunction
Ask about the impact of symptoms on daily functioning, employment, family life, and physical activity
Ask about sleep, appetite, low mood, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress symptoms, particularly given his military background
Ask if he has tried any treatments for his symptoms and whether they were helpful
Ask about his social history including smoking, alcohol use, occupation, and home situation
Ask about his ideas, concerns, and expectations
Make a working diagnosis of possible fibromyalgia

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you Peter for explaining everything again today. I know this has been going on for a long time and has had a big impact on your life, especially with work and day-to-day activities.*

*I want to start by reassuring you that your blood test results are all normal. They do not show any evidence of rheumatoid arthritis. That is reassuring news.*

*From everything you have told me, your examination, and the normal blood tests, your symptoms fit best with a condition called fibromyalgia. Have you heard about this before?*

*Fibromyalgia is a long-term condition that tends to flare from time to time, causing widespread pain, fatigue, and tiredness. It does not mean there is damage to your joints or muscles, and it is not something that will cause long-term harm, but it can be very distressing and exhausting. Are you following me so far?*

*One of the key parts of managing fibromyalgia is understanding your symptoms better. I would encourage you to keep a simple symptom diary and use a technique called pacing, which means balancing activity and rest rather than pushing through pain and then crashing afterwards.*

*I would also like to refer you to physiotherapy for a graded exercise programme, and offer you talking therapy (CBT), which helps change how the brain processes pain and improves coping strategies.*

*For pain management, as paracetamol and ibuprofen have not been effective, we can try a low dose of amitriptyline taken in the evening. We would start at a very low dose. I should mention that this is an off-label use of the medication.*

*Given the impact on your work and finances, I would also like to refer you to our social prescribing team to help with financial support and benefits eligibility.*

*If you develop any new or worrying symptoms such as worsening weakness, numbness, problems with your bladder or bowels, unexplained weight loss, or thoughts of harming yourself, please seek urgent medical advice.*
management: No need for a face-to-face review, as he has already been examined and there are no new red flag symptoms
Advise him to keep a symptom diary to identify potential triggers and support better self-management
Provide advice on pacing – balancing activity and rest, breaking tasks into smaller manageable activities, resting before feeling exhausted, and gradually increasing activity over time
Offer referral to physiotherapy for tailored graded exercise programmes
Offer cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) to help change how the brain processes pain, improve coping strategies, and reduce psychological distress

For pain management, offer low-dose amitriptyline starting at 10 mg taken 2 to 4 hours before bedtime; inform him of common side effects such as drowsiness and dry mouth; explain this is an off-label use
Offer referral to the social prescriber to provide advice on financial support, benefits eligibility, and signposting to local support services
Offer written information and leaflets about fibromyalgia for further reading

Safety-net clearly and advise him to seek urgent medical advice if he develops thoughts of suicide or self-harm, progressive weakness, numbness, bowel or bladder dysfunction, unexplained weight loss, or night sweats
Arrange follow-up in four weeks to assess response to treatment
learningPoints:
Fibromyalgia is a chronic pain disorder of unknown cause. It is more common in women, who are affected around ten times more frequently than men. To diagnose fibromyalgia, symptoms must have been present for **at least three months**, and there should be no other condition that would otherwise explain the pain.

Fibromyalgia is associated with widespread pain, fatigue, headaches, morning stiffness, paraesthesia, and a sensation of swollen joints despite no objective swelling on examination. Other common associated features include depression, anxiety, sleep disturbance, and cognitive difficulty.

Management focuses on education and non-pharmacological approaches: keeping a symptom diary, pacing, cognitive behavioural therapy, and physiotherapy.

Pharmacological management may include antidepressants such as duloxetine, amitriptyline, citalopram, fluoxetine, paroxetine, or sertraline. These medications are used **off-label** in fibromyalgia.

Referral to rheumatology is only necessary if there are concerns about inflammatory arthritis or if the patient does not improve despite appropriate primary care management.

title: Blood in Vomit After Heavy Alcohol Use

patientData.name: Liam Osborne
drugHistory: Not currently on any regular medication

recentConsultation.notes: Patient booked an urgent appointment to discuss some concerns.

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *Hi doctor, I had an episode of vomiting yesterday and noticed some blood.*

If Asked to Explain Further: You were out with friends yesterday and drank more alcohol than usual — about six cans of beer over two hours, followed by around five shots of whiskey. About 30 to 40 minutes later, you started vomiting. You had three episodes in total. During the last episode, you noticed small specks of blood in the vomit. This has not happened again since. You are feeling better now.

ONLY say below if asked:

You do not currently have any other symptoms and you feel well in yourself.

**Social History:** You live in a student hostel with friends. You are studying artificial intelligence at university. You drink alcohol every day, usually around four cans of beer daily, and have been doing this for the last one year. You do not smoke and you do not use illicit drugs.

**Ideas:** You are not sure what caused the blood in your vomit.

**Concerns:** You are worried about seeing blood when you vomited and want to make sure it is nothing serious.

**Expectations:** You would like the GP to explain what happened and advise you on what to do next.

If the doctor offers a face-to-face consultation: Decline and explain that you have an important school assignment to finish, but you can attend tomorrow.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about the onset and number of episodes of vomiting
Ask whether the blood in the vomit was a large volume or small streaks or specks of blood
Ask about associated symptoms including epigastric pain, heartburn, chest pain, difficulty swallowing, black stools, or diarrhoea
Ask about red flag symptoms of anaemia including dizziness, syncope, shortness of breath, or palpitations
Ask about use of over-the-counter medications such as NSAIDs that may contribute to symptoms
Ask about any past history of similar episodes
Ask about social history including alcohol intake, smoking, illicit drug use, occupation, and home situation
Ask about CAGE questions to assess alcohol dependence
Ask whether he experiences any alcohol withdrawal symptoms when he does not drink
Ask about the patient's ideas, concerns, and expectations
Make a working diagnosis of a likely Mallory-Weiss tear or alcohol-induced gastritis

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you Liam for explaining everything so clearly today. I can understand why seeing blood when you vomited would be worrying, especially at your age.*

*From what you have told me, this episode is most likely due to repeated, forceful vomiting after drinking a large amount of alcohol. This can cause a small tear in the lining where the food pipe meets the stomach, called a Mallory–Weiss tear, or irritation of the stomach lining. The good news is that these usually heal on their own and, as the bleeding was very small and has not happened again, there are no signs of anything serious at the moment. Does that make sense so far?*

*I would still like to see you face to face so I can examine your tummy and check your observations, just to be safe. If you are not able to come in today, we can arrange this for tomorrow.*

*To help the lining of your stomach heal, I would like to start you on a medication called omeprazole. You would take one tablet once a day for four weeks.*

*I also want to talk about alcohol. The amount you are currently drinking is above recommended limits, which can cause problems with the liver and lead to other health issues over time. I would strongly advise cutting down. If you feel you might struggle with this, we can refer you to local alcohol services. I would also recommend some blood tests including liver function tests to make sure everything is okay.*

*If you vomit blood again, if your stools turn black, or if you develop dizziness, fainting, worsening tummy pain, or heart racing, please seek urgent medical advice or go to A&E if symptoms are severe.*
management: Offer a face-to-face appointment to assess the abdomen and check observations; if he declines today, arrange for the next day as there is no immediate urgency
Offer blood tests including liver function tests to assess for alcohol-related liver injury given his one-year history of heavy alcohol intake
Advise him that he needs to reduce his alcohol intake, as ongoing heavy drinking is harmful
Offer referral to local alcohol support services to help him cut down safely and reduce the risk of withdrawal symptoms
Offer omeprazole 20 mg once daily for four weeks to aid mucosal healing and reduce gastric acid irritation

Safety-net clearly: advise him to seek urgent medical advice by contacting the urgent GP service or NHS 111 if out of hours if vomiting blood recurs, stools become black, or he develops dizziness, abdominal pain, fainting, or palpitations; advise attending A&E if symptoms are severe
Arrange follow-up in four weeks to review symptoms
learningPoints:
Mallory-Weiss syndrome (MWS) is a common cause of non-variceal upper gastrointestinal bleeding. It results from longitudinal mucosal tears, usually at the gastro-oesophageal junction, caused by sudden rises in intra-abdominal pressure during vomiting, retching, or coughing.

The classic presentation is haematemesis following repeated retching or vomiting. Bleeding is usually mild and self-limiting, meaning conservative medical management is sufficient in most cases.

Alcohol-induced gastritis is another common cause of upper gastrointestinal bleeding in people who binge drink and may coexist with a Mallory-Weiss tear. However, if bleeding persists, stools become dark and tarry, or the patient develops features of haemodynamic compromise such as dizziness, palpitations, or syncope, urgent admission via A&E for immediate assessment and resuscitation may be required.

title: Chest Pain Misdiagnosed as Gastritis

patientData.name: Emma Swindon
drugHistory: Not currently on any regular medication

recentConsultation.notes:
**Triage Notes:** 2 months history of recurrent vomiting. Patient reported ongoing vomiting on the day of attendance with approximately six episodes. Vomiting was non-bloody.

**Assessment:** Urine pregnancy test was negative. Blood tests and medical review were planned; however, the patient left the department before these could be completed.

**Outcome:** The patient left the department prior to full clinical assessment and investigations.

**Dr James Patel, ST5 Emergency Medicine Registrar**

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *Hello doctor. Can you prescribe me some medication for gastritis?*

If Asked to Explain Further: You were seen in A&E yesterday because of chest pain. You had a heart tracing (ECG) and blood tests done, and you were told the results were normal. A nurse suggested your symptoms might be due to gastritis and advised you to see your GP for treatment.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:
The chest pain is located in the centre of your chest and feels like a dull, squeezing ache. The first episode happened four weeks ago while walking up the stairs at work. The second episode occurred yesterday afternoon while carrying heavy shopping bags. On both occasions, you had to stop what you were doing for the pain to settle. The pain resolved after about 5 to 6 minutes of rest. You do not have chest pain now.

**Social History:** You smoke 20 cigarettes per day and have done so for around 30 years. You do not drink alcohol. You work as a mortgage broker. You live with your husband and two children.

**Family History:** Your father died from a heart attack at the age of 62.

**Ideas:** You think this is gastritis because the nurse in A&E suggested this.

**Concerns:** You do not have any particular concerns.

**Expectations:** You would like the GP to prescribe medication for gastritis.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about the location, onset, and nature or character of the chest pain
Ask about aggravating and relieving factors for the pain (stable angina is typically precipitated by physical exertion and relieved by rest)
Ask whether the chest pain occurs only with exertion or also at rest (pain at rest suggests acute coronary syndrome and requires urgent hospital assessment)
Ask whether the chest pain radiates anywhere, for example to the neck, shoulders, jaw, or arms
Ask how long the pain lasts before resolving (stable angina pain usually lasts less than 15 minutes)
Ask whether she currently has chest pain
Ask about associated symptoms including shortness of breath, palpitations, dizziness, nausea, or sweating
Ask about any past cardiac history or previous similar episodes
Ask about respiratory symptoms such as cough or recent flu-like illness
Ask about gastrointestinal symptoms including heartburn, vomiting, and regurgitation, to help rule out gastritis
Ask about social and lifestyle factors including smoking, alcohol use, physical activity level, and diet
Ask about family history of heart attack or stroke
Ask about the patient's ideas, concerns, and expectations
Make a working diagnosis of stable angina

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you, Emma, for explaining everything clearly today. I understand why you were told this might be gastritis, and it is completely reasonable that you are asking for treatment. However, after going through your symptoms carefully, I am concerned that this chest pain is more likely to be coming from your heart rather than your stomach.*

*The reason for my concern is that the pain comes on with exertion, such as walking upstairs or carrying heavy shopping, and then settles when you rest. That pattern is very typical of a condition called stable angina. Is this something you have heard of before?*

*Angina happens when there is narrowing in the blood vessels that supply the heart. Because of this narrowing, the heart muscle does not get enough blood and oxygen during activity, which causes the chest pain you are experiencing. When you stop and rest, the demand on the heart reduces and the pain settles.*

*Given your smoking history and family history of heart disease, it is important that we take this seriously and investigate it properly.*

*What I would like to do next is arrange for you to be seen face to face so I can examine your heart and repeat an ECG. I would also like to arrange some blood tests including cholesterol levels.*

*I am also going to start you on two medications today. One is aspirin, which helps reduce the risk of heart attacks, and the other is a spray called glyceryl trinitrate, or GTN. If you get chest pain again, stop what you are doing and rest, then use one spray under your tongue. If the pain has not eased after five minutes, use a second spray. If the pain is still there five minutes after that, call 999 immediately.*

*I will also refer you urgently to the rapid access chest pain clinic. You should be seen within two weeks.*

*One very important thing is that smoking significantly increases the risk of heart disease, and stopping is one of the most effective ways to protect your heart. I can refer you to our smoking cessation service to help you quit successfully.*

*If you develop chest pain at rest, worsening pain, pain lasting more than 15 minutes, or symptoms such as breathlessness, dizziness, or collapse, please call 999 straight away.*
management: Offer a face-to-face appointment for a cardiovascular examination and repeat ECG
Arrange blood tests including lipid profile, full blood count, urea and electrolytes, and liver function tests
Start aspirin 75 mg once daily, unless contraindicated, and prescribe glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) spray

Advise that if chest pain occurs, she should stop and rest, use one spray of GTN; if pain has not eased after five minutes use a second spray; if pain has still not eased five minutes after the second dose she should call 999 for an ambulance
Offer an urgent referral to the rapid access chest pain clinic (RACPC); explain that she should be seen within two weeks for further investigations to confirm the diagnosis
Advise on smoking cessation and offer referral to smoking cessation services
Advise on maintaining a healthy lifestyle, including regular physical activity within tolerance and a balanced diet

Safety-net clearly: advise her to call 999 if she develops chest pain at rest, worsening or more frequent pain, pain lasting more than 15 minutes, or associated symptoms such as breathlessness, dizziness, or collapse
Arrange follow-up after she has been seen in the rapid access chest pain clinic
learningPoints:
**Stable angina** typically presents as chest pain or discomfort that occurs predictably with physical exertion or emotional stress, settles within minutes of rest or with sublingual GTN, lasts less than 15 minutes, and follows a consistent pattern. Suspected stable angina should be referred urgently to a rapid access chest pain clinic.

**Unstable angina** refers to chest pain that suggests an acute coronary syndrome. This includes chest pain occurring at rest, lasting longer than 15 minutes, worsening in frequency or severity, occurring with less exertion than before, or chest pain that does not reliably settle with rest or GTN. **Unstable angina requires urgent hospital admission.**

title: Safeguarding Concerns – Child with Unexplained Injury

recentConsultation.notes: Patient's mother, Toni Beckham (age 30), booked an urgent appointment to discuss some concerns about her child. Toni has a history of substance abuse (cannabis) and alcohol misuse; she completed a drug and alcohol rehabilitation programme one year ago. She is not currently on any regular medication.

patientStory:
**Opening Statement (Mother's brief):** *Hello doctor. Has the safeguarding team contacted you?*

If Asked to Explain Further: Your son, Harry, who is 3 years old, was taken to A&E 2 weeks ago because he had a bruise on his hand. This happened while he was playing with your partner, Desmond. X-rays were done and everything was fine. However, the doctors in A&E said they would be making a safeguarding referral. Since then, you have been very worried because you do not want your child to be taken away.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:

Desmond is not the biological father of your son, Harry. You were not present when the incident happened. Your partner told you that he was playing with Harry in the garden when Harry fell and bruised his arm. The doctors said they were concerned about the type of injury and some findings on the X-ray and explained that they would be making a safeguarding referral.

If asked about your partner: Desmond is 40 years old. He drinks alcohol excessively, including in front of your child. He can be temperamental, but you love him. He has hurt you physically once in the past, but you do not consider this serious. He is currently unemployed, helps you with childcare, and is on Universal Credit.

**Social History:** You live with your partner and your son. You work as a waiter in a bar. You do not smoke or use illicit drugs currently. You previously attended alcohol and drug misuse rehabilitation.

**Ideas:** You think the safeguarding team may take your child away.

**Concerns:** You are worried because you have a history of cannabis and alcohol misuse recorded in your notes, and you think this will lead to the safeguarding team taking your child away.

**Expectations:** You would like the GP to remove the cannabis and alcohol misuse history from your medical records.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Clarify the patient's understanding of why a safeguarding referral was made and what concerns were raised in A&E
Ask about the events leading to the child's injury, including when it happened, who was present, and what actions were taken afterwards
Ask about the child's current condition, including whether the injury has healed, whether the child is still in pain, and where the child is currently
Ask about the child's behaviour, including whether he appears withdrawn, fearful, or less engaged than usual
Ask whether the child is eating and drinking normally, is up to date with immunisations, and whether there are any concerns about his development
Ask if there has been any previous history of injuries, accidents, or hospital attendances involving the child
Ask about the home situation, including who lives at home and whether there are any other children in the household
Ask about the partner, including his role in the household, alcohol use, smoking, or illicit drug use, and whether there has been any abusive behaviour towards the patient or the child
Ask whether the patient feels safe at home
Ask about the patient herself, including occupation, financial situation, smoking, alcohol use, and illicit drug use
Ask about her ideas, concerns, and expectations
Consider safeguarding concerns relating to a child with an unexplained injury, and potential domestic abuse risk

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you Toni for explaining everything so openly today. I can hear how worried and upset you are, and that is completely understandable.*

*I want to reassure you first that a safeguarding referral does not automatically mean that a child will be taken away. Safeguarding is about making sure children are safe and supported, and in most cases the aim is to keep families together wherever it is safe to do so.*

*I also want to be honest with you about your medical records. Past histories of cannabis and alcohol misuse cannot be removed from your records. As doctors, we have an ethical and professional responsibility to keep records accurate and factual. Does that make sense?*

*I want to reassure you that safeguarding teams usually seek your consent before accessing your medical records where possible. However, information may be shared without consent if there are concerns about a child's safety.*

*Toni, some of the things you have told me today do raise concerns about your safety and your child's safety. Because of that, it is important that I make a referral to the safeguarding team today.*

*The children's safeguarding team are likely to contact you within the next 24 to 48 hours. Their role is to assess the situation and offer support where needed, not to blame you.*

*If at any point you feel unsafe at home, or if you are worried about your partner's behaviour towards you or your son, please seek help urgently. That could mean calling the police on 999 if there is immediate danger.*
management: Inform her that past histories of cannabis and alcohol misuse cannot be removed from her medical records, as medical records must be accurate, factual, and reflect relevant past health information
Explain that there is an ethical and professional responsibility to keep medical records accurate; removing this information could affect the management of her condition in future
Explain that safeguarding teams usually seek consent to access medical records where possible, but information may be shared without consent if there are concerns about a child's safety

**Offer to make an urgent referral to children's safeguarding** regardless of whether a referral was made by the hospital; note that safeguarding is everyone's responsibility, and given that two weeks have passed since the incident without contact, the original referral may have been missed

Inform her that the child safeguarding team is likely to contact her within the next 24 to 48 hours to gather further information; reassure her that their aim is to support families and keep children with their parents wherever it is safe to do so
Encourage her to engage openly and honestly with safeguarding professionals and to attend any appointments or assessments arranged
Safety-net clearly: advise her to seek urgent help by calling 999 if she feels unsafe at home or if she becomes concerned about her partner's behaviour towards her or her child
Offer follow-up with a telephone review within 24 to 48 hours to check whether safeguarding services have made contact and to provide further support
learningPoints:
Safeguarding is everyone's responsibility. Healthcare professionals have a legal, ethical, and professional duty to act when there are concerns about the safety or wellbeing of a child or vulnerable adult.

In this scenario, although the mother reports that the hospital made a referral, it is important not to assume it has been received or acted upon. Hospital referrals can occasionally be delayed, missed, or misdirected. Given that two weeks have passed since the incident without any contact, this raises a red flag that the safeguarding referral may have been missed.

According to the GMC, confidential information can be shared without consent if required by law or necessary to protect a child. Even if a parent objects, information should usually be shared when a child is at risk of abuse or neglect, as safeguarding the child's welfare takes priority.

Medical records must remain accurate and factual and cannot be altered to remove relevant past history.

title: Panic Attacks and Agoraphobia Following Cancer Treatment

patientData.name: Mark Goldman
pastMedicalHistory: Prostate cancer – completed radical radiotherapy, currently in remission (PSA 0.4 ng/mL)

recentConsultation.notes:
**Reason for attendance:** 999 call for shortness of breath, palpitations, and feeling of impending doom. Second ambulance attendance for similar symptoms.

**On scene findings:** Symptoms resolved on crew arrival. No chest pain reported.

**Clinical assessment:** 12-lead ECG: Normal sinus rhythm. No acute ischaemic changes. Observations: BP 132/78 mmHg, HR 76 bpm, RR 16 breaths per minute, SpO₂ 97% on air, Temperature 36.6°C.

**Outcome:** Hospital conveyance offered, but patient declined. Patient assessed to have capacity. Safety-net advice given.

**Plan/advice:** Advised urgent GP review due to recurrent symptoms to exclude underlying cardiac cause.

**Urology Letter – 5 months ago:** Mr Goldman completed radical radiotherapy for prostate cancer 6 weeks ago. Disease currently well controlled. PSA 0.4 ng/mL, consistent with good post-treatment response. PSA monitoring every 6 months in line with standard UK post-radiotherapy surveillance.

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *Hello doctor, the ambulance crew asked me to contact you.*

If Asked to Explain Further: You have been experiencing shortness of breath, which occurs whenever you think about going outside. The symptoms started gradually and have been getting worse. They began after you completed radiotherapy for prostate cancer about 6–7 months ago.

ONLY say below if asked:

When you feel breathless, your heart starts racing. You do not experience any chest pain. The symptoms only occur when you think about going outside and do not happen at other times.

Your wife has become frustrated and upset because you are no longer able to help with shopping, go out with her, or visit your grandchildren.

Your mood, sleep, and appetite are generally fine. You do not have any thoughts of suicide or self-harm.

**Social History:** You do not smoke, and you do not drink alcohol. You live with your wife. You are a retired primary school teacher. Your wife currently does the shopping and cooking. You are still able to manage activities around the house but are unable to leave the house.

**Ideas:** You are not sure why this is happening.

**Concerns:** You are concerned because these symptoms are significantly affecting your life.

**Expectations:** You would like the GP to help resolve this problem.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about the onset, duration, and progression of the shortness of breath
Ask what triggers the symptoms and confirm whether they are situational, for example occurring only when thinking about or attempting to leave the house

Ask about associated symptoms during episodes, including palpitations, sweating, trembling, dizziness, a choking sensation, fear of losing control, fear of dying, or avoidance of situations that may provoke breathlessness
Ask about the frequency of episodes and whether symptoms resolve spontaneously
Ask about chest pain, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, wheeze, cough, fever, leg swelling, or reduced exercise tolerance, to help exclude cardiac or respiratory disease
Ask whether there was any specific incident that triggered the onset of symptoms
Ask about mood, sleep, and appetite
Ask directly about thoughts of suicide or self-harm
Ask about common symptoms associated with cancer or cancer treatment, including pain, constipation, or vomiting
Ask about the impact of symptoms on daily activities, independence, and relationships
Ask about social and lifestyle history including smoking, alcohol use, and home situation
Ask about the patient's ideas, concerns, and expectations
Make a working diagnosis of panic attacks with agoraphobia

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you Mark for explaining everything so clearly today. I can see how frightening and limiting these symptoms have been for you, especially as they are stopping you from leaving the house and enjoying time with your wife and grandchildren.*

*From everything you have told me, and taking into account the normal assessments carried out by the ambulance crews, your symptoms are most consistent with panic attacks. Panic attacks can cause very real physical symptoms such as sudden breathlessness, a racing heart, dizziness, and a strong sense of fear.*

*An important part of what you have described is that these symptoms mainly happen when you think about going outside or trying to leave the house. This pattern has a name, and it is called agoraphobia. Agoraphobia means a fear of being in situations where you feel you might not be able to escape or get help if symptoms come on. It often develops alongside panic attacks. Does that make sense?*

*The most effective treatment for panic attacks with agoraphobia is a talking therapy called cognitive **behavioural** therapy, or CBT. CBT helps you understand how anxiety affects the body and teaches techniques to manage panic symptoms. It also involves gradual, supported exposure to situations you have started to avoid, helping you rebuild confidence step by step.*

*While you are waiting for therapy, there are some practical steps that can help, such as avoiding caffeine and learning simple breathing and grounding techniques.*

*We also have the option of medication while you are waiting for talking therapy. If we do start medication, symptoms can sometimes feel slightly worse in the first one to two weeks before they begin to improve.*

*If your symptoms change in nature, start happening without anxiety triggers, are associated with chest pain, collapse, or other new worrying symptoms, or if you develop thoughts of harming yourself, please seek urgent medical attention.*
management: Acknowledge his symptoms and validate how distressing and limiting this has been for him
Explain that his symptoms are most consistent with panic attacks, which can cause very real physical symptoms such as breathlessness, palpitations, dizziness, and a fear response
Offer referral for cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) as first-line treatment, focusing on graded exposure and anxiety management techniques
Advise avoiding anxiety-provoking substances, for example caffeine, as these can worsen panic symptoms
Reassure him that many people respond well to CBT; explain that while he is waiting for therapy, medication is an option if symptoms are significantly affecting his quality of life
If he is open to medication, offer an SSRI such as sertraline, escitalopram, or paroxetine, which are licensed treatments for panic disorder
If medication is started, explain that symptoms can sometimes worsen in the first one to two weeks before improving, and advise close monitoring

Safety-net clearly: advise him to seek urgent medical help if his symptoms change in nature, occur without anxiety triggers, are associated with chest pain, collapse, or other new concerning symptoms, or if he develops thoughts of suicide or self-harm
Arrange follow-up in two weeks if medication is started, or in four weeks if CBT alone is pursued
learningPoints:
Agoraphobia is a fear of being in situations where escape may feel difficult or where help may not be available. These situations often trigger intense anxiety or panic attacks, leading people to avoid places such as shops, public spaces, or leaving the house altogether.
