Agoraphobia is different from social anxiety disorder. **Social anxiety disorder** is the fear of being judged, criticised, or embarrassed in social situations. In **agoraphobia**, the fear is about feeling unsafe or unable to escape if symptoms occur, not about social judgement.

Cancer can have a significant psychological impact. **Anxiety disorders, including panic attacks and agoraphobia, can develop after successful cancer treatment.** This may be related to the emotional toll of the cancer journey, fear of symptoms returning, loss of the safety of regular medical follow-ups, or fear of experiencing panic symptoms away from help.

title: Request to Stop Medication and Remove Supervision in Schizophrenia

patientData.name: Jeffrey Sweeney
pastMedicalHistory: History of attempted suicide (jumped from bridge into canal during psychotic episode one year ago)
Detained under the Mental Health Act one year ago

recentConsultation.seenBy: Letter from Adult Psychiatry – 1 year ago
recentConsultation.notes:
**Dear GP,**

Re: Jeffrey Sweeney, 24-year-old male.

Thank you for your ongoing care of Mr Jeffrey Sweeney. I am writing to provide an update following his recent compulsory psychiatric admission and subsequent discharge into the community.

Mr Sweeney has a background of high-functioning autism, schizophrenia, and recurrent depressive disorder. He has a significant history of severe psychotic episodes associated with both suicidal and violent ideation, including command auditory hallucinations instructing him to harm himself and others. He made a serious suicide attempt by jumping from a bridge into a canal.

He was detained under the Mental Health Act and remained an inpatient for approximately one month. On discharge, a robust risk management and support plan was put in place, including a dedicated mental health support worker who remains with him at all times.

**Dr Eleanor White, MBChB, MRCPsych – Consultant Psychiatrist**

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *Hello doctor, I want you to write a letter saying that I have capacity so that my mental health support worker can stop following me everywhere and telling me what to do. I also want to increase my working hours from 10 hours per week to full-time work (40 hours a week) as well as stop my medications as I feel better.*

If Asked to Explain Further: You had a severe relapse of your schizophrenia about one year ago. During that time, you nearly harmed yourself and others and were admitted to hospital. After discharge, you were allocated a mental health support worker who supervises you closely and accompanies you when you go out. You feel much better now and want more independence.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:

There is no bullying or mistreatment from the mental health support workers. They are kind and supportive, but you feel restricted.

You have not experienced any side effects from your medications.

**Social History:** You live in supported living accommodation. You get on well with staff and other residents and have friends there. You do not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs.

**Ideas:** You believe the support workers were needed in the past, but you feel well now and think they are no longer necessary.

**Concerns:** You do not have any concerns.

**Expectations:** You want the GP to write a letter stating that you have capacity, allowing you to stop being supervised, increase your working hours, and stop your medications.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask why the patient wants a letter stating that he has capacity
Ask why he wants to stop his medication and whether he has experienced any side effects
Ask what he understands about his diagnoses and why the mental health support worker was put in place after his last admission
Ask about his current mental state, including mood, thought disorder, hallucinations, or delusional beliefs
Confirm when his last relapse or psychotic episode occurred
Ask directly about any current or recent thoughts of suicide, self-harm, or harm to others
Ask about any safeguarding concerns, including whether he has felt bullied, verbally abused, physically abused, or mistreated by his mental health support workers
Ask about his current employment, what his role involves, and why he wishes to increase his working hours
Ask about social and lifestyle factors, including where he lives, smoking status, alcohol intake, and illicit drug use
Ask whether he has discussed his concerns or wishes with the Community Mental Health Team
Ask about the patient's ideas, concerns, and expectations

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you, Jeffrey, for explaining how you are feeling today. I can understand why you want more independence, especially as you are feeling much better now.*

*I want to be open with you. I am not able to write a letter saying that you have capacity to stop your support worker, stop your medication, or make changes to your care plan. That is not because I do not trust you or think you are unwell, but because decisions like this need to be made by your mental health team and your consultant psychiatrist, who know your history in detail and are responsible for keeping you safe.*

*It may help to explain how capacity works. We do not routinely write letters to confirm capacity, because everyone is assumed to have capacity unless there is evidence otherwise. Capacity is also decision-specific and time-specific. Bigger or higher-risk decisions, such as stopping medication or changing levels of support, may need specialist assessment and guidance.*

*It is also important that you do not stop your medication suddenly. Even when people feel well, stopping medication without specialist review can lead to a relapse, which could put you at risk again.*

*What I can do is contact your Community Mental Health Team today and let them know how you are feeling. They can arrange a proper review to look at whether it is safe to reduce supervision, review your medication, and discuss increasing your working hours in a gradual and supported way.*

*The safest way to work towards more independence is step by step, with the mental health team involved, rather than making sudden changes.*
management: Explain that the GP cannot provide a letter declaring capacity to stop supervision, stop medication, or change care arrangements, as these decisions sit with the Community Mental Health Team and Consultant Psychiatrist

Explain that everyone is assumed to have capacity unless proven otherwise, and that capacity is decision-specific and time-specific; everyday decisions are usually within capacity, but higher-risk decisions such as stopping medication or reducing supervision require specialist assessment
Reassure him that this is not about taking control away from him, but about ensuring changes are made with him in a safe and supported way
Advise strongly against stopping medication abruptly, explaining that sudden discontinuation significantly increases the risk of relapse, with potential risk to himself and others
Offer to contact and inform the Community Mental Health Team about his concerns so they can arrange a multidisciplinary review
Advise that any increase in working hours should be gradual and agreed with the mental health team, rather than an immediate move to full-time work, as increased stress can trigger a relapse

Safety-net clearly: advise him to seek urgent help from mental health services or emergency services if he experiences a return of hallucinations, suicidal thoughts, thoughts of harming others, worsening mood, or loss of control
Reassure him that you will update him as soon as you hear back from the Community Mental Health Team
learningPoints:
Mental capacity is decision-specific and time-specific. This patient may have capacity for day-to-day decisions such as what to wear, where to go locally, or working limited hours. However, the decisions he is requesting — stopping antipsychotic medication, ending constant supervision, and increasing work to full time — are high-risk, complex decisions.

Because of his recent severe psychotic relapse, history of suicide attempt and risk to others, and ongoing involvement of the Community Mental Health Team, the GP cannot provide a letter declaring capacity for these high-risk decisions, which require specialist psychiatric capacity assessment and risk management in the patient's best interests and public safety.

title: Cannabinoid Hyperemesis Syndrome

patientData.name: Bella Beaconsfield
pastMedicalHistory: Regular cannabis use for the past 6–7 months

recentConsultation.seenBy: A&E Discharge Summary – Two Weeks Ago
recentConsultation.notes:
**Triage Notes:** 2 months history of recurrent vomiting. The patient reported ongoing vomiting on the day of attendance with approximately six episodes. Vomiting was non-bloody.

**Assessment:** Urine pregnancy test was negative. Blood tests and medical review were planned; however, the patient left the department before these could be completed.

**Dr James Patel, ST5 Emergency Medicine Registrar**

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *Hi doctor, I have been feeling sick and vomiting on and off for about two months and it is starting to worry me.*

If Asked to Explain Further: Two months ago, you started having repeated episodes of vomiting. The episodes come on suddenly. When they occur, you vomit uncontrollably, having around four to five episodes within thirty minutes to one hour. You tend to have a flare almost once every week, and it is starting to affect your work.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:

You have noticed that your symptoms tend to flare when you are most stressed. You sometimes feel bloated, and your bowel motions can be hard and pellet-like, but this has been the case for a long time and is not a new symptom. There is no blood in your vomit or stools. You have not lost weight, and you are usually able to keep fluids down. You are not pregnant and have done a recent negative pregnancy test. You use cannabis regularly, most days, and have done so for the last six to seven months.

**Social History:** You work as an administrative officer in a retail company. You do not smoke cigarettes. You smoke cannabis regularly. You do not drink alcohol. You live with your partner.

**Ideas:** You think stress may be causing your symptoms.

**Concerns:** You are worried that if this continues, it may start to affect your work, as you often have to take time off during flares.

**Expectations:** You want medication or advice on what to do to stop this.

If the doctor advises you to stop using cannabis, ask whether cutting down rather than stopping completely would be enough.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask when the vomiting episodes started and how symptoms have progressed over time
Ask how many episodes of vomiting occur in a typical day and during a flare
Ask about the contents of the vomit, specifically whether there is any blood or bile
Ask whether the patient is able to keep fluids down between episodes
Ask about any known triggers, including emotional stress or anxiety, infections, certain foods, prolonged periods without food, dehydration, or menstrual periods
Ask about associated symptoms such as nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, constipation, bloating, or unintentional weight loss
Ask how the vomiting is affecting the patient's day-to-day activities, work, and quality of life
Ask about symptoms of dehydration, including headache, dry mouth or lips, dizziness, increased thirst, lethargy, and reduced urine output
Ask about the date of her last menstrual period and acknowledge the recent negative pregnancy test
Ask about social and lifestyle history, including smoking, alcohol intake, illicit drug use — particularly **cannabis use** — occupation, and home situation
Explore the patient's ideas, concerns, and expectations
Make a diagnosis of **cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome**

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you Bella for explaining everything so clearly. From everything you have told me, the most likely explanation for your symptoms is something called cannabis-induced vomiting, or cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome.*

*This is a condition that can happen in people who use cannabis regularly. It can cause repeated episodes of nausea and vomiting over weeks or months, and the episodes can come on quite suddenly, just as you have described. Stress can often make the symptoms worse, which fits with what you have noticed.*

*The most important part of treatment is stopping cannabis completely. Anti-sickness medication can help in the short term, but the vomiting usually continues if cannabis use carries on. Does that make sense? I appreciate that this may be difficult, but I want to reassure you that you are not on your own. We have local services that can support you if you would like help to stop.*

*To your question about whether cutting down would be enough — I am afraid cutting down is not usually sufficient; complete stopping is what is needed for the vomiting to fully resolve.*

*I would also like to see you face to face to examine your abdomen and arrange some blood tests, just to make sure there is nothing else contributing. In the meantime, I can prescribe some anti-sickness tablets to use when your symptoms occur.*

*If at any point the vomiting becomes persistent, you are unable to keep fluids down, you notice blood in your vomit or stools, you develop severe tummy pain, unintentional weight loss, or symptoms of dehydration, please seek urgent medical attention.*
management: Offer a face-to-face appointment to perform an abdominal examination and arrange blood tests including urea and electrolytes, full blood count, liver function tests, and HbA1c
Advise the patient to keep a symptom diary to help track the frequency and severity of symptoms and identify any additional triggers
Offer antiemetic treatment for symptomatic relief, for example prochlorperazine 10 mg three times daily to be used when required

Advise that **stopping cannabis use completely** is the most effective way to prevent further episodes of vomiting; explain that cutting down is insufficient and symptoms typically persist if use continues
Explain that anti-sickness medication may provide short-term relief but will not fully resolve symptoms if cannabis use continues
Offer support for stopping cannabis use and explain that local drug misuse services are available
Discuss strategies to manage stress, including breathing and relaxation exercises, regular physical activity, yoga, and talking therapies

Provide safety-net advice to seek urgent medical review if vomiting becomes persistent, if she is unable to keep fluids down, if there is blood in vomit or stools, if severe abdominal pain develops, if there is unintentional weight loss, or if there are signs of dehydration
learningPoints:
Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (CHS) is associated with regular, long-term cannabis use and presents with recurrent or cyclical episodes of severe nausea and vomiting. Cannabis contains several active compounds that act on receptors within the brain and gastrointestinal system, altering gastric motility, delaying gastric emptying, and affecting lower oesophageal sphincter function.

A key management point is that **symptom resolution requires complete cessation of cannabis use**. **Reducing cannabis intake is insufficient** and symptoms typically persist if use continues. Early recognition, non-judgemental history taking, and clear patient education are essential.

Standard antiemetic medication may be used to provide symptomatic relief. If there is poor response to conventional antiemetics, **topical capsaicin 0.1% cream** may be considered, applied to the abdomen. **Amitriptyline** may also be considered for prevention of recurrent flares; however, the evidence supporting its use is limited.

title: Chronic Tension-Type Headache with Cervicogenic Component

patientData.name: Catherine Birchwood
drugHistory: Not currently on any regular medication

recentConsultation.seenBy: Dr James McDonnell (Clinical Practitioner Access Role) – 3 weeks ago
recentConsultation.notes:
**Presenting complaint:** Headache ongoing for two months, described as a tight band around the head. Associated nausea but no vomiting. No red flag features reported.

**Examination:** Fundoscopy satisfactory in both eyes with no concerning features. Blood pressure 120/70 mmHg. Neurological examination normal.

**Impression:** Tension-type headache.

**Plan:** Patient was reassured. Advised on stress management techniques and use of simple analgesia such as paracetamol and ibuprofen. Safety-net advice given regarding red flag symptoms.

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *Doctor, I am back because my headaches are still there and have not improved.*

If Asked to Explain Further: You have had a headache for almost 3 months. The headache occurs almost every day. The pain is located across the whole frontal area of your head and feels like a tight band. You feel nauseated, but you have not vomited.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:

The headache is worse when you move your neck backwards, particularly when lifting your head upwards. You take paracetamol and ibuprofen, which help temporarily, but the headache keeps returning. You use these medications around five to six times per month. Your last menstrual period was seven days ago.

**Social History:** You work as a customer service agent in a media company, and your job involves long periods of sitting. You do not smoke and do not drink alcohol. You live with your husband and two children. You eat a balanced diet and exercise regularly. You are not currently under significant stress.

**Ideas:** You think your headaches may be migraines rather than tension-type headaches.

**Concerns:** You are worried it could be something serious, as the headaches have not resolved.

**Expectations:** Your husband feels you should be referred for a head scan or to see a specialist.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about the location, onset, character, frequency, and duration of the headaches, and whether the pain radiates
Ask about relieving and aggravating factors
Ask about associated symptoms, including nausea, vomiting, blurred vision, lacrimation, nasal congestion, aura, photophobia, and neck pain
Ask about trauma to the head or neck
Screen for red flag symptoms, including rash, fever, neck stiffness, slurred speech, weakness or paraesthesia, and unintentional weight loss
Ask about features of raised intracranial pressure, such as early morning headaches, vomiting, or headache worsened by coughing or straining

Ask about analgesic use and frequency to exclude **medication overuse headache** (if she takes ibuprofen on 15 or more days per month, or codeine or triptans on 10 or more days per month, consider medication overuse headache)
Ask how the symptoms have affected daily functioning and quality of life
Ask about mood and sleep
Ask about social history, including smoking, alcohol intake, occupation, stress, caffeine intake, and hydration
Explore the patient's ideas, concerns, and expectations
Make a diagnosis of chronic tension-type headache coexisting with a cervicogenic headache

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you, Catherine, for explaining everything so clearly. You mentioned that you were worried this could be a migraine or something more serious. From everything you have told me, your symptoms do not fit with migraine, and there are no concerning features to suggest anything serious, especially as your examination three weeks ago was normal.*

*From what you have described, this fits best with what we call a tension-type headache, along with an element coming from your neck and posture, which we call a cervicogenic headache. When tension-type headaches become more frequent and persistent over time, we describe them as chronic. These types of headaches are very common and can be uncomfortable and frustrating, but they are **not dangerous**.*

*There is no need for scans at this stage. I understand why you were worried, but based on the information we have, imaging would not be helpful.*

*Because these headaches have been happening frequently, using painkillers too often can actually make headaches worse over time. To reduce that risk, I would suggest starting a medication called amitriptyline, taken at night. It is not being used as a painkiller here but to prevent the headaches from coming as often. We would start at a low dose.*

*Alongside this, I would recommend keeping a headache diary so we can track triggers and see what helps. I will also refer you to physiotherapy, as working on neck movement, strength, and posture often makes a big difference with this type of headache.*

*If at any point you develop new symptoms such as weakness, speech problems, vision changes, or a sudden severe headache, I would want you to seek urgent medical advice straight away.*
management: No need for a face-to-face review at present, as she has already been examined and red flag features have been excluded
Offer a headache diary to help monitor triggers, frequency, severity, and response to treatment
Offer amitriptyline 10 mg at night as preventive treatment, given the chronic nature of her headaches and the risk of medication overuse headache
Explain the risk of medication overuse headache and advise limiting simple analgesia for acute attacks to fewer than 15 days per month
Reassure her that brain imaging is not routinely indicated in the absence of red flag symptoms or abnormal neurological findings
Advise optimising posture and workplace ergonomics, including regular breaks from prolonged sitting and screen use
Offer a referral to physiotherapy to help improve neck range of motion, strength, and posture
Provide clear safety-net advice to seek urgent medical review if she develops new neurological symptoms, a sudden severe headache, visual disturbance, or systemic symptoms
Arrange follow-up in 4 to 6 weeks to review symptom control and response to treatment
learningPoints:
**Chronic tension-type headache** is defined as a tension-type headache occurring on **15 or more days per month for more than three months**, in the absence of medication overuse. It often presents as a persistent, bilateral, tight or pressing headache.

Chronic tension-type headache may coexist with secondary headache disorders, such as **cervicogenic headache**, where pain arises from the cervical spine and is commonly triggered by neck movement or prolonged poor posture.

The key aim in managing chronic tension-type headache is to reduce headache frequency and prevent medication overuse headache. Preventive treatment, such as low-dose amitriptyline, is recommended when headaches are frequent or persistent.

Cervicogenic headache is managed primarily with physiotherapy, targeted exercises to improve neck mobility and strength, and ergonomic adjustments.

title: Chest Tightness and Anxiety in a Young Student

recentConsultation.notes: Patient has booked a routine telephone consultation to discuss some concerns.

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *Hi doctor, I think I might have asthma, or maybe I am having a heart attack.*

If Asked to Explain Further: You have been experiencing episodes of chest tightness that occur randomly — while studying, lying in bed, or spending time with friends. This has been happening for around three to four months. The most recent episode occurred last night while watching television and lasted around 25 minutes before settling on its own.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:

Each episode usually lasts 15 to 25 minutes. If you hold your breath or take a deep breath, the chest tightness improves or disappears. You do not have chest pain or shortness of breath. Occasionally the chest tightness is accompanied by a racing heartbeat.

You are currently very stressed, as you are working while preparing for your A-levels. You often stay up late and sleep very little, as you use energy drinks and caffeine to study after work. You are working to support your mother, as your parents have recently divorced and your father has moved out, leaving you both to manage household bills.

**Social History:** You do not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. You work as a coffee shop attendant and live with your mother.

**Ideas:** You think this might be asthma or a heart attack.

**Concerns:** You are worried about these possibilities because of what your colleagues have told you.

**Expectations:** You would like the GP to offer you medication to help with the symptoms.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about the onset, duration, frequency, and pattern of chest tightness
Ask about whether the symptoms are intermittent or constant, and if intermittent, how long each episode lasts
Ask about triggers and relieving factors
Ask about whether symptoms are improving, worsening, or unchanged
Ask about cardiac-associated symptoms, including chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations, dizziness, or syncope
Ask about respiratory symptoms, including cough, wheeze, nocturnal symptoms, exercise-induced symptoms, or recent viral illness
Ask about panic or anxiety features, including sweating, trembling, fear of dying, tingling around the lips, and nausea
Ask about mood and sleep
Ask about family history of sudden cardiac death or heart disease
Ask about social and lifestyle factors, including recent stress, caffeine or energy drink consumption, smoking, alcohol intake, illicit drug use, and occupation
Ask about the impact of symptoms on his daily activities
Ask about the patient's ideas, concerns, and expectations
Make a diagnosis of possible anxiety-related episodes or panic attacks

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you, Leo, for explaining everything so clearly. I can see why you are worried, especially after what your colleagues said about asthma and heart attacks. From what you have told me, your symptoms do not fit with asthma or a heart attack.*

*What this sounds most consistent with is anxiety-related chest tightness, sometimes called panic or anxiety attacks. These can cause very real physical symptoms such as chest tightness and a racing heart. Stress, lack of sleep, and energy drinks can all make this worse. Are you following so far?*

*Would you be happy for me to book you a face-to-face appointment so I can examine your heart and chest, and arrange an ECG and some basic blood tests, mainly to rule out any other contributing causes?*

*I understand that you were hoping for medication to stop this straight away. At this stage, the most effective treatment is actually addressing the triggers, rather than starting tablets.*

*Cutting down on caffeine and energy drinks, improving your sleep routine, and using breathing and relaxation techniques can make a big difference. Talking therapy is another option that can help you understand your symptoms better and give you more control over managing them.*

*I also want to say that it sounds like you are carrying a lot right now — working, studying for your A-levels, and supporting your mum. That is a great deal of pressure for anyone. I can refer you to our social prescriber, who may be able to help you access some support.*

*If at any point you develop chest pain that does not settle, ongoing shortness of breath, collapse, or worsening symptoms, please seek urgent medical help.*
management: Offer a face-to-face review for cardiovascular and respiratory examination
Offer an ECG and baseline blood tests to exclude other abnormalities and provide reassurance
Advise reducing caffeine and energy drink intake, as these can contribute to chest tightness and palpitations
Advise establishing regular sleeping patterns and good sleep hygiene
Discuss stress-relief strategies, including regular physical activity, relaxation and breathing techniques, yoga, and talking therapies
Discuss ways to balance A-level preparation with work commitments, including taking regular breaks and setting realistic study schedules
Offer referral to talking therapies to help manage anxiety-related symptoms
Offer referral to the social prescriber who can help with financial or practical support
Provide clear safety-net advice to seek urgent medical attention if he develops chest pain, persistent shortness of breath, collapse, or worsening symptoms
Arrange follow-up in four weeks to review progress and symptom improvement
learningPoints:
This station highlights the importance of a thorough, structured assessment of chest symptoms in young patients, where anxiety-related causes are common but serious pathology must first be excluded. Careful history-taking to assess red flag cardiac and respiratory features, alongside exploration of psychosocial stressors, is essential.

Anxiety or panic-related chest tightness can present with real physical symptoms, including chest tightness and palpitations, and is often exacerbated by stress, sleep deprivation, and stimulant use such as caffeine and energy drinks. Management should focus on reassurance, lifestyle modification, and addressing underlying stressors, with investigations used judiciously to provide reassurance and exclude pathology.

title: Fatigue and Diarrhoea in a Young Vegan

patientData.name: Emeka Obi
drugHistory: Not currently on any regular medication

recentConsultation.notes: Patient has booked a routine video consultation to discuss some concerns.

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *Hi doctor, I feel tired all the time and this has been ongoing for the last 6 to 7 months.*

If Asked to Explain Further: For the past 6 to 7 months, you have been feeling tired all the time. You are not sure what is causing this, but your mum advised you to book an appointment.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:

You changed your diet about one year ago and now follow a vegan diet. You mainly eat pasta and green vegetables. You sometimes experience cramps and diarrhoea. The diarrhoea can last for about a week and then settles, and this has been happening on and off for the past 6 to 7 months. There is no blood or mucus in the stool. There has been no weight loss or loss of appetite. You also experience some bloating. Your sleep, mood, and appetite are good.

You are currently at university studying sports science and hope to become a football coach. The tiredness is manageable, but at times it prevents you from attending your regular football coaching sessions.

**Social History:** You do not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. You live with your parents. There is no family history of bowel problems that you are aware of. You are a university student and things are going well.

**Ideas:** You are not sure what is causing your tiredness.

**Concerns:** You have no specific concerns.

**Expectations:** You would like the GP to identify the cause of your tiredness.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask what the patient means by feeling tired all the time, whether it is physical tiredness, mental tiredness, or both
Ask how long it has been ongoing and whether it started gradually or suddenly
Ask if there is anything that makes the tiredness better or worse
Ask about mood, sleep, and appetite to screen for psychological causes
Ask about symptoms of obstructive sleep apnoea, including snoring, witnessed apnoeic episodes, and daytime sleepiness
Ask about any recent flu-like illness or infection
Explore dietary history to assess for poor nutritional intake or vitamin deficiencies such as vitamin B12, folate, and iron
Ask about symptoms suggestive of vitamin deficiency, particularly in the context of a vegan diet, including poor concentration, tingling, numbness, or glossitis
Ask about gastrointestinal symptoms including abdominal pain, change in bowel habits such as diarrhoea, and any blood in the stool
Ask about endocrine causes including diabetes with polyuria and polydipsia, and thyroid disease with heat or cold intolerance and palpitations
Screen for red flag symptoms of malignancy, including weight loss, night sweats, new lumps or masses, or a persistent cough
Ask how the symptoms have affected the patient's daily life, studies, and functioning
Explore social history including smoking, alcohol intake, illicit drug use, and any recent stressors
Ask about family history of medical conditions, particularly bowel conditions such as coeliac disease
Explore the patient's ideas, concerns, and expectations
Make a diagnosis of possible nutritional deficiency (vitamin B12 or folate) in the context of a vegan diet, or coeliac disease or inflammatory bowel disease given intermittent diarrhoea

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you Emeka for explaining all that, it is really helpful. From what you have told me, there are a few possible reasons why you may be feeling tired. One of the common causes, especially with a vegan diet, is low levels of certain vitamins such as vitamin B12 or folate. This is because many people get vitamin B12 from animal sources such as meat, fish, and dairy products. Sources for vegans are limited, and it is therefore common for people following a vegan diet to develop vitamin B12 deficiency.*

*Also, your bowel symptoms such as **diarrhoea** and bloating make us think about conditions like coeliac disease. Coeliac disease is a condition where the body reacts to foods containing gluten, such as pasta, which you mentioned you eat quite a lot.*

*What we need to do next is arrange some blood tests to check your vitamin levels, your thyroid function, your blood count, and to screen for coeliac disease. I would also like to arrange a stool test to check for any inflammation in the bowel. In addition, it would be helpful to see you face to face so I can examine you properly, including checking for any lumps and examining your tummy.*

*In the meantime, it would be important to make sure your diet contains enough essential nutrients. With a vegan diet, vitamin B12 is particularly important. You can get this from foods such as fortified breakfast cereals, unsweetened soya drinks, yeast extract such as Marmite, and nutritional yeast flakes.*

*Once the results are back, we will review them together and decide on the best treatment.*
management: Offer a face-to-face examination to assess for lymphadenopathy and perform an abdominal examination
Offer blood tests including vitamin B12, folate, ferritin, vitamin D, coeliac screen, thyroid function tests, full blood count, CRP, HbA1c, liver function tests, and faecal calprotectin

Advise the patient that if any vitamin deficiency is confirmed, this will be treated with appropriate replacement, and if coeliac disease is suspected, he will be referred to a specialist for confirmatory testing; explain that management of coeliac disease involves a gluten-free diet

Advise that in the meantime, he can optimise his vegan diet to ensure adequate intake of vitamin B12; suggest options such as fortified breakfast cereals, unsweetened soya drinks, yeast extract (Marmite), and nutritional yeast flakes
Advise that for his tiredness, he can keep a symptom diary, pace his activities, prioritise tasks, and plan rest periods
Offer follow-up to review his results once available

Provide safety-netting: if he develops worsening symptoms or new symptoms such as tingling in his arms or legs, blurred vision, or confusion, he should seek urgent medical advice as this may indicate significant vitamin B12 deficiency affecting the nerves
learningPoints:
This station focuses on the structured assessment of fatigue as an undifferentiated presentation in primary care. Feeling tired all the time is common and requires a systematic approach.

**Vitamin B12 deficiency** is the most common and clinically significant deficiency in individuals following a vegan diet, as it is found almost exclusively in animal products. A vitamin B12 supplement may be required.

This station also highlights the importance of linking associated symptoms to guide diagnosis. In this case, gastrointestinal symptoms such as diarrhoea and bloating raise the possibility of **coeliac disease** or **inflammatory bowel disease**, which should be appropriately investigated.

title: Dangerous Drug Interaction – Verapamil and Bisoprolol

patientData.name: Vikram Chatterjee
pastMedicalHistory: Myocardial infarction (6 months ago, treated with primary PCI and stenting to the proximal LAD)
Ventricular ectopics with non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (diagnosed 2 days ago)
drugHistory: Verapamil 40 mg three times daily (newly prescribed by cardiology – not yet dispensed)

recentConsultation.notes:
**Dear GP,**

Thank you for referring Mr Vikram Chatterjee, who presented with a four-week history of palpitations.

I reviewed him in the cardiology clinic. His ECG and 3-day Holter monitoring demonstrated ventricular ectopic beats and two short runs of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia.

Echocardiography showed no evidence of structural heart disease, with a preserved ejection fraction of 55%.

I have explained the diagnosis to him and commenced Verapamil 40 mg three times daily.

I will review him again in six weeks to assess his symptom response. In the meantime, please continue Verapamil 40 mg three times daily on repeat prescription.

**Dr Patrick Hughes MBChB, FRCP – Consultant Cardiologist**

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *Hi doctor, the pharmacist would not let me have the new medication the cardiologist prescribed for me. She asked me to speak to you.*

If Asked to Explain Further: You had been experiencing palpitations and saw a GP, who referred you to a cardiologist. The cardiologist carried out some heart tests and prescribed a medication to help with the palpitations. You are still experiencing palpitations. They have not worsened and occur once every 2 to 3 days. You do not have any other symptoms.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:

**Social History:** You do not smoke or drink alcohol. You live with your wife. You are a businessman and own an Indian restaurant. You maintain a good diet and exercise regularly.

**Ideas:** You are not sure why the pharmacist refused to dispense the medication.

**Concerns:** You are worried that the medication may be important for your safety.

**Expectations:** You would like the GP to explain why you cannot have the medication.

If the doctor explains that you cannot take the medication and that it may be unsafe with bisoprolol, you should ask whether the specialist made an error and whether taking the medication could have been dangerous for you. You should become angry and frustrated, and ask the doctor how to make a complaint, as you would like to raise one.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Start by acknowledging that you can see the patient has recently seen a cardiologist for palpitations and ask him to explain in his own words what has happened
Ask about current palpitations, including whether he is still experiencing them and whether they have worsened, improved, or remained the same
Ask about associated symptoms including syncope, dizziness, shortness of breath, chest pain, and exertional symptoms
Ask whether he is still taking all his current medications, particularly bisoprolol
Ask how the symptoms have affected his daily life
Explore social history including smoking, alcohol intake, diet, and exercise level
Ask about family history of heart disease or sudden cardiac death
Ask whether the pharmacist explained why the medication was not dispensed
Recognise a potential drug interaction between verapamil and bisoprolol, which may increase the risk of bradycardia and heart block

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you Vikram for explaining all that, I can understand why this situation would be worrying for you.*

*From what you have told me, and from the letter from the cardiologist, the new medication prescribed is verapamil. The reason the pharmacist has not given this to you is because verapamil and one of your current medications, bisoprolol, should generally not be taken together. **Both of these** medications can slow the heart rate and can potentially be dangerous. Are you following me so far?*

*At this stage, it is difficult to say exactly why this was prescribed, as I do not have enough information. It may be an oversight, but I cannot be certain. What we can do now is contact the cardiology team, inform them about the potential interaction, and seek further guidance from them.*

*In the meantime, you can continue taking your usual medications as prescribed, but it is important that you do not start the verapamil until we have clarified this. What is reassuring is that the pharmacist has picked this up, and you have not started the medication, so there has been no harm to you. Does that make sense?*

*If you would like to raise a concern or make a complaint, you are absolutely entitled to do so. You would need to contact the hospital's Patient Advice and Liaison Service, known as PALS. You can write to them, send an email, or raise your concern verbally, and they will investigate and get back to you.*

*Although I do not expect this to happen, if you develop worsening palpitations, chest pain, shortness of breath, dizziness, or if you faint, please seek urgent medical attention by calling 999.*
management: Explain that verapamil and bisoprolol should generally not be taken together as they can both slow the heart rate and may increase the risk of bradycardia or heart block, which can be dangerous

Explain that this may be a prescribing oversight; however, you do not have enough information at this stage to determine why it was prescribed in this way, and you will clarify this with the cardiology team
Offer to contact the cardiology team to inform them about the potential interaction between verapamil and bisoprolol and to seek further advice
Advise the patient to continue his current medications, including bisoprolol, until further specialist advice is obtained

If the patient wishes to make a complaint, advise that this can be done through the hospital Patient Advice and Liaison Service (PALS), as the issue relates to secondary care; the complaint can be made by writing (sending an email or letter), or raising it verbally
Offer to follow up with the patient once you have heard back from the cardiology team
Provide safety netting that if he develops worsening palpitations, chest pain, shortness of breath, dizziness, or syncope, he should seek urgent medical attention by calling 999
learningPoints:
This station focuses on recognising and managing potentially dangerous drug interactions.

When used together, bisoprolol and verapamil can increase the risk of bradycardia, asystole, severe hypotension, and heart failure.

This station also assesses ethical and professional practice. The clinician should be open and honest with the patient about the potentially dangerous drug interaction while maintaining a non-accusatory approach. It is important not to prematurely attribute blame to the specialist, as there may be clinical reasoning that is not yet clear. The appropriate approach is to acknowledge the concern, ensure patient safety by withholding the medication, and promptly seek clarification from the cardiology team.

title: Amitriptyline-Induced Urinary Symptoms in a Migraine Patient

patientData.name: Adam Churchill
pastMedicalHistory: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (mildly enlarged prostate on examination)
drugHistory: Symbicort 200/6 Turbohaler, one puff twice daily and one puff as required for symptom relief

recentConsultation.notes:
**Dear GP,**

**Re: Adam Churchill | 70-year-old male**

Thank you for referring this patient to the neurology clinic for assessment of recurrent headaches. He describes a history consistent with migraine. An MRI scan of the brain has been performed and is normal. He was previously treated with pizotifen 1.5 mg once daily, which was initially effective but has since lost its benefit. This has now been discontinued. We have commenced amitriptyline 25 mg at night as prophylaxis, with scope to increase to 75 mg at night if required and tolerated.

**Dr David Brown – Consultant Neurologist**

**Seen by Dr Clinton Diwe (Clinical Practitioner role) – 1 week ago**

Presenting complaint: Urinary symptoms including hesitancy, nocturia, and frequency. No red flag symptoms.

Examination: Blood pressure 130/78 mmHg, pulse 68 bpm. PR examination: Mildly enlarged prostate. Urinalysis: Negative for all parameters.

Plan: Blood tests sent for PSA and U&Es. Urine sent for culture. Follow up arranged.

bloodTestResults.summary: PSA, renal function and urine culture all normal.

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *Hi doctor, I would like to discuss my blood test and urine results.*

If Asked to Explain Further: The doctor sent you for these tests because you have been having problems passing urine. You have been going more often than usual, especially at night, and when you try to pass urine it takes a while to get started.

This has started to affect your daily life. You do not go out in the evenings as much anymore or meet your friends for tea because you keep needing to use the toilet. Your friends have started asking questions about why you are going so often and spending a long time in the toilet, which you find quite embarrassing. You also wake up frequently at night due to these symptoms.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:

You have noticed that these symptoms started after you began taking amitriptyline. The medication has helped control your headaches, but you then started to notice these urinary problems.

**Social History:** You do not smoke or drink alcohol. You are a retired train driver. You live with your wife. You enjoy playing golf and spending time with your friends most days.

**Ideas:** You are not sure what is causing your symptoms, but you think it may be related to the new medication, amitriptyline.

**Concerns:** This is affecting your day-to-day life as you now avoid going out with your friends.

**Expectations:** You would like the doctor to help manage these symptoms.

**Question for the Doctor:** If the doctor does not mention it, ask whether this could be related to amitriptyline, as you noticed the symptoms started after starting this medication.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Start by acknowledging that you can see he was reviewed for urinary symptoms and was sent for blood and urine tests
Ask him to describe the symptoms that led to these investigations
Ask about the onset of symptoms
Ask about other lower urinary tract symptoms including urgency, straining, intermittency, terminal dribbling, feeling of incomplete bladder emptying, and poor stream
Ask about symptoms of urinary retention including inability to pass urine, abdominal pain, or suprapubic discomfort
Ask about bowel symptoms such as constipation, which may worsen urinary symptoms
Ask about red flag symptoms for prostate cancer including new onset back pain, bone pain, haematuria, weight loss, and night sweats
Ask about family history of prostate cancer
Ask whether the symptoms started after initiating amitriptyline and whether the medication has helped his headaches
Ask how the symptoms have affected his daily life and mood
Ask about social history including smoking, alcohol intake, occupation, and home situation
Ask about intake of caffeine or caffeinated drinks
Explore the patient's ideas, concerns, and expectations
Make a diagnosis of amitriptyline-induced urinary symptoms

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you Adam for explaining all that, it is **really helpful**. Your blood tests, including your kidney function and the blood test to assess your prostate, have come **back** normal. We also tested your urine for infection, and this was normal as well, which is reassuring.*

*From what you have told me, and looking at the timing of your symptoms, the most likely cause is a side effect of amitriptyline. This medication can affect how the bladder works, which explains the urinary symptoms you are experiencing. Does that make sense?*

*We have a couple of options going forward. **As** you mentioned that amitriptyline has helped with your headaches, one option is to reduce the dose to 10 mg. This may help improve your urinary symptoms and may still provide some benefit for your headaches. However, it is also possible that reducing the dose may not control your headaches, and your urinary symptoms may persist, but it is a reasonable option to try. Alternatively, we can switch to a different medication for migraine prevention such as topiramate or candesartan. What would you prefer?*

*It would also help to reduce caffeine intake, especially in the evening, as this can worsen urinary symptoms.*

*I would like to review you again in about four weeks to see how your symptoms are and whether your headaches remain controlled.*

*Although I do not expect this to happen, if you find that you are unable to pass urine, develop severe tummy pain, notice any blood in your urine, or develop new back pain, please seek medical advice urgently.*
management: Explain to the patient that amitriptyline is the most likely cause of his urinary symptoms due to its anticholinergic side effects

Offer options including reducing the dose of amitriptyline to 10 mg; explain that urinary symptoms may still persist, and his headache control may be less effective, but it is a reasonable option to try

Alternatively, offer switching to another migraine prophylaxis such as topiramate 25 mg once daily, with gradual dose increase if needed, or candesartan 16 mg once daily; **note that candesartan (an ARB) should not be offered in patients already taking an ACE inhibitor, as ACE inhibitors and ARBs should not be used together**

Inform the patient about potential side effects: topiramate can cause gastrointestinal upset and increase the risk of kidney stones, so advise maintaining good fluid intake; candesartan can cause dizziness and cough
Advise reducing caffeine intake, especially in the evening, as this can worsen urinary symptoms
Arrange follow up in 4 weeks to assess both migraine control and whether urinary symptoms have improved

Provide safety netting that if urinary symptoms persist, worsen, or if he develops weight loss, haematuria, or new back pain, he should seek medical advice promptly; advise seeking earlier review if his migraine symptoms worsen
learningPoints:
This station highlights the importance of recognising common medication side effects in primary care. Amitriptyline has anticholinergic properties and can cause urinary symptoms such as hesitancy, frequency, and incomplete bladder emptying, particularly in older males and those with underlying prostatic enlargement.

In patients with benign prostatic hyperplasia, anticholinergic medications can increase the risk of urinary retention. Therefore, their use should be approached with caution, especially in those with significant lower urinary tract symptoms.

Management should involve shared decision making, including discussing options such as dose reduction, discontinuation, or switching to an alternative medication, while balancing symptom control and side effects.

**If dose reduction is offered**, it is important to inform the patient that this may lead to **poorer headache control**, that the urinary symptoms may still persist, and that there remains a **risk of urinary retention**.

title: Exertional Calf Pain in a Smoker

patientData.name: Jeremy Bryant
pastMedicalHistory: Nil – no previous medical history recorded
drugHistory: Not currently on any regular medication

recentConsultation.notes:
**Dear GP,**

**Re: Jeremy Bryant, 55-year-old male**

Jeremy self-referred to our service with a history of cramp-like pain in both calves on walking.

An Ankle Brachial Pressure Index (ABPI) assessment was performed using a handheld Doppler.

ABPI Results:
- Right ABPI: 0.80
- Left ABPI: 0.76

Doppler Waveform Analysis: Biphasic waveforms with reduced amplitude bilaterally, consistent with mild to moderate reduction in arterial flow on the right and moderate reduction on the left.

Jeremy has been advised to arrange follow up with his GP for further assessment and ongoing management.

**Mr Daniel Mansfield BSc (Hons) Podiatry, HCPC Registered Podiatrist**

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *Hi doctor, the podiatrist asked me to see you. He said he would send you a letter about a test he did on my legs.*

If Asked to Explain Further: You have been experiencing cramping pain in both calves for the past 5 months. The pain comes on after walking for about 15 minutes and is relieved by rest after around 6 to 10 minutes. This is now affecting your work as a postman, as you have to stop frequently while walking. You have not noticed any pain at rest or at night. You have not noticed any ulcers or colour changes in your feet.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:

**Social History:** You smoke 20 cigarettes per day and have done so for 30 years. You do not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. You work as a postman. You live with your wife.

**Ideas:** You are not sure what is causing your symptoms.

**Concerns:** You are worried because this is affecting your job as a postman and your ability to walk.

**Expectations:** You would like the GP to provide a solution to stop the pain.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Acknowledge that you have reviewed the podiatry letter regarding the test on his legs and ask the patient to explain, in his own words, the symptoms he has been experiencing
Ask about the pain, including onset, nature, and any relieving or aggravating factors
Ask whether the pain is bilateral or unilateral
Ask about walking distance before the pain comes on, how long it takes to settle with rest, and whether this has worsened over time

Ask about red flag symptoms of acute limb ischaemia (the 5 Ps), including pain at rest or night time pain, paresis (weakness in the lower limbs), paraesthesia (numbness, decreased sensation or tingling), a perishingly cold limb, and pallor (change in colour of the limb)
Ask about other associated symptoms, including non-healing ulcers or wounds on the legs and hair loss on the legs or feet
Ask about swelling or redness in the legs to help exclude deep vein thrombosis
Ask about chest pain, shortness of breath, and palpitations to screen for co-existing cardiovascular disease
Ask about the impact of symptoms on the patient's life, including his occupation
Ask about smoking, alcohol intake, diet, and lifestyle
Ask about the patient's ideas, concerns, and expectations
Make a diagnosis of intermittent claudication secondary to peripheral arterial disease, supported by reduced ABPI values

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you Jeremy for explaining all that, it is **really helpful**. From what you have told me, and from the test results the podiatrist sent, this looks like a condition called peripheral arterial disease. Is this something you have heard of before?*

*What this means is that the blood vessels supplying your legs have become narrowed, so when you walk and your muscles need more blood, they are not getting enough. That is why you get the cramping pain, and it improves when you rest. Does that make sense so far?*

*The reassuring thing is that you are not getting pain at rest or at night, which tells me this is at an earlier stage, and there is a lot we can do to manage it and improve your symptoms.*

*The most important thing we need to focus on is improving your blood flow and reducing your future risk of heart problems or stroke. One of the biggest factors here is smoking. Stopping smoking is the most effective step you can take to prevent this from getting worse. Is this something you would be willing to consider?*

*We will also start you on medications to protect your blood vessels. This includes a cholesterol-lowering tablet called a statin and a blood-thinning medication to reduce the risk of clots.*

*Another very important part of treatment is exercise. Regular walking actually helps improve the blood supply over time. I will refer you to a supervised exercise programme where they will guide you on how to do this safely.*

*We will also arrange to have your blood pressure checked and carry out some blood tests.*

*Although I do not expect this to happen, if you notice any sudden worsening of the pain, pain at rest, your leg becoming very cold, pale, numb, or weak, it is important that you seek urgent medical attention by calling 999.*
management: Explain to the patient that his symptoms and test results are consistent with peripheral arterial disease, where there is reduced blood flow to the legs due to narrowing of the arteries
Offer blood tests to screen for associated conditions, including HbA1c, cholesterol, lipid profile, liver function tests, renal function tests, and full blood count
Advise the patient that his blood pressure will be checked when his blood tests are taken
Offer a statin such as atorvastatin 80 mg once daily for cardiovascular risk reduction
Offer antiplatelet therapy such as clopidogrel 75 mg once daily to reduce cardiovascular risk
Offer referral to physiotherapy for a supervised exercise programme, encouraging regular walking to the point of pain, resting, and then continuing, as this helps improve symptoms over time
Advise smoking cessation as this is the most important step to slow disease progression; offer referral to a smoking cessation service if the patient wishes
Advise on lifestyle modification, including a healthy diet, weight management, and regular physical activity
Offer support for work, providing a fit note with amended duties to support him in the workplace if needed

Provide safety netting for signs of acute limb ischaemia, including sudden worsening pain or rest pain, pallor, paraesthesia, paralysis, or a perishingly cold leg, and advise him to seek urgent medical attention by calling 999
Offer follow up in 4 to 6 weeks to review symptoms and response to treatment
learningPoints:
Intermittent claudication typically presents as pain in the calves that occurs during walking and is relieved by rest. The hallmark feature is pain that develops after walking a predictable distance and usually resolves within about 10 minutes of rest.

Red flag features that indicate the need for urgent vascular referral include pain at rest, which may be worse at night, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, a perishingly cold limb, and paralysis.

The Ankle Brachial Pressure Index (ABPI) is a key diagnostic tool in primary care:
- Less than 0.5 suggests chronic limb-threatening ischaemia and requires urgent referral
- 0.9 or less suggests the presence of peripheral arterial disease
- 0.91–0.99 indicates PAD may be present; further investigation required if clinically suspected
- 1.0–1.4 is considered normal
- Greater than 1.4 may suggest arterial calcification (e.g. in diabetes or rheumatoid arthritis)

Management focuses not only on symptom control but also on reducing cardiovascular risk through smoking cessation, antiplatelet therapy, statins, and supervised exercise programmes for 3 months.

title: Diagnosis of COPD Following Spirometry

patientData.name: Peter Hunter
drugHistory: Not currently on any regular medication

recentConsultation.seenBy: Seen by Debbie Burton (Respiratory Nurse specialist) – 2 days ago
recentConsultation.notes:
**A&E Discharge Summary – 3 weeks ago**

Peter Hunter attended A&E with a history of productive cough with yellowish sputum and progressively worsening breathlessness. Significant smoking history of approximately 30 cigarettes daily for 30 years.

Chest X-ray: Satisfactory, no acute abnormalities identified.

Treatment: Prednisolone 30 mg once daily for 5 days; Doxycycline 200 mg stat on day 1, followed by 100 mg once daily for a total of 5 days.

He was advised to follow up with his GP for further assessment, including consideration of spirometry.

**Spirometry Results (Post-Bronchodilator)**

| Parameter | Measured | Predicted | % Predicted |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| FEV₁ | 2.40 L | 3.20 L | 75% |
| FVC | 3.70 L | 4.30 L | 86% |
| FEV₁/FVC | 0.65 | 0.75 | — |

Bronchodilator Reversibility: FEV₁ increase +100 mL (5%), No significant reversibility.

Flow-Volume Loop: Concave expiratory limb demonstrated. Volume-Time Curve: Prolonged expiratory phase. Test quality: Good and reproducible.

Patient advised to follow up with GP to discuss results.

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *Hi doctor, I have been asked to make this appointment to discuss the results of the breathing test I did for my breathing problems.*

If Asked to Explain Further: You have been experiencing shortness of breath for the past 3 months, which has been gradually worsening.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:

You become short of breath with activities such as walking about 200 to 300 metres, hurrying while walking, or playing with your grandchildren, and you often have to stop to catch your breath. You have also noticed a cough that occurs throughout the day. The cough is productive of clear sputum and has been present for 3 months. You do not feel breathless at rest. You do not have chest pain or breathlessness at night.

You were previously treated for a chest infection 3 weeks ago. You feel better in yourself, and the sputum has changed from yellow to clear, but the cough and breathlessness are still present.

**Social History:** You smoke 30 cigarettes per day and have done so for 30 years. You do not drink alcohol. You live with your wife. Your grandchildren visit every weekend. You are a retired electrician.

**Ideas:** You are not sure what is causing your symptoms.

**Concerns:** You are worried because you are now finding it difficult to play with your grandchildren.

**Expectations:** You would like the GP to explain the results and help improve your symptoms.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Acknowledge that you have reviewed the spirometry results and ask the patient to explain, in his own words, the symptoms he has been experiencing
Ask about the shortness of breath, including onset, progression, and severity
Ask about functional limitation, including how far he can walk and what activities bring on symptoms
Ask whether he is breathless at rest or only on exertion
Ask about associated respiratory symptoms including cough, sputum production, and wheeze
Ask about features suggestive of heart failure, including orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, and leg swelling
Ask about chest pain and palpitations to help exclude angina
Ask about red flag symptoms to rule out malignancy, including weight loss, night sweats, and haemoptysis
Ask about past respiratory infections and whether he has required steroids, antibiotics, or hospital admission due to chest symptoms in the last year
Ask about social history including smoking, alcohol intake, home situation, occupation, diet, and the impact of his condition on daily functioning
Ask about the patient's ideas, concerns, and expectations
Make a diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you Peter for explaining all that, it is **really helpful**. From what you have told me, and from the breathing test results, this is consistent with a condition called chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, also known as COPD. Is this something you have heard of before?*

*COPD is a **long term** condition where the airways become narrowed and inflamed, which makes it harder for air to move in and out of the lungs. This is why you are experiencing breathlessness and a persistent cough. It can also flare up from time to time, especially with infections. Does that make sense so far?*

*The main cause of this is smoking, and stopping smoking is the most important step we can take to slow the condition down and prevent it from getting worse. Is this something you would be willing to consider?*

*In terms of treatment, we will start you on a regular inhaler that helps to **open up** your airways and improve your breathing. This is a combination inhaler called **Anoro** Ellipta, which you will use every day. We will also give you another inhaler (salbutamol) to use only when you feel more breathless.*

*I will arrange for our COPD nurse to go through how to use the inhalers with you and provide you with a personalised COPD plan.*

*You mentioned that your breathlessness is affecting how you play with your grandchildren. I would also like to refer you to a pulmonary rehabilitation programme, which has been shown to significantly improve breathlessness and quality of life.*

*We will also arrange some blood tests and ensure your vaccinations such as flu and pneumonia vaccines are up to date.*

*Although I do not expect this to happen, if you develop worsening breathlessness, chest pain, coughing up blood, or **feel** generally unwell, please seek urgent medical attention.*
management: Offer to start a LAMA + LABA combination inhaler (for example, Anoro Ellipta or Ultibro Breezhaler), as the patient is in Group B (mMRC score 2 or more, fewer than 2 exacerbations per year, no hospital admissions for COPD)
Offer a short-acting bronchodilator (SABA such as salbutamol) with a spacer device for relief of breakthrough symptoms if required
Advise smoking cessation as this is the most important step to slow disease progression; offer referral to a smoking cessation service and discuss support options if he is willing
Offer referral to pulmonary rehabilitation to improve breathlessness, exercise tolerance, and quality of life
Offer vaccinations including annual influenza vaccine and pneumococcal vaccine
Offer baseline blood tests including full blood count to check for anaemia or polycythaemia
Offer referral to a COPD nurse, who will provide inhaler technique training and help develop a personalised COPD self-management plan

Provide safety netting that if he develops worsening breathlessness, chest pain, haemoptysis, or becomes systemically unwell, he should seek urgent medical attention by contacting the GP or calling NHS 111 if out of hours
Offer follow up in 4 to 6 weeks to review symptoms, inhaler technique, and response to treatment
learningPoints:
COPD is a common chronic lung condition and should be suspected in people aged over 35 years who have a risk factor, such as smoking or occupational or environmental exposure, and present with symptoms including exertional breathlessness, chronic or recurrent cough, or regular sputum production.

A post-bronchodilator ratio of FEV₁/FVC of less than 0.7 on spirometry confirms persistent airflow obstruction and supports the diagnosis.

This station emphasises the updated GOLD classification adopted by NICE, where patients are grouped based on symptom burden and exacerbation history to guide management. **Group A and B patients** have 0 or 1 exacerbation per year without hospital admission. **Group A** patients have mMRC 0–1 (not troubled by breathlessness except during strenuous exercise). **Group B** patients have mMRC 2 or more (short of breath when hurrying or on minimal exertion). **Group E** patients have 2 or more exacerbations within a year or at least one hospital admission due to COPD.

Management should be holistic and include smoking cessation, pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccinations, inhaler technique education, and a personalised self-management plan.

title: Infected Eczema with Possible Head Lice

recentConsultation.notes: No significant recent consultations. Patient's mother, Helen Fowler, is calling to discuss concerns regarding her daughter.

patientStory:
**Opening Statement (Mother's brief):** *Hi doctor, I think my daughter's eczema is flaring up again and I need some stronger treatment.*

If Asked to Explain Further: Your daughter has had a flare of eczema on the back of her neck and scalp for the last 3 days. She has been scratching both areas continuously.

You have been using her steroid cream (Eumovate) and E45 cream on her neck. However, this has not improved the rash and it seems to be getting worse. You have noticed some yellowish crusting at the back of her neck.

You have also noticed some white flakes on her scalp when combing her hair. Your ex-husband's wife mentioned that she noticed your daughter scratching her scalp, did wet combing, and saw a live louse, which she believes was removed.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:

The rash on her neck is dry and not oozing or bleeding. She is otherwise well. She is eating, drinking, and passing urine normally. There has been no known contact with anyone else who has head lice or an itchy scalp.

**Social History:** She lives with you but spends time with her father occasionally. She attends nursery.

**Ideas:** You think this might be head lice because the symptoms started while she was staying with her father, and his partner mentioned that she found lice during wet combing.

**Concerns:** You are worried because her symptoms usually improve with steroid treatment, but this time they are not responding to steroids.

**Expectations:** You would like stronger treatment to help settle the rash.

**Questions for the doctor:** Can she still attend nursery? Do you need to inform the nursery? Could this be due to her father or his partner not washing her hair properly?

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about the rash, including onset, duration, location, and progression
Ask about the nature of the rash, including redness, crusting, discharge, oozing, and itching
Ask about associated systemic symptoms such as fever, lethargy, poor oral intake, or reduced urine output

Ask about scalp symptoms, including itching, rash, and whether any lice or eggs have been seen; note that a live louse must be found to confirm active head lice infestation, and an itchy scalp alone is not sufficient to make the diagnosis
Ask about contact with others who may have head lice
Ask about previous eczema flares and frequency of flares per month
Ask what treatments have been used and whether they have been effective
Ask about symptoms to help exclude safeguarding concerns, including whether the child appears withdrawn or has any marks, injuries, or wounds on the body
Ask about the impact of the rash on sleep and daily activities
Ask about social history, including nursery attendance and home situation
Ask about the parent's ideas, concerns, and expectations
Make a diagnosis of possible secondary bacterial infection (impetigo) due to itching from head lice or eczema

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you Helen for explaining all that, it is **really helpful**. I understand you were wondering whether this could be head lice, especially as her symptoms started while she was staying with her father and his partner mentioned finding lice.*

*It is possible that your daughter may have had head lice. With her background of eczema, the itching can cause small breaks in the skin. These breaks can then allow **bacteria** to enter and lead to a skin infection called impetigo. This would explain the yellow crusting you have noticed at the back of her neck. Does that make sense so far?*

*Another important clue here is that the steroid cream is not helping and may even be making things worse. When the skin becomes infected, steroid creams on their own do **not treat** the infection and can sometimes allow it to worsen. This pattern strongly points towards a skin infection like impetigo rather than eczema alone.*

*In terms of what we can do next, it would be **really helpful** to see the rash more closely. If you are happy to do so, you could send us a clear photograph of the affected areas, and I can review it and guide you further.*

*If it does look like a skin infection, we can start treatment with an antiseptic cream called hydrogen peroxide, which you would apply three times a day for 5 days. I would advise that you avoid using the steroid cream on that area for now, as it may make things worse. You can continue using her moisturising creams regularly to keep the skin well hydrated. Are you happy with that?*

*As you have not seen any live lice, it is possible that the wet combing may have already taken care of it. However, if you are still concerned about head lice, wet combing is an effective method for both detecting and treating them.*

*Regarding nursery, if this were head lice alone, she would be able to attend as normal. However, as we are concerned about a possible skin infection, it would be best for her to stay off nursery until 48 hours after starting treatment, as it can be contagious.*

*I also want to reassure you that head lice are not related to poor hygiene. They can occur in clean hair, and they spread through direct head-to-head contact rather than how often hair is washed.*
management: Explain to the mother that it is possible that head lice, on a background of eczema, has led to increased itching, causing breaks in the skin and resulting in a secondary infection, which explains the yellowish crusting
Offer a face-to-face assessment to have a closer look at the scalp and the back of the neck; if this is not possible, advise sending a clear photograph for review

Advise that if the appearance suggests infection, treatment can be started with a topical antiseptic such as hydrogen peroxide 1% cream or a topical antibiotic such as fusidic acid 2%, applied three times daily for 5 days
Advise keeping the child's nails short and avoiding scratching to reduce further skin damage and the risk of infection
Advise continued regular use of emollients such as E45 cream multiple times daily; advise avoiding topical steroids on the affected infected area as this may worsen the infection

Reassure her that as she did not find any head lice, it is possible that the wet combing carried out by her ex-husband's wife was effective; if she remains concerned, she can repeat wet combing, as it is an effective method for both diagnosing and treating head lice

Advise that the child can continue to attend nursery if this is due to head lice alone; however, as impetigo is suspected, advise that she should remain off nursery until 48 hours after starting treatment, as it can be contagious
Reassure the mother that head lice are not related to poor hygiene; they spread through direct head-to-head contact rather than how often hair is washed
Provide safety netting that if the child develops fever, worsening redness, spreading rash, pain, or becomes systemically unwell, she should seek urgent medical attention
learningPoints:
This station highlights the importance of recognising secondary bacterial skin infection. Constant scratching, for example from head lice, can lead to breaks in the skin and subsequent infection such as impetigo.

It is important to note that the use of topical steroids on impetigo can worsen the infection. Steroids suppress the local immune response, allowing bacterial infections such as Staphylococcus or Streptococcus to spread, while potentially masking symptoms — a phenomenon known as impetigo incognito.

Head lice should be diagnosed by identifying a live louse. An itchy scalp alone is not sufficient to make the diagnosis.

Wet combing is both a diagnostic and treatment method. If head lice is confirmed, the recommended treatment involves repeated wet combing sessions over 2 weeks, typically on days 1, 5, 9, and 13. It is also important to treat all affected household members on the same day to prevent reinfection.

title: Paramedic Query on Palpitations Management

patientData.name: Graham Telford
drugHistory: Not currently on any regular medication

recentConsultation.notes: Paramedic Sally Overstone is calling on behalf of Graham Telford regarding palpitations.

patientStory:
**Opening Statement (Paramedic's brief):** *Hello doctor, I am calling for some advice regarding Graham Telford, a 49-year-old male who I believe is a patient at your practice.*

If Asked to Explain Further: You attended a 999 call made by Graham's wife. Graham reports palpitations that have been ongoing for the past three months. Today's episode felt particularly frightening to him, which prompted the call for an ambulance. You are unsure whether he needs to be conveyed to Accident and Emergency or whether he can be managed safely in the community.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:

He reports occasional shortness of breath associated with the palpitations, although this does not occur with every episode. There is no associated chest pain, dizziness, or syncope, and the palpitations are not triggered by exertion.

There is no family history of sudden cardiac death.

Previously, he experienced approximately one episode every two to three days. However, he is now experiencing at least one episode per day.

He describes the palpitations as regular in nature. Each episode typically lasts around 10 minutes before resolving spontaneously, although today's episode lasted up to 15 minutes.

He has recently started a new job as a restaurant manager, which has been quite stressful. To cope, he drinks up to ten cups of coffee per day.

You have performed an ECG, which shows normal sinus rhythm with no abnormalities and a rate of 89 beats per minute.

His observations are stable: pulse rate 84 bpm, blood pressure 130/70 mmHg, temperature 36.1°C, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute. Chest is clear with no murmurs.

**Ideas:** You are unsure what is causing his palpitations.

**Concerns:** You are concerned because his symptoms are becoming more frequent, and you are unsure whether he requires hospital assessment.

**Expectations:** You would like clear guidance from the GP on whether to convey him to hospital or manage him in the community.

If the doctor asks to speak to the patient, explain that he is hearing impaired and finds it difficult to communicate over the phone.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Thank the paramedic for attending the patient and for calling to discuss the case
Ask about the onset and progression of the palpitations, including frequency and whether symptoms are worsening or stable over time
Ask about the nature of the palpitations, including whether they feel fast, regular, or irregular
Ask about the duration of each episode
Ask for associated red flag features, including chest pain, shortness of breath, dizziness, syncope, exertional symptoms, and any family history of sudden cardiac death or cardiac disease
Ask about potential triggers such as stress, anxiety, caffeine, or energy drink intake
Ask about sleep pattern, mood, and symptoms of anxiety
Ask whether an ECG and a full set of observations have been performed, and request the results
Ask about social history, including smoking, alcohol intake, recreational drug use, occupation, and home situation
Ask about the paramedic's ideas, concerns, and expectations, as well as those of the patient
Make a diagnosis of likely benign palpitations related to excess caffeine intake and stress

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you Sally for explaining everything so clearly and for the assessment you have **done** for Graham, that is really helpful. From what you have described, he is currently stable, his observations are within normal limits, and his ECG shows a normal sinus rhythm, which is reassuring.*

*Based on the history, this sounds most in keeping with benign palpitations, likely related to his high caffeine intake and the stress from his new role. It is reassuring that there are no red flag features such as chest pain, collapse, or exertional symptoms to suggest a more serious cause at this stage.*

*I think, given how stable he is at the moment, we could safely manage him in the community rather than taking him to hospital, as long as you are comfortable with that as well.*
