*It would be helpful if we could encourage him to gradually reduce his caffeine intake to no more than one to two cups per day and avoid energy drinks or other stimulants. Supporting him with stress management, such as improving sleep and considering ways to reduce work-related pressure would also be beneficial.*

*I can arrange some blood tests for him, including thyroid function, blood sugar, full blood count, liver function, kidney function, and cholesterol levels, just to ensure there are no other contributing factors. I will organise an appointment with the nurse and send him a confirmation.*

*Please let him know that if his symptoms worsen or do not improve, he should contact us, and we can consider further investigations such as a 24-hour ECG or a 3-day Holter monitor.*

*Meanwhile, it would also be helpful for him to keep a symptom diary to identify any triggers and patterns related to his palpitations.*

*Would you be happy to advise him on the red flag symptoms to watch out for, such as chest pain, worsening shortness of breath, severe dizziness, or fainting or collapse, and that he should seek urgent medical attention by calling 999 if any of these occur?*

*I will send him a text message summarising everything we have discussed, including what to do next and the warning signs to look out for.*
management: Thank the paramedic for the detailed assessment
Advise that there are no red flag features to suggest an immediate life-threatening cause, so hospital conveyance is not required at this stage
Explain that the likely cause of his palpitations is related to excessive caffeine intake and stress
Inform the paramedic to advise the patient to significantly reduce caffeine intake, ideally limiting it to no more than one to two cups per day, and to avoid energy drinks or other stimulants
Encourage stress management strategies, including adequate rest, regular sleep, and relaxation techniques; advise that he may discuss with his employer to explore ways of reducing work-related stress
Advise the patient to keep a symptom diary, noting the timing, duration, and any triggers of the palpitations
Offer to organise baseline blood tests, including thyroid function tests, full blood count, HbA1c, urea and electrolytes, liver function tests, and lipid profile
Advise that if his palpitations persist, worsen, or do not improve, he should seek review, and further investigations such as a 3-day Holter monitor will be considered

Ask the paramedic to provide clear safety-net advice to the patient to seek urgent medical attention by calling 999 if symptoms change, including chest pain, syncope, severe dizziness, worsening shortness of breath, or prolonged episodes
Inform the paramedic that you will send the patient a text message summarising everything discussed, including the management plan and red flag symptoms
learningPoints:
Palpitations are a common presentation, and while many cases are benign, it is important to systematically exclude red flag features such as chest pain, syncope, exertional symptoms, and a family history of sudden cardiac death, which may indicate a serious underlying cardiac condition.

In a patient who is clinically stable with no red flag features, it is safe to advise on possible triggers such as caffeine and stress, while carrying out basic investigations including thyroid function tests, HbA1c, lipid profile, urea and electrolytes, and liver function tests to exclude any underlying abnormalities.

A watch-and-wait approach can then be taken to see if symptoms improve with lifestyle modification before proceeding to further investigations such as a 24-hour ECG or a 3-day Holter monitor, with appropriate safety-netting in place.

title: Parental Request for Antidepressants in an Adolescent

patientData.name: Sandra Olderman
drugHistory: Not currently on any regular medication

recentConsultation.notes:
**Seen by Dr Aisha Abdul (Clinical Practitioner role) – 2 months ago**

Presenting complaint: Seen with mum. Mum reports that the patient is anxious, withdrawn, and generally has a low mood ongoing for one month. No known triggers. Attending school and managing well. No thoughts of suicide.

Examination: Vitals stable. Maintaining eye contact. No pressure of speech. No delusions or signs of psychosis.

Impression: Depression.

Plan: Referred to CAMHS. Safety-netting advice given.

patientStory:
**Opening Statement (Mother's brief):** *Hello doctor, we recently saw a private psychiatrist who recommended that my daughter should be started on antidepressants. They advised fluoxetine 10 mg. Please can you prescribe this?*

If Asked to Explain Further: Your daughter was seen by the GP two months ago and was thought to have depression. She was referred to CAMHS, but you were informed that the waiting time is currently around six months. You felt this was too long to wait, so your husband used private health insurance to arrange a consultation with a private psychiatrist. The psychiatrist assessed her, confirmed a diagnosis of depression, and advised that she should start antidepressant medication. You were told that prescribing it privately would involve a cost, but that the GP could prescribe it under the NHS. The psychiatrist recommended fluoxetine 10 mg.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:

Sandra has been low in mood and feels anxious about going to school. She is withdrawn at home and has lost interest in activities she previously enjoyed. There are no clear triggers. Her sleep and appetite are both normal, but she does not engage in activities as she used to.

She continues to attend school, and there have been no concerns raised by teachers. She has not reported any bullying.

**Social History:** Non-smoker, no alcohol use, no illicit drug use. She lives with both parents and her older brother. Family life is stable.

**Ideas:** You believe she is depressed.

**Concerns:** You are worried that her symptoms may worsen while waiting to be seen by CAMHS.

**Expectations:** You would like the GP to prescribe the recommended medication.

If asked about your daughter's whereabouts, say that she is currently at school.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about the onset and progression of her low mood, including whether it is improving, worsening, or staying the same, and whether it is persistent or intermittent
Ask about associated depressive symptoms, including poor sleep or increased sleep, reduced or increased appetite, and any weight changes
Ask about possible triggers, including stressors at school, changes in circumstances, or any recent loss or significant life event
Screen for risk by asking about any thoughts of self-harm, suicidal ideation, plans, or previous attempts
Ask if she has been unwell in any way recently
Ask about her social relationships, including whether she has friends and whether she is in any romantic relationships
Explore anxiety symptoms, including what she feels anxious about and any avoidance behaviours
Ask about school functioning, including attendance, academic performance, relationships with peers and teachers, and any concerns about bullying
Ask about any family history of depression or other mental health conditions
Ask about social history, including home situation and any history of substance use
Confirm details of the private psychiatric assessment, including diagnosis, recommendations, and whether any written communication is available
Assess the mother's ideas, concerns, and expectations, particularly regarding starting medication
Make a diagnosis of depression

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you Katie for explaining everything so clearly, and I can completely understand why you are concerned about Sandra, especially with the long wait to be seen by CAMHS. You have done the right thing by seeking help early and exploring other options.*

*From what you have told me, it does sound like Sandra is experiencing symptoms of depression, and I understand why the private psychiatrist has suggested starting medication. Fluoxetine is in fact the first-line antidepressant used in young people when medication is needed.*

*However, in the UK, we usually start this type of medication in children and young people under specialist guidance, such as through CAMHS. This is because they need closer monitoring and support when starting treatment. **So** at this stage, it would be safest for us to involve CAMHS before initiating medication. Does that make sense so far?*

*In the meantime, there are still very effective things we can do to support Sandra. Talking therapies, particularly cognitive **behavioural** therapy, can be very helpful. I can provide you with some information to read, and you can go through it together with Sandra as well.*

*In regards to getting her seen by CAMHS, we can let them know that her symptoms are ongoing and see if there is any possibility of expediting her appointment. At home, simple measures can also make a difference, such as maintaining a regular routine, encouraging good sleep, gentle physical activity, and keeping communication open so she feels supported.*

*It would also be helpful for us to check for any physical causes that can sometimes present with similar symptoms to low mood. This includes checking vitamin levels such as B12, folate, and iron, as well as thyroid function. How would you feel about us arranging these tests?*

*If at any point you notice that she is talking about harming herself, expressing suicidal thoughts, or if her mood significantly worsens, it is important to seek urgent help by contacting NHS 111 or local mental health crisis services.*

*I would also like to arrange a follow-up in about 4 to 6 weeks, ideally with Sandra present, so we can review how she is getting on and decide on the next steps together.*
management: Acknowledge the mother's concerns and thank her for seeking help early
Explain that depression in young people is best managed with a combination of psychological support and, where appropriate, medication, but this should usually involve specialist input such as CAMHS
Advise that GPs do not usually initiate antidepressants in young people under the age of 18, and this is typically done under specialist guidance
Explain that cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is very effective, and offer referral to appropriate services
Offer to write to CAMHS to request an expedited appointment if possible, given the ongoing symptoms
Offer blood tests to check for other conditions that can present with similar symptoms, including vitamin B12, folate, and iron deficiency, as well as thyroid function tests
Encourage supportive measures at home, including maintaining a routine, good sleep hygiene, regular physical activity, and open communication
Discuss school support, including informing the school if appropriate so that additional support can be provided

Provide safety-netting by advising the mother to seek urgent help if there are any concerns about self-harm, suicidal thoughts, or significant deterioration in mood, including contacting local mental health crisis services or NHS 111
Offer follow-up in 4 to 6 weeks, ideally with Sandra present, to review progress and reassess
learningPoints:
Depression in children is a condition that GPs must be confident in recognising and assessing. The key symptoms of depression include persistent sadness or low mood, which may present as irritability in young people, and loss of interest or pleasure in usual activities.

During assessment, it is important to consider and exclude other conditions that can mimic depressive symptoms, such as anaemia, hypothyroidism, and viral illnesses.

Management primarily involves psychological interventions, particularly cognitive behavioural therapy, alongside referral to CAMHS for specialist input. GPs do not usually initiate antidepressants in children under the age of 18, as this requires specialist involvement and close monitoring.

This case also highlights an important medico-legal principle: according to GMC guidance in *Good Medical Practice* (2024), doctors must recognise and work within the limits of their competence. If prescribing based on another healthcare professional's recommendation, the GP must be satisfied that the prescription is appropriate and safe. In this scenario, initiating antidepressant medication in a young person without specialist involvement would not be within the GP's scope of competence.

title: Incidental Pulmonary Fibrosis on CT Scan

patientData.name: Alice Bedford
drugHistory: Nitrofurantoin 50 mg at night (started 18 months ago for prophylaxis against recurrent UTIs)

recentConsultation.notes:
**CT Chest Report**

Clinical Indication: General health check-up (private insurance screening)

**Findings:** Bilateral, predominantly basal and subpleural reticular opacities. Areas of interlobular septal thickening are noted, with early honeycombing seen in the posterior lower lobes. Mild traction bronchiectasis is present. No focal consolidation identified. No suspicious pulmonary nodules or masses. No pleural effusion or pneumothorax. No significant mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy.

**Impression:** Imaging features are in keeping with early pulmonary fibrosis, with a basal and subpleural predominance, early honeycombing, and traction bronchiectasis.

Clinical correlation is advised. Referral to a respiratory specialist and consideration of pulmonary function testing is recommended.

**Dr James Whitaker, MBBS, FRCR – Consultant Radiologist**

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *Hello doctor, I recently had a full health check through my private health insurance as part of a routine assessment, and they did a CT scan. They told me they found something in my lungs and advised me to discuss this with my GP.*

If Asked to Explain Further: You feel completely well in yourself. This was part of a routine full body health check arranged through your private health insurance. You were told that something was found in your lungs, but you are not sure what it means.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:

You do not have any symptoms and feel well in yourself.

If asked about nitrofurantoin: You have been taking it for the past 18 months. It was prescribed by a urologist due to recurrent urinary tract infections. This has been effective, and you have not experienced a urinary tract infection for approximately one year.

**Social History:** You do not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. You live with your husband and work as a finance analyst for a bank.

**Ideas:** You are not sure what this finding means.

**Concerns:** You are worried because something has been found despite feeling completely well.

**Expectations:** You would like the GP to explain the scan results.

**Questions for the GP:** What is pulmonary fibrosis? Is this condition curable? What might have caused this? If the doctor mentions that your medication may have contributed, ask if stopping the medication would allow your lungs to return to normal. Also ask whether the side effect was not discussed prior to you starting the medication, and whether it is a common side effect. If the doctor suggests referral to a specialist, ask what the specialist is likely to do.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask why the CT scan was carried out in the first place
Ask if she has any respiratory symptoms such as cough, shortness of breath, reduced exercise tolerance, wheeze, or chest pain
Ask whether she has noticed any constitutional symptoms such as weight loss, fatigue, fevers, or night sweats
Ask about any history of tuberculosis, pneumonia, or recurrent chest infections
Ask about symptoms suggestive of connective tissue disease, including joint pains, rashes, dry eyes, dry mouth, Raynaud's phenomenon, or muscle weakness
Ask about social history, including smoking, alcohol use, and home situation
Ask about the patient's occupation and work history (risk occupations include livestock farming or bird keeping, hairdressers, construction workers, plumbers, miners, or demolition workers)
Ask about any family history of lung disease
Explore the patient's ideas, concerns, and expectations
Make a diagnosis of pulmonary fibrosis and consider nitrofurantoin-induced lung toxicity as an important possible cause

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you Alice for explaining everything, and I can understand why this has come as a surprise, especially as you are feeling completely well. You have done the right thing by following this up.*

*From the scan results, there are some early changes in the lungs that we call pulmonary fibrosis. Have you heard of this before?*

*This is a condition where there is some scarring in the lungs. Sometimes this can happen on its own without a clear cause, and sometimes it can occur after previous chest infections. In your case, one possible cause is the medication nitrofurantoin, especially as you have been taking it for a longer period.*

*Does that make sense so far?*

*In terms of your question about whether this is curable, if this is related to the medication, stopping it can prevent things from getting worse and may even lead to some improvement, particularly as we have picked this up early. However, any **scarring** that has already formed may not **completely reverse**. The important thing is that we act early to prevent progression.*

*You also asked what might have caused this and why this was not discussed before. I am sorry if this was not explained to you at the time. Side effects like this are quite rare, and nitrofurantoin is generally a safe and commonly used medication. However, in rare cases, particularly with long-term use, it can affect the lungs.*

*The next step would be to involve a respiratory specialist who can assess this in more detail. They may arrange further tests such as breathing tests to assess your lung function.*

*For now, I would advise that we stop the nitrofurantoin and look at alternative ways of managing your urinary infections. We can start with some simple measures, such as drinking plenty of fluids, avoiding tight or non-breathable underwear, and wiping from front to back after using the toilet.*

*If you notice any symptoms such as shortness of breath, a persistent cough, chest discomfort, or reduced exercise tolerance, please let us know promptly so we can review you sooner.*
management: Offer an urgent referral to a respiratory specialist; explain that they may arrange further tests such as spirometry and, in some cases, more detailed investigations such as a lung biopsy if needed
Inform her that pulmonary fibrosis is a rare side effect of long-term use of nitrofurantoin

Advise the patient to stop nitrofurantoin and discuss alternative ways of managing her recurrent urinary tract infections, including lifestyle measures such as maintaining adequate hydration, avoiding delaying urination including after sexual activity, and wiping from front to back

Explain that if this is caused by the medication, stopping nitrofurantoin can prevent the condition from worsening and may lead to some improvement; however, any scarring that has already developed in the lungs may not completely reverse
Offer baseline blood tests, including ESR, CRP, full blood count, and an autoimmune screen, to exclude other possible causes
Provide safety-netting by advising her to seek medical attention if she develops symptoms such as shortness of breath, persistent cough, chest pain, or reduced exercise tolerance
learningPoints:
Pulmonary fibrosis is a long-term condition in which the lung tissue becomes thickened, stiff, and scarred, making it harder for the lungs to expand and take in oxygen effectively.

Nitrofurantoin is one of the medications known to be associated with adverse pulmonary reactions, particularly with long-term use. It is therefore important to always review medication history when new lung findings are identified.

Management involves prompt cessation of the suspected offending agent, early referral to a respiratory specialist for further assessment, and baseline investigations to exclude alternative causes such as autoimmune disease.

title: Recurrent Epistaxis

patientData.name: Juliana Alban
drugHistory: Co-codamol 30/500 mg, 1 to 2 tablets every 4 to 6 hours as required

recentConsultation.notes:
Dear GP,

Juliana attended A&E with a nosebleed. The bleeding was identified as anterior epistaxis and was successfully cauterised, with good haemostasis achieved.

Observations were stable. Blood pressure 130/78 mmHg, pulse 89 bpm.

She was prescribed Naseptin cream to be applied to both nostrils twice daily. She was advised to avoid nasal trauma, including nose picking, and to avoid strenuous activity for a few days.

**Dr Emily Carter, Emergency Medicine Registrar**

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *Hello doctor, I have had another episode of nosebleed again.*

If Asked to Explain Further: You have been experiencing recurrent nosebleeds for the past 6 months. You were seen in A&E 1 week ago where the bleeding was treated, and you were given a cream to apply twice daily. Today, you had another episode of nosebleed about 30 minutes ago.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:

The most recent episode occurred from your left nostril, which is the same side it usually comes from. You usually get at least one episode every 2 weeks, but it is becoming more frequent, now around 2 episodes every 2 weeks.

You do not have any other symptoms apart from the nosebleeds. When they occur, you lean backwards and pinch the hard part of your nose to try to stop the bleeding.

You have hypertension and osteoarthritis, and you take your prescribed medications regularly. For your osteoarthritis, you have been using over-the-counter ibuprofen tablets, which you started around 6 to 7 months ago as they helped with your knee pain. You do not take co-codamol regularly because you find that ibuprofen works better, and you do not use the ibuprofen gel.

**Social History:** You do not smoke, drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. You work as a store manager in a large retail supermarket and live with your husband.

**Ideas:** You think your high blood pressure may be causing the nosebleeds.

**Concerns:** You are worried because the episodes are becoming more frequent.

**Expectations:** You would like the doctor to advise you on what to do.

**Questions for the Doctor:** Can you please show me what to do when I have a nosebleed? I am not sure if I am doing it correctly because it never seems to work. I usually lean backwards and pinch the hard part of my nose. Is that right?

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about the onset and progression of the nosebleeds
Ask if she is currently having an episode and when the last episode occurred
Ask whether the bleeding is from one nostril or both; note that bleeding from one nostril is more suggestive of an anterior bleed, whereas bleeding from both nostrils may suggest a posterior source
Ask about the severity of the bleeding and whether there are any clots
Ask what she does during an episode to stop the bleeding
Ask about local nasal causes such as nose picking, trauma, recent upper respiratory tract infection, chronic rhinosinusitis, nasal dryness, or use of nasal sprays
Ask about symptoms of anaemia such as fatigue, dizziness, palpitations, chest pain, or shortness of breath
Ask if she has experienced bleeding from other sites, such as gum bleeding, easy bruising, or blood in the stool or urine, to exclude a bleeding disorder

Ask about red flag symptoms that may suggest malignancy, including weight loss, night sweats, unilateral nasal obstruction, persistent nasal discharge, facial pain, hearing loss, or persistent lymphadenopathy
Ask about medication use, including anticoagulants and over-the-counter medications such as aspirin or NSAIDs
Ask about any family history of bleeding disorders
Ask about smoking, alcohol use, occupation, and home situation
Explore the patient's ideas, concerns, and expectations
Make a diagnosis of recurrent epistaxis, likely worsened by regular use of over-the-counter ibuprofen tablets

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you Juliana for explaining everything so clearly. I can understand why this is worrying you, especially as the nosebleeds are becoming more frequent.*

*From what you have told me, this sounds like what we call epistaxis, which is just a medical term for a nosebleed. Nosebleeds are quite common and can sometimes occur without a specific cause. However, one thing that may be contributing **in** your case is the use of ibuprofen tablets, as these can increase the risk of bleeding. Does that make sense so far?*

*In terms of what to do next, would it be okay if I arrange a face-to-face appointment so I can examine your nose properly and rule out any other more serious causes? We can also arrange some blood tests.*

*For now, I would advise that you stop taking ibuprofen tablets. Instead, you can use paracetamol, or the ibuprofen gel for your knee pain. If your pain is not well controlled, we can arrange another appointment to explore other options.*

*You can continue using the Naseptin cream, and it would be helpful to apply it up to four times a day to support healing. It is also important to avoid picking or blowing your nose, as this can trigger further bleeding.*

*In terms of your concern about your blood pressure, it was well controlled when it was checked recently in hospital, so it is unlikely to be the cause. We can recheck it when you come in just to be sure.*

*When you do get a nosebleed, the best way to manage it is to sit upright, lean **forward**, and pinch the **soft** part of your nose firmly for 10 to 15 minutes without letting go. Leaning backwards can actually make things worse, so it is best to avoid that.*

*If the bleeding lasts longer than 20 minutes despite doing this, becomes very heavy, or if you feel unwell with symptoms like dizziness or shortness of breath, you should seek urgent medical attention.*
management: Offer a face-to-face appointment to examine the nostrils and look for any local causes such as polyps or masses that may be contributing
Offer blood tests, including full blood count to check for anaemia, liver function tests, and a coagulation profile to assess for clotting abnormalities
Advise that she can continue using Naseptin and increase application to four times daily
Advise discontinuation of ibuprofen tablets, as these can contribute to bleeding and worsen nosebleeds
Offer alternative pain relief such as paracetamol with or without codeine, or topical ibuprofen gel
Advise avoiding nose blowing or picking to reduce further trauma
Reassure her that her blood pressure was well controlled at her recent A&E visit and is unlikely to be the cause of her nosebleeds; offer to recheck blood pressure at the face-to-face appointment
Reinforce correct first aid for epistaxis by advising her to sit upright, lean forward, and pinch the soft part of the nose firmly for 10 to 15 minutes without releasing pressure

Provide safety-netting by advising her to seek urgent medical attention if bleeding lasts longer than 20 minutes despite applying pressure, becomes heavy, or is associated with symptoms such as dizziness, shortness of breath, palpitations, or weakness
Offer follow-up to discuss the blood test results once they are available
learningPoints:
Most cases of epistaxis are self-limiting and benign. Common local causes include nose picking, nasal fractures, septal irritation or perforation, foreign bodies, or blunt injury. Inflammatory causes include infections such as chronic sinusitis, allergic rhinitis, or nasal polyps.

Medications are an important and often overlooked cause. Topical agents such as decongestants or corticosteroids, as well as substances like cocaine, can contribute. Systemic medications including anticoagulants, antiplatelets, and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs can impair clotting and increase the risk of bleeding.

Although less common, tumours must also be considered, including benign causes such as angiofibroma and malignant conditions such as squamous cell carcinoma, particularly in older patients or those with red flag symptoms.

title: Sexual Health Advice in a Lesbian Patient

patientData.name: Victoria Barnett
pastMedicalHistory: Missed cervical screening for the second time
drugHistory: Not currently on any regular medication

recentConsultation.notes: Numerous text messages and letters sent to patient's home address regarding missed cervical screening. Patient has booked a video consultation to discuss some concerns.

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *Hello doctor, I read an article saying that lesbians can contract sexually transmitted infections, including HIV, and I would like to understand how this is possible and whether I should get tested.*

If Asked to Explain Further: You recently read an article about sexually transmitted infections in women who have sex with women, which has made you worried about your own risk. About 3 months ago, you went out partying and had a sexual encounter with a woman who is bisexual. You currently have no symptoms but are concerned about possible exposure.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:

You shared sex toys with the bisexual partner. You do not have a regular partner and have occasional sexual encounters. Your last sexual contact was 3 months ago. You usually have sex with women, and your last partner was a bisexual female.

If asked about cervical screening: You did not feel it was necessary as you believe cervical cancer risk was mainly in women who have sex with men. Ask the doctor whether you are at risk of getting the virus that causes cervical cancer even if you do not have sex with men.

**Social History:** You do not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. You live alone and work as a web application developer.

**Ideas:** You believe that lesbians are not at risk of sexually transmitted infections.

**Concerns:** You are worried after reading the article and feel that you may now be at risk.

**Expectations:** You would like the GP to explain your risk and advise whether you need testing.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Acknowledge her concerns and explore what she has understood from the article
Signpost that you will be asking some personal questions to better understand her risk
Ask about her sexual lifestyle, including number of sexual partners, gender of partners, and whether partners are female or bisexual, as well as practices such as use of sex toys and oral sex
Ask whether protection was used during sexual activity, including use of dental dams for oral sex or condoms on sex toys
Ask about any past history of sexually transmitted infections and whether she has ever been tested before
Screen for symptoms of sexually transmitted infections, including vaginal discharge, itching, pelvic pain, dysuria, bleeding after sex, or genital lesions
Ask about her menstrual history, including any abnormal bleeding or intermenstrual bleeding
Acknowledge that she has missed two cervical screening appointments and explore her reasons for this
Ask about social history, including smoking, alcohol use, illicit drug use, occupation, and home situation
Explore her ideas, concerns, and expectations regarding STI risk and testing

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you Victoria for explaining everything so clearly. I can understand why reading that article has made you worried, and it is really good that you have come to discuss this.*

*Just to clarify, women who have sex with women can still get and pass on sexually transmitted infections. This can happen through things like sharing sex toys, oral sex, especially if there are any cuts or sores, and contact with bodily fluids. So although the risk may be different compared to sexual relationships with men, it is not zero. Does that make sense so far?*

*In terms of your situation, as your last sexual contact was about 3 months ago, it would be appropriate to offer you a full sexual health screen. This would include tests for infections such as HIV, chlamydia, gonorrhoea, and syphilis. We can arrange this through a sexual health clinic, or if you would prefer, we can organise the tests here in the practice. How would you feel about that?*

*You also mentioned cervical screening. It is a common misconception that it is only needed for women who have sex with men, but that is not the case. The virus that causes cervical cancer, called HPV, is passed on through skin-to-skin contact during sexual activity, not just through penetration. This means it can be transmitted between women as well. So it is still very important that you attend for cervical screening. Does that make sense?*

*In terms of reducing your risk going forward, simple measures can help, such as avoiding sharing sex toys or using condoms on them. If they are shared, they should be cleaned thoroughly with soap and water between use. You can also consider using protection such as dental dams during oral sex.*

*If you notice any symptoms such as unusual discharge, pain when passing urine, lower abdominal pain, or any sores, please let us know.*
management: Explain that women who have sex with women can still get and pass on sexually transmitted infections, including HIV, HPV, herpes, and bacterial infections, particularly through sharing sex toys, oral sex, and contact with bodily fluids

Offer referral to a sexual health clinic and explain that they can provide a full sexual health screen, including tests for HIV, chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis, and other relevant infections; if she prefers, offer to arrange testing in primary care
Address her misconception regarding cervical screening and explain that HPV can be transmitted between women, so cervical screening remains important regardless of sexual orientation
Strongly encourage her to book a cervical smear and explain its role in preventing cervical cancer

Discuss safer sex practices, including using condoms on sex toys, avoiding sharing them or cleaning them thoroughly with soap and water between use, and considering the use of dental dams for oral sex
Offer written information or leaflets about STI risk and safer sex practices

Provide safety-netting by advising her to seek medical attention if she develops symptoms such as abnormal vaginal discharge, painful urination, lower abdominal pain, genital ulcers, or any other concerns
learningPoints:
Women who have sex with women can still acquire and transmit sexually transmitted infections. Risk depends on sexual practices rather than sexual orientation alone.

Infections such as chlamydia can be transmitted through the exchange of bodily fluids, while herpes and genital warts can be passed through direct skin-to-skin contact, including during oral sex or through shared contact between partners. Sharing sex toys without protection or cleaning can also increase the risk of transmission.

Human papillomavirus is particularly important, as nearly all cases of cervical cancer are associated with this virus. HPV is transmitted through skin-to-skin contact during sexual activity, including between women. This means that women who do not have sex with men are still at risk of HPV infection and therefore cervical cancer.

Cervical screening remains essential regardless of sexual orientation, as it detects early changes in cervical cells before they develop into cancer.

furtherResources.title: Cervical Screening For Lesbian And Bisexual Women
Sexual Health For Lesbian And Bisexual Women

title: Rectal Bleeding in Young Male

patientData.name: Nick Parsons
pastMedicalHistory: External haemorrhoids noted on examination 3 months ago
drugHistory: Not currently on any regular medication

recentConsultation.seenBy: Seen by Dr Peter Bexley (Clinical Practitioner role) – 3 months ago
recentConsultation.notes:
**Presenting complaint:** Patient was concerned about the risk of prostate cancer as his uncle was recently diagnosed. No weight loss, new back pain or urinary symptoms reported.

**Examination:** Prostate examination performed with verbal consent. Chaperone declined. Prostate felt smooth with no masses. Some external haemorrhoids noted, non-bleeding and non-tender.

**Observations:** Blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 100% on air, pulse 82 bpm.

**Impression:** Normal findings. PSA test offered.

**Note entry – 2 months ago:** PSA 1.2 ng/mL (0–4 ng/L) – normal. Patient informed via text and reassured. Warning signs of prostate cancer discussed.

bloodTestResults.summary: PSA 1.2 ng/mL – normal. No other recent blood tests available.

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *Hello doctor, I have had bleeding from my back passage for the last 2 days.*

If Asked to Explain Further: You noticed fresh red blood when wiping after opening your bowels yesterday, and it happened again today. This has made you worried, which is why you booked this appointment.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:

The blood is not mixed with the stool. You notice it on the tissue after opening your bowels. Your stools are normal, and you do not have constipation or diarrhoea.

You do not have any pain, weight loss, or night sweats.

There is a family history of bowel cancer in your father at age 75 and prostate cancer in your uncle on your father's side at age 80.

If asked about sexual history: You are bisexual and have sex with both men and women. You engage in anal sex and are both the receptive and insertive partner.

**Social History:** You do not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. You live alone and work as a tattoo artist, running your own shop.

**Ideas:** You are not sure what is causing the bleeding.

**Concerns:** You are worried that the bleeding could be cancer or related to your sexual activity.

**Expectations:** You would like the GP to explain what might be going on.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask about the onset of PR bleeding, including duration, frequency, and whether it is increasing or resolving
Ask about the colour of the blood, including whether it is dark red or fresh bright red
Ask whether the blood is mixed with the stool, on the surface of the stool, or only seen on wiping
Ask about any associated anal pain during or after passing stool
Ask about associated abdominal pain, constipation, or diarrhoea
Ask about symptoms suggestive of colorectal cancer, including weight loss, fatigue, loss of appetite, or night sweats
Ask about symptoms of anaemia such as dizziness, palpitations, chest pain, or shortness of breath
Ask about any history of haemorrhoids, anal fissures, or previous similar episodes
Ask about recent sexual history, including anal intercourse, any trauma, pain, or bleeding associated with it, and use of protection
Ask about risk of sexually transmitted infections, including discharge, ulcers, or rectal pain
Ask about medication use, including anticoagulants, antiplatelets, or NSAIDs
Ask about family history of bowel cancer and clarify the age of diagnosis
Ask about social history, including smoking, alcohol use, and occupation
Explore the patient's ideas, concerns, and expectations
Make a diagnosis of rectal bleeding, likely due to haemorrhoids

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you Nick for explaining everything so clearly. I can understand why you are worried, especially with your family history, as bleeding from the back passage can sometimes be associated with cancer.*

*However, reassuringly, you do not have symptoms such as weight loss, change in bowel habits, or blood mixed with the stool. From what you have described, especially the blood being seen on wiping and not mixed with the stool, this is most likely due to **haemorrhoids**. Is that something you have heard of before?*

*I can also see from your previous consultation that my colleague examined you and found haemorrhoids at that time, which further supports this being the likely cause. Haemorrhoids are swellings of blood vessels in or around the back passage, and they can cause bleeding.*

*The next step would be to arrange a face-to-face appointment so I can examine you properly, with a chaperone present, and confirm the diagnosis. Would you be happy for me to arrange this?*

*In the meantime, there are a few things that can help. Increasing fibre in your diet, drinking plenty of fluids, and avoiding straining when opening your bowels can reduce irritation. It is also important not to sit on the toilet for long periods, and keeping the area clean and dry will help with healing.*

*You can also try over-the-counter treatments such as haemorrhoid creams like Anusol, which can be used for about 7 days, morning and evening, and after opening your bowels to help with symptoms.*

*In terms of your concern about whether this could be related to your sexual activity, haemorrhoids are not caused by sexual orientation. However, it is still important to continue practising safe sex.*

*If you notice that the bleeding becomes heavy, continues, starts mixing with the stool, or if you develop symptoms such as weight loss, change in bowel habit, dizziness, or shortness of breath, please seek medical attention promptly.*
management: Offer a face-to-face appointment for examination, including abdominal examination and digital rectal examination to confirm the diagnosis
Advise on conservative management, including increasing dietary fibre intake, maintaining adequate hydration, and avoiding straining during bowel movements
Advise on the importance of good anal hygiene; the anal area should be kept clean and dry to promote healing and reduce irritation
Advise avoiding prolonged sitting on the toilet
Advise that he can purchase over-the-counter haemorrhoid treatments such as creams or suppositories (for example Anusol cream) to be used morning and night and after bowel movements for up to 7 days
Reassure him that his symptoms are more likely due to haemorrhoids and are less likely to be due to cancer or his sexual orientation; encourage him to continue safe sex practices

Provide safety-netting by advising him to seek medical attention if bleeding becomes heavy, persists, is mixed with stool, or if he develops weight loss, a change in bowel habit, or symptoms of anaemia such as dizziness, palpitations, or shortness of breath
Offer follow-up in 4 weeks to review symptoms and ensure improvement
learningPoints:
Fresh red blood seen on wiping and not mixed with stool is most commonly due to haemorrhoids, whereas blood mixed with stool or associated with systemic symptoms should raise concern for more serious pathology such as colorectal cancer.

In this case, the patient has no red flag symptoms suggestive of colorectal cancer, and the history of fresh red blood on wiping, along with a previous examination confirming haemorrhoids, makes a benign cause the most likely diagnosis.

A safe primary care approach is to arrange a face-to-face examination to confirm the diagnosis, provide appropriate conservative management, and offer clear safety-netting with follow-up to ensure symptoms improve.

If symptoms do not improve, persist, or if red flag features develop, then appropriate escalation, including a FIT test and referral for further investigations, is warranted.

title: Iron Deficiency and Low Folate

patientData.name: Patrick Perkins
pastMedicalHistory: Bereavement (wife died one year ago from breast cancer)
drugHistory: Not currently on any regular medication

recentConsultation.seenBy: Seen by Mary Preston (Advanced Nurse Practitioner) – 2 weeks ago
recentConsultation.notes:
**Presenting complaint:** Feeling tired all the time and reports back pain. No red flag symptoms.

**Examination:** Blood pressure 130/70 mmHg, pulse 78 bpm, temperature 36.1°C, oxygen saturation 98% on air. No tenderness on examination of lower back and straight leg raise normal bilaterally.

**Impression:** Tired all the time with mechanical back pain.

**Plan:** For TATT blood tests and review with results.

bloodTestResults.summary: Ferritin low at 10 µg/L and serum folate low at 2.0 µg/L, suggesting iron deficiency and folate deficiency. Haemoglobin within normal limits.

rows.test: B12, U&Es, Bone profile, CRP, ESR, TSH, LFTs

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *Hello doctor, I am here to discuss my blood test results, if that is okay.*

If Asked to Explain Further: You have been feeling tired all the time for over 3 months and also had some back pain. You saw a nurse practitioner who arranged blood tests to look for a cause of your symptoms.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:

Your back pain has now resolved. It was in your lower back, a dull ache that came and went, but it is now better. You do not have any urinary or bowel symptoms, no weight loss, and no bleeding from anywhere.

You are still able to manage your daily activities such as shopping and cleaning despite the tiredness.

Your sleep and mood are okay.

Your diet has not been very good since your wife, who used to cook, passed away one year ago from breast cancer. You miss her a lot. You usually have toast in the morning and rely on processed or packaged foods for lunch and dinner as you do not know how to cook.

**Social History:** You live alone and are a retired bus driver. You do not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs.

**Ideas:** You are not sure what is causing your symptoms.

**Concerns:** You do not have any specific concerns.

**Expectations:** You would like to discuss your blood test results.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Acknowledge that you have reviewed the previous consultation notes, but ask the patient to explain in his own words what led to the blood tests
Ask about the onset and progression of his tiredness, including whether it is getting worse, improving, or staying the same
Ask if there are any factors that make the tiredness better or worse
Ask about his back pain, including location, onset, character, and whether it radiates
Ask about bleeding from any part of the body, including blood in urine, blood in stool, or vomiting blood
Ask about symptoms suggestive of anaemia, including headache, shortness of breath, dizziness, palpitations, or reduced exercise tolerance
Ask about gastrointestinal symptoms such as abdominal pain, vomiting, difficulty swallowing, heartburn, change in bowel habit, or any abdominal or rectal lumps
Ask about lower urinary tract symptoms, including frequency or nocturia, to exclude possible prostate pathology
Ask about cancer red flag symptoms, including weight loss, night sweats, or loss of appetite
Ask about dietary intake
Ask about family history of cancer
Ask about social history, including smoking, alcohol use, and home situation
Explore the patient's ideas, concerns, and expectations
Explain that the blood results show low ferritin and low folate, suggesting iron deficiency and folate deficiency, which are likely contributing to his tiredness

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you Patrick for taking the time to discuss your results. I can see from your blood tests that your iron levels and folate levels are a bit low, and this is likely contributing to why you have been feeling tired. Does that make sense so far?*

*The next step is to treat this and also understand why it has happened. In your case, your diet may be playing a role, especially as you mentioned it has been difficult to prepare meals since your wife passed away. I am sorry to hear about your loss.*

*To help with this, I would like to start you on iron tablets and folic acid supplements to bring your levels back up.*

*The iron tablets can sometimes cause side effects such as an upset stomach, constipation, or diarrhoea, but these usually settle on their own. If they become troublesome, please let us know.*

*While it is likely that your diet is contributing to the low iron and folate levels, it is important that we do not miss any other possible causes. I would like to arrange some further tests, including a stool test to check for any hidden blood in your stools. I am not saying that you have cancer, but at your age, it is something we routinely check to be safe. Is that okay with you?*

*We will also arrange a blood test to check for conditions such as coeliac disease. If any of these tests come back abnormal, we may need to refer you for further investigations, such as a camera test to look at the stomach or bowel.*

*We will repeat your full blood count in about 4 weeks to make sure things are improving.*

*If you notice any new symptoms such as difficulty swallowing, change in bowel habits, blood in your stool, weight loss, or if you feel more dizzy or unwell, please let us know straight away.*
management: Offer further investigations, including a FIT test and coeliac screening, to rule out other causes of iron and folate deficiency
Start iron supplementation with ferrous sulfate 200 mg once daily for 3 months, and folic acid 5 mg daily for 4 months
Advise dietary modification, including increasing intake of iron-rich foods such as red meat, green leafy vegetables, and fortified cereals, as well as folate-rich foods such as broccoli and peas
If meal preparation is a struggle, offer referral to a social prescriber who can support access to local community meal services such as Meals on Wheels
Explain that if any investigations return abnormal results, further referral for specialist assessment, including possible endoscopy, may be required
Arrange repeat blood tests, including full blood count, in 4 weeks to assess response to treatment

Provide safety-netting by advising him to seek medical attention if he develops symptoms such as difficulty swallowing, new-onset heartburn, change in bowel habit, blood in the stool, vomiting blood, unintentional weight loss, or worsening symptoms of anaemia such as dizziness, palpitations, or shortness of breath
learningPoints:
Non-anaemic iron deficiency is a common finding in primary care. This occurs when iron stores are low (low ferritin) but haemoglobin remains within the normal range. Iron deficiency develops in stages, beginning with depletion of iron stores before progressing to anaemia, making haemoglobin a late marker of deficiency.

For this patient, his poor diet and coexisting folate deficiency alongside low iron make a nutritional cause likely. However, it is important not to assume this without excluding other causes. Further investigations such as a coeliac screen and FIT test are necessary to rule out underlying pathology.

Note that when both iron and folate deficiency are present, this can mask the typical microcytosis seen in iron deficiency, resulting in a normal mean cell volume. Repeating the full blood count in 4 weeks is important to monitor response to treatment and check for the development of anaemia.

title: Heavy and Painful Periods in an Adolescent

patientData.name: Samantha White
drugHistory: Not currently on any regular medication

recentConsultation.notes: No significant recent consultations. Patient's stepmother, Lisa McCarthy, has booked a telephone consultation on Samantha's behalf.

patientStory:
**Opening Statement (Stepmother's brief):** *Hello doctor, Samantha has been having heavy periods and I would like to get some help for her.*

If Asked to Explain Further: Samantha has been having heavy and painful periods since she started menstruating at the age of 10, and this has not improved.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:

Samantha is aware that I will be seeking the GP's help for her today, and her father is also aware.

She is not currently on her period. Her last menstrual period was 1 week ago, and the bleeding usually lasts around 4 days, with a regular 28-day cycle. During her periods, she uses Tampax Super Plus and Ultra absorbency products, but despite this, she goes through them very quickly, sometimes using up to 5 to 6 per day.

You are not sure if she passes clots.

She always has significant crampy pain during her periods in her lower tummy. She has tried ibuprofen and paracetamol, but these have not helped.

Sometimes the pain can be so severe that she misses school during the first 2 days of her periods.

She is not in a romantic relationship and is not sexually active as far as you are aware.

Her biological mother passed away 6 years ago following a road traffic accident.

She is currently in school. She enjoys playing football and attends football training every weekend.

**Social History:** She does not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. She lives at home with you, her biological father, and her half-brother and sister.

**Ideas:** You think she has heavy and painful periods.

**Concerns:** You are concerned because her symptoms seem to be getting worse and you want help for her.

**Expectations:** You would like the GP to offer treatment and support.

If the doctor suggests contraception, explain that you had similar symptoms when you were younger and found contraception helpful, but you are unsure if this would be appropriate for Samantha as she is not sexually active.

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Clarify consent or parental responsibility to discuss the patient (e.g. confirm that Samantha is aware of the call and happy for her symptoms to be discussed, or confirm parental responsibility)
Ask about the history of heavy periods, including onset, duration, and whether symptoms are worsening
Ask about menarche, last menstrual period, cycle length, duration of bleeding, and whether there is any bleeding between periods
Ask about how heavy the flow is, including number of pads or tampons used and presence of clots
Ask about associated lower abdominal or pelvic pain
Ask about any abnormal vaginal discharge or urinary symptoms
Ask about symptoms of anaemia, including dizziness, palpitations, shortness of breath, or tiredness
Ask about sexual history sensitively, including whether she is sexually active
Ask about social history, including smoking, alcohol use, illicit drug use, home situation, and school attendance
Ask about family history of heavy periods or bleeding disorders
Ask about the impact on quality of life, including school attendance, sports, and social activities
Ask what she has tried so far to manage her symptoms
Explore the stepmother's ideas, concerns, and expectations
Make a working diagnosis of primary dysmenorrhoea with menorrhagia

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you Lisa for explaining everything so clearly, and I can understand why you are concerned about Samantha, especially as this has been going on for some time and is affecting her school.*

*From what you have described, Samantha's symptoms sound like what we call heavy and painful periods. This is quite common in young people, especially in the first few years after starting periods, and is usually due to how the body produces certain hormones during the menstrual cycle. Does that make sense so far?*

*The next step would be for me to see Samantha in a face-to-face appointment so I can assess her properly and also speak with her directly. We can also arrange a blood test to check if she may be anaemic, as heavy periods can sometimes lead to low blood levels, which can make her feel tired.*

*In terms of treatment, there are medications that can really help. There are tablets such as tranexamic acid, which can reduce the amount of bleeding, and anti-inflammatory medications like mefenamic acid, which can help with both pain and bleeding. These are taken during her periods.*

*We also have the option of hormonal treatments such as the contraceptive pill, which is taken daily and can help regulate and control periods. You mentioned that contraception has helped you in the past, and I want to reassure you that this can be used purely for the management of heavy and painful periods, not just for contraception, and is suitable regardless of whether Samantha is sexually active.*

*I can also provide some information for both of you to read before the appointment, so you can think about which options might suit her best.*

*If at any point Samantha becomes very tired, dizzy, short of breath, or develops palpitations, it is important to seek medical attention urgently, as this could mean she has lost a significant amount of blood.*
management: Offer a face-to-face appointment to assess the patient, including observations and abdominal examination; note that as the patient has never been sexually active, a bimanual or speculum examination is not indicated at this stage; if there is concern regarding underlying pathology such as fibroids, a transabdominal pelvic ultrasound scan should be considered as a first-line non-invasive investigation
Offer blood tests, including full blood count, to check for anaemia
Offer medical management, including tranexamic acid with or without mefenamic acid or other NSAIDs during periods

Discuss hormonal options if symptoms are not controlled, including the combined oral contraceptive pill, explaining that this is commonly used for regulating periods and reducing pain and bleeding, not just for contraception
Offer written information or leaflets for both the patient and her stepmother to review before the appointment
Advise lifestyle measures, including maintaining a healthy diet, adequate hydration, and regular exercise

Provide safety-netting by advising that if she develops symptoms such as dizziness, palpitations, shortness of breath, or extreme tiredness, she should contact the GP urgently or NHS 111 if out of hours, as this may indicate significant blood loss
learningPoints:
Primary dysmenorrhoea is the most likely diagnosis when menstrual pain starts within 6 to 12 months after menarche, once cycles become regular. The pain is typically cramping in nature, felt in the lower abdomen, and may radiate to the back or inner thighs. It usually begins shortly before or at the onset of menstruation and lasts up to 72 hours.

Secondary dysmenorrhoea should be considered when symptoms do not follow this typical pattern. It is more likely when pain starts after several years of previously painless periods, is not limited to menstruation, or is associated with other gynaecological symptoms such as dyspareunia, abnormal vaginal discharge, heavy menstrual bleeding, intermenstrual bleeding, or postcoital bleeding.

title: Persistent Menorrhagia Despite Treatment

patientData.name: Ashling O'Brien

**Presenting complaints:** Patient reports recurrent heavy menstrual periods for the past year. The periods are slightly painful, but the pain is manageable and not a major concern to her.

**Recent investigations:** Ultrasound scan done 1 week ago was normal with no identified cause. Cervical smear up to date and negative. Sexually transmitted infection screen – negative. Full blood count: haemoglobin 122 g/L (normal). Normal thyroid function tests.

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *Hello doctor, my periods are very heavy and I really need something to stop them.*

If Asked to Explain Further: Your periods have been heavy for the past 18 months. You have had scans, STI screening, and a cervical smear, all of which were normal. You were told this can sometimes happen without a clear cause, but your symptoms are not improving.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:

You are currently on your period, which started yesterday, and it is heavy.

You have been taking tranexamic acid and mefenamic acid as prescribed, but they do not seem to be helping. Your periods last 5 to 6 days and occur every 30 days. They are regular. They can be painful at times, but the pain is manageable and not a concern for you.

You do not have any bleeding between periods. You are sexually active with your husband of 10 years. You are not on any contraception. Your husband has had a vasectomy. You also took a pregnancy test 2 weeks ago, which was negative.

Your sister has also had similar symptoms, with heavy periods, and she is now 47 years old and still experiencing them.

**Social History:** You work as a theatre nurse. You do not smoke or drink alcohol. You live with your husband and 2 kids.

**Ideas:** You are not sure what is causing this.

**Concerns:** You are travelling to Italy to attend a friend's wedding in 3 days' time. You were planning to wear a white dress and are worried about staining. You would like something to stop your period.

**Expectations:** You would like the GP to prescribe something to stop your periods.

Ask about her menstrual history, including last menstrual period, cycle length, duration of bleeding, any intermenstrual bleeding, and possibility of pregnancy

Ask about symptoms of anaemia, including dizziness, palpitations, shortness of breath, or tiredness

Ask about the impact on quality of life, including work, social activities, and daily functioning

Explore her ideas, concerns, and expectations
Make a working diagnosis of heavy menstrual bleeding, likely dysfunctional uterine bleeding

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you Ashling for explaining everything so clearly. I can understand why this is particularly stressful for you, especially with your friend's wedding coming up and your travel plans.*

*From what you have told me, it sounds like your heavy periods are not being well controlled with the current medications, which can happen sometimes.*

*In terms of helping you in the short term, especially with the wedding in a few days, there is a medication we can use called norethisterone. This is a hormone tablet that can help reduce or temporarily stop the bleeding. It is taken three times a day for a short course, and it may take up to 48 hours to start reducing your bleeding. How do you feel about trying this?*

*As with any medication, there are some risks to be aware of. Very rarely, it can increase the risk of blood clots. To reduce this risk, it is important to stay well hydrated and keep moving, especially during your travel. If you notice any symptoms such as leg swelling or pain, chest pain, shortness of breath, or coughing up blood, you should seek urgent medical attention. Does that make sense?*

*Because you have been bleeding heavily, I would also like to repeat your blood test to check your blood levels, just to make sure you have not become anaemic.*

*Once you are back from your trip, it would be a good idea for us to review things properly and discuss longer-term options to manage your periods. One option is a hormonal coil, such as the Mirena, which can be very effective in reducing heavy bleeding. I will provide you with a leaflet to read more about the Mirena coil, so you can consider whether this might be a suitable option for you.*

*If at any point you feel very dizzy, short of breath, have a racing heartbeat, or feel extremely tired, please seek medical help urgently by contacting the GP surgery or NHS 111 if out of hours, as this could be a sign of significant blood loss.*
management: Offer repeat blood tests, including full blood count, to reassess for anaemia given ongoing bleeding
Offer short-term treatment with norethisterone 5 mg three times a day for 10 days to help stop the bleeding; explain that it may take up to 48 hours to reduce the bleeding
Inform her about the rare risk of blood clots with norethisterone; advise her to stay well hydrated and keep mobile, especially during travel, to reduce this risk

Advise her on red flag symptoms of blood clots, including leg pain or swelling, chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath, or coughing up blood, and to seek urgent medical attention if these occur

Explain that once she returns from the wedding, it would be important to review long-term management options, including the levonorgestrel intrauterine system (e.g. Mirena coil), which can help control heavy periods

Provide safety-netting by advising her to seek medical attention if she develops symptoms such as dizziness, palpitations, shortness of breath, or extreme tiredness, which may indicate significant blood loss
Offer follow-up after she returns from her trip to review symptoms and discuss ongoing management options
learningPoints:
Menorrhagia is a common presentation in primary care, particularly in women of reproductive age. In women around the age of 45, it is important to consider perimenopause as a potential cause, as this can present with heavier, longer, or more irregular periods, often alongside symptoms such as hot flushes, irritability, and difficulty with concentration.

Management of heavy menstrual bleeding involves both short-term urgent reduction of ongoing bleeding and long-term strategies. For acute reduction of bleeding, options include norethisterone or tranexamic acid, with or without an NSAID such as mefenamic acid.

For long-term management, options include the levonorgestrel intrauterine system (Mirena coil), the combined oral contraceptive pill if suitable, norethisterone, or the use of tranexamic acid during menstruation.

title: Post-Partum Breast Pain

recentConsultation.notes: Patient has booked an urgent video consultation to discuss some concerns.

patientStory:
**Opening Statement:** *Hello doctor, I have pain in my left **breast** and it is getting worse.*

If Asked to Explain Further: Your left breast has been painful for the past 2 days. It feels hot to touch and the pain has been getting worse.

ONLY SAY BELOW IF ASKED:

The breast pain is a dull, constant ache, and it only affects your left breast. The right breast is fine.

You had a fever last night and your temperature was 38 degrees Celsius. You have noticed an area of redness on your left breast, starting from around the nipple and extending to the upper part of the breast.

You have not noticed any lumps or rashes. You have been taking paracetamol, but it has not helped much.

You gave birth 7 days ago via vaginal delivery and everything went well. Your baby, David, is well and has no issues with feeding or in his mouth. You are both breastfeeding and supplementing with formula.

**Social History:** You live with your mother and older sister. The father of your child is not involved, and you have not spoken to him for 6 months. You feel well supported by your family. You are not currently working and receive Universal Credit. You do not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs.

**Ideas:** You are not sure what is causing this, but your mother mentioned it might be something normal.

**Concerns:** You are worried about whether it is safe to continue breastfeeding.

**Expectations:** You would like the doctor to advise you on what to do next.

**Questions for the Doctor:** Can I still continue to breastfeed? If the doctor advises continuing breastfeeding, ask: Can this infection pass to my baby? If I am prescribed antibiotics, are they safe to take while breastfeeding?

markingScheme.heading: Data Gathering and Diagnosis
points: Ask if the symptoms are affecting one breast (unilateral) or both breasts (bilateral)
Ask about the onset and progression of breast pain, including whether it is getting better, worse, or staying the same
Ask her to characterise the pain and specifically ask about deep burning pain (deep burning pain may suggest ductal infection and may require milk culture)
Ask about the location of the pain and whether it is localised to one area or affecting the whole breast
Ask about associated symptoms such as redness, warmth, swelling, areas of hardness, or any lumps
Ask about nipple discharge or nipple changes, including cracks or bleeding
Ask about systemic symptoms, including fever, chills, or feeling generally unwell
Ask if she is breastfeeding; if yes, ask about any difficulties such as poor infant attachment or latching issues
Ask about predisposing factors such as eczema, trauma, use of tight bras, feeding from one breast only, or mixed feeding
Ask about red flag symptoms for breast cancer, including lumps in the armpit, unintentional weight loss, or night sweats
Ask about medication use, including analgesia taken so far

Ask about social history, including smoking, alcohol use, illicit drug use, how she is coping at home, how the baby is doing, whether the baby is feeding well and growing well, any fever in the baby, and any whitish coating on the baby's tongue suggestive of oral thrush
Explore her ideas, concerns, and expectations
Make a diagnosis of lactational mastitis

exampleExplanation:
*Thank you Olympia for explaining everything so clearly. I can understand that this must be quite uncomfortable for you, especially so soon after giving birth.*

*From what you have described, this sounds like something we call mastitis, which is an infection or inflammation of the breast that can happen during breastfeeding. It often causes pain, redness, warmth, and sometimes fever, just as you have described. Are you with me so far?*

*What I would like to do next is arrange a face-to-face appointment today so I can examine your breast in the presence of a chaperone. This is important because, in some cases, this condition can lead to a collection of **fluid** called an abscess, which may need drainage. **So** it is important that we rule this out. Would you be happy for me to arrange this?*

*Because you have had a fever and your symptoms are getting worse, I would recommend starting antibiotics to treat the infection. The antibiotic is called flucloxacillin, and you would take it four times a day for 10 days. I can see from your records that you do not have any allergies. Is that **still** correct?*

*This antibiotic is safe to take while breastfeeding. The important thing to know is that it is safe to continue breastfeeding, even from the affected breast. In fact, continuing to feed or express milk helps clear the infection more quickly. If it feels too painful or your baby does not want to feed from that side, you can express milk instead until things improve. How do you feel about that?*

*You mentioned that you are worried about passing the infection to your baby if you continue breastfeeding. I would like to reassure you that it is safe to continue breastfeeding. The infection does not pass to the baby through breast milk, and in fact, breast milk contains protective factors that help your baby fight infections. Does that make sense?*

*In the meantime, there are some simple things that can help. You can take regular pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen if suitable. Applying cold compresses for about 10 minutes can help reduce pain and swelling. It is also important to rest and stay well hydrated.*

*If you notice that the pain, redness, or swelling is getting worse, if your heart is racing, if you develop shivering or feel very unwell, or if you have any concerns, please contact us urgently or NHS 111 if out of hours.*

*I will arrange a follow-up in about 10 days to check that your symptoms have improved.*
management: Offer a face-to-face appointment to assess the breast and rule out an abscess that may require drainage
Advise that as her symptoms have worsened over the last 24 hours, antibiotics are indicated; prescribe flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for 10 days and confirm there are no allergies
Advise that she can use ibuprofen for pain relief if there are no contraindications

Advise her to continue breastfeeding from the affected breast if she is able, as this helps with recovery; if breastfeeding is too painful or the baby refuses to feed, advise her to hand express milk to maintain supply until she can resume breastfeeding
If the nipple is cracked or painful, advise expressing milk from that breast until it heals
Reassure her that it is safe to continue breastfeeding; the infection does not pass to the baby through breast milk, and breast milk contains protective factors that help the baby fight infections
Advise her to rest and wear a well-fitting, supportive bra
Offer to send leaflets and videos on breastfeeding techniques; if she continues to have difficulty, offer referral to a midwife or breastfeeding specialist for further support

Provide safety-netting by advising her to seek urgent medical attention by contacting the GP surgery or NHS 111 out of hours if symptoms worsen, if she develops rigors, chills, a fast heart rate, feels increasingly unwell, or if there is no improvement within 48 hours of starting antibiotics
Follow up in 10 days after completion of antibiotics
learningPoints:
Lactational mastitis is a common complication in the early postpartum period, typically presenting with unilateral breast pain, redness, warmth, and systemic symptoms such as fever. It is important to recognise that it can occasionally be bilateral, although this is less common. In lactating women, milk stasis is usually the primary underlying cause, where accumulated milk leads to an inflammatory response that may or may not progress to infection.

The most common organism associated with infective mastitis is Staphylococcus aureus.

NICE advises that a breast milk culture should be considered if symptoms do not improve after 48 hours of first-line treatment, if mastitis is recurrent or atypical, if a hospital-acquired infection is suspected, or if there is severe deep burning breast pain suggestive of ductal infection.

A key learning point is addressing common misconceptions. Many women worry that they should stop breastfeeding due to the risk of passing infection to the baby. However, the World Health Organization (WHO) advises that it is safe to continue breastfeeding, even in the presence of infection. Continued breastfeeding or expressing milk is important, as it helps resolve milk stasis and supports recovery.

title: Confidentiality in a Third-Party Query

Dear Colleague,

Mrs Elizabeth Canterbury was seen in our clinic for assessment following an optometry referral due to raised intraocular pressure and suspected glaucoma.
